Its `accept` where `in` values may too, as a github trigger's do. Either parameter is required or has a default, so the trigger never fills empty: one that is neither is refused when the package is read. Its `server` and `event` take no placeholder.
  - A trigger made with `POST /v2/triggers` is unchanged: its `server` is still a saved Composio server's name.
- The console applies a template whose setup is only parameters (no MCP tool, no key) from its own screen: Apply is the main action there and Configure on its card, and "Set it up with an agent" is the second way. A template with more to set up keeps Run as its main action. On such a template that reads mail (an `email_*` tool or an email trigger), Apply waits for a mailbox saved under Settings → Email and links there, instead of being refused.
- `email_send` asks a person in two more cases, even when it is set to allow:
  - after a run has sent 5 emails, each further send asks, saying "this run has sent N emails". This stops two auto-responders that answer each other from looping. The count is the run's own record of sends that went out (a send denied, refused or failed doesn't count), so a pause doesn't reset it. A subagent's sends count toward its run's cap, across a pause too. Sends the model makes at once count each other: past the cap, one of them may go unasked and the rest ask.
  - on a run an email trigger started, a send that reaches anyone outside that email's thread asks, naming them ("eve@example.com is outside this email's thread"). The thread's people are the account's own address and every From, To and Cc of the thread's messages. A run whose agent reads the whole account (`scope: "mailbox"` on `email_read`), and any run no email started, is held to the cap alone.

  The approval says why: its `summary` ends "Asks because …", and the card's arguments carry it as `asked_because`. With accounts off (no one can approve), such a send is refused in those words. A tool's own ask is a new field of the server's tool entry (`asks`), so the gate carries no email code.
- Three fixes from the computer milestone's QA: `apps.launch` no longer says it opened a url that a running Firefox never got, the Screen tab no longer says "released" right after a person allows a parked run, and the "Asked your approval" row sits above a park's rows on the Timeline.
  - computerd: a url for an app that already runs is handed over by a second launch. Firefox takes it only over a session bus, and an app here has none, so that launch put up Firefox's "Firefox is already running" box while the call answered that it opened. Now a launch that shows a dialog of its own instead, or whose launcher fails, is ended (its box goes) and the call fails `unsupported`, naming the dialog and saying to open the url in the running window or to terminate the app and launch it with the url. A launcher that hands the url over and ends (Chromium's), or a second instance with a window of its own, still answers.
  - Console: a desktop or phone kept at a park is opened again by the resume, so after an answer in time the Screen tab says "Waiting for the desktop. Its screen shows here once it is up." until the screen is back, not "This desktop has been released.". A page opened on a parked run now says what the run waits for and until when, even if it never saw the desktop live.
  - Timeline: the approval row sits right below its call's row, as the ask came at the call. A park's "The desktop is kept…" row and the resume's "It's the same desktop, as the wait left it." row now come after it, not before.
- Two fixes for runs that wait on a person and for a server whose process is briefly held up.
  - An answer sent just as a run paused on its question could leave the run reading working/idle for good, never resumed. This happened when no hold of the person's time fit the run's cap (so the run parked), or when the run had nothing to hold open, and the answer landed while the park let the browser session go. The answer started a turn that the park then cut, and nothing was left to wake the run. Now the answer waits for the park and resumes the run from it, and one that lands before the park starts is the run's next turn in the same claim.
  - With the runner beside the server (the default), a write could fail with "the store stayed locked past its busy wait: database is locked" when the process was held up for about 10 s (a synchronous call, a long pause, a loaded machine) while a transaction of the other side was open or just starting. The SQLite store's wait for the write lock now gives back the time the process was held up when the holder is a transaction of the same process, as that transaction's own deadline already does. A wait on another process's write still ends after the busy wait, as before.
- The OpenAPI document capped the email account's password at 320 characters while the server took 1,024. Both now read one cap, 1,024, so a long OAuth-style token is valid in the document too. The tool catalog's email tool summaries are now the tools' own descriptions, so `email_send`'s says `rejected` and `note`.
- An email trigger starts watching at its first poll, which the server runs at once when the trigger is made, turned on again or edited, instead of a separate start step. A create or a turn-on waits for that poll (10 seconds at most) before it answers, or, when an edit of the trigger's source while it runs drops it, for the poll after the edit, so its answer carries `last_check` and mail after it starts runs. Mail that came while it was off still starts no run, and an edit of its filter or `every_s` still keeps its place. Three things change:
  - mail that lands during the create or turn-on call itself, or past the 10 seconds when the mail server is that slow, counts as already there;
  - a server that can't be reached at creation writes no history line (the trigger's `last_check` says so); the first check that signs in says "Couldn't check INBOX until now; watching from now: the N messages there won't start runs.";
  - a sign-in refused at creation is one of the three in a row that turn the trigger off, as a refusal at any check is.

  The note on turning it on again reads as a creation's ("Watching INBOX from now: the N messages already there won't start runs.").
- `GET /agents/{id}/learning/cost` counts only served runs on its after side: runs a learned workflow finished (`workflow`) or ran first and handed back (`handed_back`). A `replay` checks a new revision on a graded input and serves no one, and a run by hand after the takeover is not the workflow's, so neither moves `summary.after`, `times_cheaper`, `withheld` or `hand_backs`. The new `summary.after_state` says why `after` is null when it is: `no_served_runs` (no learned workflow has taken over) or `cost_unknown` (runs were served, none with a known cost); `priced` otherwise. The Learning tab says each figure's base: the headline and the chart's after line read "all-in over N served runs", a state with no served run priced is said in words, the "Since it learned" tile reads "medians of N runs started from what it learned", and a stopped workflow's level is "over its newest 10 priced runs" (the money rule's window, `workflows[].served`).
  The agent's learning and cost reads now take each run's launch, proposals and learning run in two batched store reads per agent instead of a few per run, and share a settled run's journal read across concurrent requests: on a 480-run agent, the cost read made 7 store calls instead of 1,549.
- An OpenRouter model whose reasoning is mandatory (`openrouter/baidu/ernie-5.5-flash-preview:free`) no longer gets reasoning effort `none` with thinking off, which OpenRouter refused on every request ("Reasoning is mandatory"). With thinking off it now reasons at its default.
- A pi run's effort now applies on an OpenRouter model that speaks Chat Completions, `openrouter/openai/gpt-6.1-sol` (pi's default on an OpenRouter key) included. Until now the route's translation sent the model no thinking level, so an effort set on such a run did nothing, and on a model that can stop reasoning (Ling 3.2 Flash) any effort was sent as reasoning off. Now the run's level reaches OpenRouter as `reasoning: { effort }`, mapped and clamped by the model's catalog entry. A run that sets an effort may cost more and take longer than it did; a run with no effort set sends what it sent before.
- A runner's renew of the claims it holds, and its claim of a batch of runs, are each a few statements on the store whatever the count, never one or two a run. On Postgres a runner holding 300 runs renewed them in about 600 round trips with every row held, so a database a few milliseconds away (a loaded host) stretched the renew past the runner's claim deadline: every claim was lost at once, and the runs were claimed again and started over, again and again.
- On Postgres, a store call that waits for one of its pool's connections while every one is in use now waits up to a write's deadline (10 s, `poolWaitMs`), not the 4 s connect timeout. A runner of 300 loops on a database a few milliseconds away queues its loops' commits behind one another for seconds, and dozens of its runs failed for good with "no connection to the store's Postgres ... it does not answer, or every connection of this store is in use" while the database answered. A new connection's connect and startup keep the 4 s bound (`connectTimeoutMs`), so a database that does not answer still fails fast, now in words that say only that. A wait past the pool's bound fails in words of its own: "no connection of the store's Postgres at ... came free within 10000 ms: all 10 of this store's connections stayed in use".
- Learning: a promotion record a beta.39 store holds as `decided: "superseded"` (a replay a newer draft cancelled) reads as `skipped` on beta.40, with `skipped_by` and a reason saying so, so the promotions list and its replay read show it decided and never "running". Nothing rewrites the stored record, and it never blocks a new draft's replay.

## 0.1.0-beta.39 (2026-11-16)

- Agent37 starts from our public box image in any account. Its provider's `prepareImage()` reads the workspace template `agentrun-box-<recipe hash>` and, when the workspace has none, registers `ghcr.io/parcha-ai/agentrun-box:<recipe hash>` under that name (`POST /v1/templates`, no build). The wait is reported to `onWait` as a pull, so a run's first claim says it is pulling, once per workspace. A refusal is the run's error in Agent37's words.
  - In Mode 2, an Agent37 sandbox and an Agent37 desktop are ready once the keys work: they mount the run's folder from the owner's Archil disk, on the image they register. A Modal or E2B sandbox and an E2B desktop are still refused.
  - A desktop that mounts the run's folder starts the `shell` group's commands and the programs `processes.start` opens in `/workspace`, as `bash` does.
  - Serve's default sandbox image (`AGENTRUN_DOCKER_IMAGE`) and its refusal of a desktop with no image are Docker's alone. A provider that prepares its image gets no image from them.
  - Breaking: `AGENT37_BOX_TEMPLATE` is gone from `@parcha/agentrun-computer`, and Agent37's descriptor has no `defaultImage`. The box template's name carries the recipe's hash; ask the provider's `prepareImage()` for it.
  - Breaking: `box/build-agent37.mjs` is gone from the package. Agent37 never builds the box: `prepareImage()` registers the published image.
- Near its cap, a run's parallel steps wait for each other instead of parking: a model request, a decision or a paid tool call (a web fetch, a search, a monid call, codemode's among them) that does not fit only because steps still running hold the room it needs waits for them to settle, and is sent once its room is back. It is refused only when what the run has spent and its own least need do not fit with nothing else running. The cap is never passed: every step is admitted by the same rule over the holds as they are then. Eight subagents started at once under a $0.50 cap, or a burst of 25 fetches and searches under a $4 cap that cost about $0.50, now finish where they parked at `spend_cap_reached`.
  - Waiters go first come, first served across the run's sessions, and only the first in line asks, so a small step never takes the room an earlier one waits for. A waiter holds nothing. It leaves the line unsent when its run is stopped, cancelled or loses its claim, and is refused in its own words when the run parks meanwhile. A step it waits on that does not settle within 10 minutes refuses it, and the run parks for a raise as before. The line reads the run's records again on a short timer (50 ms doubling to 1 s), so steps in other processes of the run wake it the same way.
  - Breaking: the budget pause's `spent_usd` is what the run spent, never what its running steps hold. The new `held_usd` says what they held when the step was refused (mostly 0), and `suggested_cap_usd` is `spent_usd` + `held_usd` + 10 × `needs_usd`. A client that read `spent_usd` as everything the cap had taken adds `held_usd`. The generated TypeScript and Python clients gain the field.
  - The refusal words keep spent and held apart: "Not sent: this run has spent $0.45 of its $0.50 cap and is holding $0.03 for steps still running; the next step, web_fetch, could cost up to $0.10 (a fetch), more than the cap leaves even once the steps still running settle. Raise the cap to at least $0.55 to continue." The console's budget pause says what is held beside what is spent.
  - A paid tool call never waits on the model request that asked for it. Claude Code books a request's cost after its calls and Codex starts a call with its response still open, so that request settles only once the call returns. A paid call made in a CLI's tool call is judged beside its session's requests still running: it is sent when it fits beside them, waits only for other steps to settle, and is refused at once when it cannot fit beside them, never left to stall for 10 minutes. It also goes ahead of steps in line that may be waiting on that request.
  - A running run's cost in the runs list is what it has spent: a step still running counts once it is answered, never at its hold.
  - Kernel: `aloneRefusal`, `runBooking`, `RunBookingOptions`, `RECORD_WAIT_MS`, `WAIT_STALL_MS`, `WAIT_POLL_FIRST_MS` and `WAIT_POLL_MOST_MS` are exported; `RunCapOptions` gains `parked`, `waitStallMs` and `stopped`; `Refusal` gains `waits` and `figures.heldUsd`; `InFlight` gains `stays`; `ModelRequest` and `ProxyRequest` gain `signal`; `ModelRequest.paid` and `RunTools.admit` gain `under`, the model session whose tool call a paid call runs in; `BudgetPending` gains `held_usd`.
- A run's cap is never passed: every model request is held at its worst case, its whole input priced uncached (at the cache-write rate when that is dearer), so a cache miss can no longer take a run past its `max_cost_usd`. The `expected` cap mode, which priced the input from the previous request's cache and let a miss go over by a bound, is gone, and with it the `cap_mode` setting.
  - Breaking, for API clients: remove `cap_mode` from what you send. A run start (`POST /agents/{agent_id}/runs`, `POST /runs`) that still sends it is refused `422` with `{"field": "cap_mode", "reason": "not_allowed"}`, and an agent definition (create or update) that still sends it is refused `422` with `definition.cap_mode` `not_allowed`. The generated clients and the CLI no longer have it (`--cap-mode` is gone). Every run now behaves as `strict` did. A stored agent revision or run launch that still holds a cap mode is read as if it had none. An inline agent's version (`POST /runs` with `external`) that first ran with a cap mode keeps it in its stored body, so running that version again with the field dropped is `409 external_body_conflict`: publish a new version and run that.
  - Breaking: `cost.overshoot_bound_usd` and the budget pause's `overshoot_bound_usd` are gone from the run's view. The generated TypeScript and Python clients and the CLI (`--cap-mode`) lose them too.
  - A request is not parked for want of room to answer: its output is clamped to what the cap has left after its input at the worst case, and it is refused only when that input plus the least answer (1,024 tokens) does not fit. The in-flight hold and the CLI harness's reserve for its answer are counted at the worst case too.
  - A Codex or OpenCode request on an OpenAI model (gpt-4o and later, the o-series, gpt-oss) is held at a local count of its input in place of its bytes, on every route: o200k_base over the body as sent, plus a tenth, 16 tokens an item and 256 a request, with encrypted reasoning at its bytes and each image at its billed size, and never above its bytes. A capped run through a gateway that parked on its bytes (a $0.50 lead list asked for $0.52) now goes on. Any other model keeps its byte bound.
  - The kernel ships OpenAI's o200k_base vocabulary file unchanged (3.6 MB, MIT, `vendor/o200k/`, checked by the sha256 tiktoken pins) and counts with it itself: no tokenizer package is a dependency. Its ranks are loaded on the first count.
  - A run whose requests read the cache spends less than it is held at, so it pauses earlier than under `expected`: raise the cap by the cached share of its input if a run that used to finish now pauses.
  - A capped run on a ChatGPT plan model (`chatgpt/…`) is admitted. Its model requests are billed to the plan: each is held at $0, its output is never limited on dollars, and it adds $0 to the cap's spend and to the wrap-up's reserve. A paid tool beside them still counts and stops the run at the cap. A model with no price that is no plan's model is still refused under a cap.
  - On a ChatGPT plan, a 429 that says the plan's usage limit is reached (`usage_limit_exceeded` or `subscription_sharing_usage_limit_exceeded`) ends the run with "Your ChatGPT plan's limit is reached. Manage usage in your ChatGPT settings, then run it again.": no retry, no switch to a key, no raise-the-cap pause.
  - Kernel: `CapModel.plan`, `PLAN_LIMIT_WORDS`, `PLAN_LIMIT_CODE`, `ProviderPolicy.finalError` and `ModelProxyOptions.onFinal` are new, and so are `ProviderPolicy.countInputLocally`, `responsesLocalInputTokens`, `localInputOf`, `o200kTokens`, `o200kModel` and `LOCAL_COUNT_MARGIN`.
  - Kernel: `CapMode`, `RecentRequest`, `CapOptions.mode`, `Admission.boundUsd`, `RefusalFigures.boundUsd`, `DECISION_OUTPUT_TOKENS` and `ModelRequest.inputTokensCounted` are gone. A decision is held at its model's most completion tokens.
- The old manual way of taking Composio's events is removed: a webhook trigger with `signature: "composio"`, a webhook subscription made by hand on Composio, and Composio's secret pasted in with Set secret. A Composio trigger (Triggers → New app trigger, source kind `composio`) is now the one way: it makes and keeps the subscription itself. A webhook trigger made the old way stops firing; delete it and make an app trigger for the same event instead.
  - A webhook trigger's create, or a change to it, with `signature: "composio"` is refused `422` under `source.signature`, in words that point to Triggers → New app trigger. `features.triggers.webhook.signatures` is `["standard", "github"]`.
  - `POST /v2/triggers/{id}/secret` takes no body: any body, `{}` too, is refused `422` before the secret changes, and the new secret is always made here. The console sends none.
  - `features.triggers.public_url` on `GET /v2/capabilities` says whether the server has a public address (`AGENTRUN_PUBLIC_URL`), never the address. Without one the console keeps New app trigger in sight but off, with the line "App triggers need this server's public address: set AGENTRUN_PUBLIC_URL and restart."; the create's `409 composio_no_public_url` stays.
  - A Composio subscription at another address (`409 composio_subscription_elsewhere`) can now only be another server's or a tool of the owner's. The refusal and the console's question before Move it here say what a move stops: "Composio sends this project's events to <url> now. Moving them here stops them arriving there: anything listening at <url> (another AgentRun server, or a tool of yours) gets no more events."
  - The README's Composio quickstart, the tutorial docs/tutorials/composio.md and the server's reference teach the app trigger alone.
- A Codex or OpenCode request straight to OpenAI is no longer counted by OpenAI before it is sent: it is held at the kernel's local o200k_base count with its margin, as a request through a gateway already is, so it never waits up to 3 seconds on `POST /v1/responses/input_tokens` first. A capped run on such a route may pause a little sooner than it did on OpenAI's exact count; the cap is still never passed.
  - Breaking, for a host of the kernel: `OPENAI_INPUT_COUNTER` is gone. A `ProviderPolicy` that named it as `countInput` drops it and sets `countInputLocally: responsesLocalInputTokens`. Anthropic's count (`countInput` on the claude-agent policy) is unchanged.
- E2B starts from our public box template in any account. Its descriptor says `prepareImage`, and its provider's `prepareImage()` answers the public template `<publishing team>/agentrun-archil-<recipe hash>` by name, with no call and no wait: the release's `box-e2b` job builds that template from the box image and makes it public.
  - In Mode 2, an E2B sandbox and an E2B desktop are ready once the key works: they mount the run's folder from the owner's Archil disk, on the box template.
  - In Mode 1, an E2B desktop starts from the box template too, instead of E2B Desktop's `desktop`: computerd starts Xvfb and xfwm4 there, and the `apps` group lists the box's apps (Firefox ESR, Mousepad, the Xfce terminal).
  - The conformance run keeps E2B's stock templates, `desktop` and `base` for kind linux, or `COMPUTER_E2B_TEMPLATE`.
  - Breaking: `E2B_BASE_TEMPLATE` and `E2B_DESKTOP_TEMPLATE` are gone from `@parcha/agentrun-computer`, and E2B's descriptor has no `defaultImage`. Ask the provider's `prepareImage()` for its template.
- Modal starts from our public box image in any account. Its descriptor says `prepareImage`, and its provider's `prepareImage()` answers `ghcr.io/parcha-ai/agentrun-box:<recipe hash>` with no call: Modal pulls the registry tag at a computer's first create in a workspace.
  - In Mode 2, a Modal sandbox is ready once the keys work: it mounts the run's folder from the owner's Archil disk, on the box image. A Modal sandbox with GPUs still mounts nothing and is refused in Mode 2, in words.
  - A computer on a host with no `extend` (Modal, Daytona) carries no `agentrun.computer.max-deadline` label: `extend` is its only reader, and the bytes go to Modal's 512 for tags.
  - Breaking: `MODAL_DEFAULT_IMAGE` is gone from `@parcha/agentrun-computer`, and Modal's descriptor has no `defaultImage`. Ask the provider's `prepareImage()` for its image.
- Learning: a replay's read and its record count its runs' outcomes once. `GET .../revisions/{digest}/replays/{replay_id}` answers them nested as `outcomes: {answered, handed_back, failed, skipped_write}`, the object a promotion record's `replay.outcomes` keeps, in place of the four top-level counts and `alone` (it was `score.n - score.handed_back`). A promotion record's `replay.skipped_write` is gone: read `replay.outcomes.skipped_write`. Upgrading: read the counts from `outcomes`.
  - `POST .../revisions/{digest}/replays` on fewer than 5 graded inputs the revision fits is 409 `replay_conflict`, before anything is reserved: no record, no run. Before, it started a replay that could only end held.
  - A decided replay's read reads its record alone, never its runs and their answers again.
- `computer_script` is gone: a desktop or phone run scripts its computer through the host's `codemode`, whose script has the computer as `computer` (its types in codemode's description), and each of its calls is a nested call, held to the run's gate and recorded on the timeline. A shell command is held to the agent's `bash` setting, a started process to `bash_background`, a file written to `write`, and a file read to `read`. An agent definition that named `computer_script` uses `codemode` instead. Codex, whose code mode takes no binding, and an MCP client of the claim's computer server (which serves the step tools and `computer_op`, never `codemode`) call the step tools and `computer_op` (`{op, args}`, an op named as `computer`'s method is, `shell.run` or `apps.open`) for what a `computer_script` script's `computer` ran. An earlier run's `computer_script` rows still read as they did.
- A tool the owner ticks when applying a template is granted, not allowed: apply writes no permission for it, and each call follows this server's tool settings, as for any granted tool. Breaking: under approvals `ask`, a ticked write now asks the owner before it runs, unless the owner allowed that tool in this server's tool settings, where before it ran unasked; a ticked read runs unasked only where the owner turned on Allow reads for its server.
  - Before, apply set every ticked tool to allow in the agent's own tool settings, so under `ask` a ticked write ran without asking, and the allow outranked the server's Allow reads rule.
  - Approvals `never` still runs every granted tool without asking, as before. A deny the owner set on the server still holds, and a template's pins are written as before (a pin whose parameter is not given still sets the tool to deny).
  - The console's apply screen says that a ticked tool is granted, that a write asks unless you allowed it in Settings or choose Never ask, and that a read follows Allow reads. The Never choice now says it runs without asking, even for writes, and that it is the one to pick when a trigger starts the agent while you're away.
  - No migration: an agent applied from a template before this release keeps the allows apply wrote. To have its writes ask, remove the `permission: allow` from those tools in its tool settings.
- The kernel's `isCatalogName` is now `isCatalogWire`, and it matches a monid endpoint's wire name by `monid__` (the name every harness calls it by), no longer by the old single `monid_`. A host that imported `isCatalogName` from `@parcha/agentrun-kernel` imports `isCatalogWire` instead.
  - An agent's monid pin is kept on its revision beside its MCP pin (`revisions.monid_pin`; Postgres migration `0012_revision_monid_pin.sql`, and a server open adds the column to a SQLite store), no longer inside the revision's body. An edit that leaves an agent's monid grants as they were reads nothing of monid's listing and keeps the pin; a grant it adds is read alone. Nothing reads a pin from an older revision's body (no compatibility path): a revision saved before this, with monid grants and no `monid_pin`, fails closed. Its runs are offered no monid endpoint, so no call runs unheld, until the agent is saved again.
  - One check holds MCP and monid grants at the save and before each run. Its words for a tool the harness would drop or retype are "The tool <catalog name> cannot be offered on <harness>: <why>." for both sources. A workflow's monid grant is refused in the MCP grant's words: "<grant>: a workflow's nodes don't bind monid endpoints here yet; grant it to an agentic agent."
  - A name that is no tool here is refused as "<name> is not a tool here: grant one of <the server's tools>, an MCP server's tool as mcp:<server>/<tool>, or a monid endpoint as monid:<provider>/<endpoint>."
  - The monid key check reads `GET /v1/endpoints?limit=1`, the listing a save pins from, which monid does not charge for.
  - A subagent given a grant gets each of the run's catalog tools that grant gives by the gate's keys, for MCP and monid alike.
- A learned workflow asks once per call, and its card says what it will do. The `learned_workflow` call's approval card lists each MCP action set to ask that the workflow can call, with the shape of its arguments (`{"tool":"mcp:linear/create_issue","args":{"title":"{title}"}}`; a `{name}` is filled in while the workflow runs). One allow lets those actions run with no second ask.
  - Each MCP node now runs as a call nested in the workflow's call, asked at the gate as its own tool. An action the card did not name (set to ask after the card was shown, or past the card's 2 KB preview) parks the run on a card of its own instead of failing the workflow. An approval passes by tool, so a tool with any action past the preview is left off the card entirely, and each of its actions asks on its own. Each check of a polled MCP node, and each attempt of a retried one, is a call of its own, and a node's call is cut when the node is (a sibling's failure, its deadline). Only the card approved for that same call counts: an earlier call's card, of the same workflow or another, never passes it. A deny of any of the workflow's MCP actions still refuses the whole call before any node runs.
  - A draft is no longer refused at learn time because its ask-set MCP actions would not all fit on one card: the ones past the card ask as they run.
  - A `learned_workflow` call that a park or a crash cut runs again from its start, where a crash used to end it interrupted and hand it back to the model. Its model, decision and call nodes answer what they answered the first time, read from the record without asking the model or the decision provider again, so each is asked and booked on the run's ledger once; an MCP call that already ran answers from its record, so nothing is sent twice. A workflow served first still hands the job back when a crash cuts it, and an ask its card did not name refuses that node.
  - A run's guard rows count the last trace each `learned_workflow` call wrote, so a call run again is counted once.
  - `NestedCalls.memo` (`@parcha/agentrun-kernel`) also takes a function, called only while nothing is recorded for its key: a rerun reads the recorded value and never calls it, and a throw of the function records nothing. `NestedCalls.call` takes an optional fourth `signal`, which the nested call runs on beside the calling one's.
  - Breaking: removed from `@parcha/agentrun-serve`'s modules: `host-calls.js` (`HostCalls`, `withHostCalls`, `hostCalls`), `learnedAskFits`, `LEARNED_ASK_CARD_BYTES` and `learnedMcpTools` (use `learnedMcpCalls`, which returns each action with its arguments), `DraftAsk` and `draftProblems`' `ask` parameter, `learnedDraftTools`' `asked` field, `RunPermissions.decide`, `SpecGate.askedFor` (the gate answers `{ ask: card }` instead) and `LearnedWorkflowRun.decide`. `LearnedWorkflowRun.mcpTools` is now a map from catalog name to the session's tool name, and `nestedOf` hands a call its nested calls.
- The console signs in with ChatGPT and says what runs without a key.
  - The first screen offers "Continue with ChatGPT" beside "Add a key". The sign-in opens OpenAI's page in a new tab, finishes by itself on the same computer, and takes the pasted address of the sign-in tab from a server elsewhere. A wrong address, an expired sign-in or a taken port reads in the server's words.
  - A waiting sign-in says until when it waits, also after a reload, and says it is finishing while the server reads the plan's models. A paste that lands after the sign-in finished on its own shows the sign-in, not a refusal.
  - Signed in, the console says who is signed in and on which plan, with OpenAI's words on usage and a "Manage usage" link to ChatGPT's settings.
  - Settings → Model keys has a ChatGPT plan row: its state, account, plan and models, and a sign-out that asks first. A sign-out OpenAI didn't confirm still signs out here, and says so in the server's words with a link to ChatGPT's settings.
  - "What runs here" lists each harness, whether it runs on this server and what it needs, on the first screen and in Settings. The no-model bar offers the ChatGPT sign-in first. On a server with no key, Codex and pi read "runs after Continue with ChatGPT".
  - Serve: on a server with no key that is not signed in, capabilities' codex and pi entries say "or sign in with ChatGPT (Settings → Model keys) to run it on your ChatGPT plan" (an expired sign-in: "sign in again"), and so does a run of an agent that names no model. Each harness entry gains `needs` (`key`, `chatgpt`) where it runs nothing for want of a key (no `chatgpt`, and no sign-in in its reason, where AGENT_MODEL names a key's model, which stays the default signed in or not); pi, which runs here with no default model, says why in its `reason`. Claude Agent and OpenCode still say they need a key. Breaking: the capabilities' harness mark is `harness/4`.
  - A run on the plan says its tokens and "Using ChatGPT plan", never $0.00 or unknown; a run that also spent dollars says them, then "+ ChatGPT plan". Plan models read "<model> · on your ChatGPT plan" in the Model picker, on an agent's page (its own model, or its harness's default when that is the plan's) and on what a workflow run's node ran on, and an agent's spend cap says it counts dollars only.
  - Serve: a run's `cost` gains `plan` (`requests`, `tokens`) for its requests on the plan, which leave `unpriced`, so a run on the plan alone has a known cost. `GET /settings/chatgpt` answers a waiting sign-in's `expires_at`.
- A server with no model key can run codex and pi on a person's ChatGPT plan. The owner signs in under `/settings/chatgpt` (OpenAI's Sign in with ChatGPT through pi-ai's own flow, finished by the loopback callback or by pasting the address the sign-in tab ended on), and models named `chatgpt/<id>` go to OpenAI's Responses API on the plan's token, billed to the plan with no price here.
  - `GET /settings/chatgpt`, `POST /settings/chatgpt/sign-in`, `POST /settings/chatgpt/sign-in/finish` and `DELETE /settings/chatgpt` (owner session only). A bad or stale pasted address is a 400 in words. Sign-out revokes the session at OpenAI, then removes it.
  - The sign-in is sealed in one row and read per request by the server and every runner, in their own processes or containers. A token renews once across all of them, 5 minutes before it ends: one holder takes a lease on the row (a compare-and-set on its sealed bytes, `SealedKeys.replaceIf`), and the others adopt the pair it writes back, so a refresh token is never used twice. A renewal sent with no answer read holds the lease to its end, since its refresh token may be spent; a fault OpenAI answers gives it back. A sign-out during a renewal stays. A refused renewal marks the sign-in expired, and runs on it fail at once in words. A 401 from OpenAI, in a pi turn or a workflow's model node, renews the token on the next request when the row still holds it.
  - Capabilities say per harness whether it runs on the plan: pi and codex do, Claude Agent and OpenCode still need a key. Models list `source: "chatgpt"`.
  - On the plan, the Codex policy sends no `max_output_tokens` and none of the keys the plan does not take, refuses a system-role message in words, and names its originator. Its turns are booked with `billing: "plan"` and no cost.
  - Kernel: a model proxy's credential may throw `CredentialUnavailable` to refuse a request in the host's words (`code: "credential_unavailable"`), and `credentialRefused` tells the host the credential a provider answered 401 to.
- A compiled workflow's answering step now runs on the agent's own model.
  - The learning checks refuse a workflow draft whose answering step (the model node that writes the key its `output.path` reads, the body step whose result a map collects there, or a composed workflow's own answering step) names tier `fast`, in words the compile turn's retry acts on: drop its tier. Legwork steps may stay on `fast`, an answer on `strong` passes, and decision nodes (judge, pick, sift) are not read. The compile prompt and its worked example say the same.
- Composio triggers are set up from here, with the key a saved Composio server already holds: "when this happens in that app, run this agent", with no curl and no secret to copy. A trigger of the new source kind `composio` names a saved Composio server, one of its toolkit's events and that event's config (GitHub's new-issue event: `{owner, repo}`), with an optional filter, an agent, what each run is asked and a cap.
  - `GET /v2/settings/mcp-servers/{name}/composio/events` lists the server's toolkit's events: each one's slug, name, description, the JSON schema of its config with the required fields, and whether Composio polls for it.
  - Making the trigger makes, in order, the Composio project's one webhook subscription at this server's address (`/v2/hooks/composio/{hook}`; its secret is sealed here and never answered or logged) when there is none, then the event's trigger instance for the account the server is connected as, then the trigger, and undoes what it made when a later step fails (a subscription whose secret can't be kept here included). A second trigger reuses the subscription. Creates, pauses, deletes, a secret's rotation and the subscription's delete on one Composio project run one at a time, so a failed create undoes only what no other trigger holds by then, the subscription is never deleted under a create still making its instance, and a rotated secret is never overwritten by an older read. The answer's `source` names what was made (`instance_id`, `hook`).
  - A delivery is checked once with the subscription's secret and starts each trigger whose instance it names (Composio's `metadata.trigger_id`) and whose filter takes it, so two triggers on two repositories never cross. A filter's conditions read the delivery, the event's data under `/data/`.
  - Refused before anything is left on Composio: no public address (`409 composio_no_public_url`, before Composio is asked anything); a subscription at another address (`409 composio_subscription_elsewhere`, naming it, unless the create says `move_subscription: true`); an account not connected (`409 composio_not_connected`, with Composio's link to connect it); several connected accounts for the toolkit (`409 composio_account_ambiguous`, naming each with when it was connected: a trigger runs as one account, so disconnect the others in Composio, and none is picked for you); an event or config Composio refuses (422, under `source.event` or `source.config`).
  - Pausing, resuming and deleting follow on Composio once the change holds here. Triggers with the same server, event and config share Composio's one instance: it is turned off only when every one of them is off, set from the triggers as they stand when Composio is asked, so a pause that reaches Composio after a later resume leaves it on (deleting the last one on, while paused ones still hold it, turns it off), and deleted with the last. A server's trigger list reads every page of Composio's instances; a trigger whose instance Composio didn't answer for reads `unknown`, never `missing`. What Composio could not do is answered beside the change (`composio: {done: false, note}`; a delete answers `200 {deleted: true, composio}` then, else 204) with what to do in Composio's dashboard. When the server turns a trigger off itself (its agent archived, five failures in a row, its connection or run gone), its instance is turned off on Composio the same way; what Composio could not do is logged with what to turn off by hand.
  - A saved server that Composio triggers still use can't be deleted (`409 composio_in_use`, naming them), a trigger still being made on it included; a trigger whose saved server was deleted while it was being made is refused and undone on Composio. `GET .../composio/triggers` lists its triggers with their state at Composio and whether the subscription is this server's; `POST .../composio/rotate-secret` rotates the subscription's secret and keeps the new one; `DELETE .../composio/subscription` deletes the subscription once no trigger uses it.
  - A template can't carry what this server sets on a composio trigger (`instance_id`, `hook`, `move_subscription`): reading such a package is refused, saying to leave them out or make the trigger from the console.
  - The console makes one: Triggers → New app trigger (its button: Create app trigger) picks a saved Composio server, one of its events (with its description; a polled one says Composio checks for it every few minutes) and the event's config, each field read from the event's schema with the required ones marked, then an optional filter on the event's data. A subscription at another address is named, and moved here only once the person picks Move it here, which sends the create that was refused; an edit to the form first withdraws the question; an account not connected is said with the link to connect it. A trigger's page shows its app, event, config and filter, and whether Composio still has its instance, and says what Composio could not follow of a pause or a delete. Edit filter changes only what you edit: a rule or condition you leave alone goes back exactly as it was, and a save with no change sends nothing. Settings → MCP servers lists a Composio server's triggers with their state at Composio and where the project's subscription sends its events, with Rotate secret.
- The console's run page grades a run. An ended run that learns has a Grade control: Right, or Wrong with what was wrong (sent as the grade's `label`; a look-back needs words, and the control says so while they are empty) and, optionally, the correct answer as a JSON object of the fields a right answer holds (`expected`). After the grade it shows "Graded wrong" and "Reviewing" while the feedback round runs, then what the round did; the Timeline shows the grade's words as "Your grade" and the round's look-back. A graded run shows its grade and takes a new one, which replaces it. Runs that don't learn, and runs that only use what was learned, have no Grade control.
  `GET /runs/{id}/learning` answers `graded` (`correct`, `source`, `graded_at`): the run's grade as its agent keeps it, absent when it has none.
- The console sets a webhook's or GitHub trigger's filter, the `accept` rules the API already took, and edits it on a trigger that exists. A rule names an event, the actions it takes (optional) and conditions on the request's body, each a field (a JSON pointer such as `/title`) and one test: "is one of", "starts with", "exists" or "is missing". A request starts a run when any rule takes it.
  - New webhook: the filter is optional. With none, every signed request starts a run, as before. With one, each request it takes starts its own run, even while an earlier run is still going, and any other request is answered and starts nothing. Under each event field, the form says what the event is for the webhook's signature: a Standard Webhooks body's `type` or GitHub's `X-GitHub-Event`.
  - "Is one of" takes one value a line. A number, `true`, `false` or `null` is that JSON value, and so is a line in double quotes (`"42"` is the text 42); any other line is its text. The trigger's page reads each condition back in the same words.
  - New GitHub trigger: each picked event takes conditions, and events the picker doesn't list can be added by name.
  - A webhook's or GitHub trigger's page has Edit filter. The save changes only the filter: a webhook keeps its URL and secret, and taking its filter away makes every signed request start a run again.
  - Editing a filter changes only what you edit. A rule or condition you leave alone is sent back exactly as it was, even one the form would not write itself (a field name ending in a space, an action with a comma in it, a condition on the whole body, rules in another order), and a save with no change sends nothing.
  - The form checks each rule's shape and the server's limits (20 rules, 20 conditions a rule, 20 values a list) before it sends. A refusal from the server shows under the field it names, in the server's words.
- The local server reads and sends email through one account of the owner's (IMAP and SMTP with an app password), saved in Settings → Email and sealed like every other secret. The account is kept whole in one sealed row, written once, so a save that fails leaves the previous account, and nothing reads one account's servers with another's password.
  - `GET`, `PUT` and `DELETE /v2/settings/email` keep the account (presets for Gmail, Fastmail and iCloud, or servers of your own; Outlook is refused in words: it needs a Microsoft sign-in this server does not do yet), and `POST /v2/settings/email/test` signs in to both servers without saving or sending anything. All four are the owner's session's alone.
  - An email trigger, `{kind: "email", mailbox?: "INBOX", every_s?: 60, accept?}`, reads the mailbox on a clock and starts a run for each new message its `accept` takes, keyed by its Message-ID. It watches from the moment it is made, its mailbox or account is changed, or it is turned on again: mail from before then starts no run, and that is said; any other edit keeps its place. A mailbox it can't reach then still makes the trigger, which starts watching at the first check that signs in. Another account saved in place of the one it read, or a mailbox the server rebuilt, starts it over from then, and that is said. A message this server sent is left. A run an email started is handed no earlier run's answer, as each message is a different sender's (a schedule's runs still are). A run's input is the message's payload as whole JSON within 16 KiB: a longer text is cut, said to be cut and marked `text_truncated: true`. The trigger shows its last check, and turns itself off (`sign_in_refused`) after the mail server refuses the sign-in three times in a row.
  - Five tools: `email_search`, `email_read`, `email_draft`, `email_send` and `email_file`. `email_send` asks a person by default, and its approval shows who it goes to and what it says; it answers `{sent, message_id, rejected?, note?}`, `rejected` listing the addresses the mail server refused (the rest got it, and nobody is sent to again). `email_read` with `thread: true` reads the thread's newest 20 messages at most, chosen by their headers before any body is fetched, and answers `truncated`, `more` and the earlier ones' ids (`omitted`) to read one at a time. `email_file` files a message under a Gmail label, where it stays in the inbox (`archive: true` takes it out), or, elsewhere, moves it out of the inbox to a folder in one call (an explicit `archive: false` is refused, as a move takes the message out of the inbox), making the label or folder if missing; its description says in one line which the saved account's server does; it answers `{filed, message_id, to, archived, subject, note?}`, the note on a move saying "moved out of the inbox to <folder>", and never deletes mail, so the trash and junk folders are refused. A run an email started reads and files only that email's thread unless the agent's `scope: "mailbox"` setting widens it, and of that thread only the messages its sender took part in (their address in From, To or Cc, as on the account's own mail to them): a Message-ID a sender writes in References, or reuses as their own, grants nothing alone: the thread is read from the message where the trigger found it, or, once it has moved, its copy from the same sender. On Gmail a thread is found by its messages' Message-ID and References; elsewhere by In-Reply-To too, with up to 5 minutes for the search, past which the tool says the server took too long. Every answer stays under the host's result bound.
  - Each email call reads as one line on a run's timeline: `Searched mail for "quarterly report" from:ana@example.com unread`, `Read <subject>`, `Drafted a reply to <to>: <subject>`, `Sent an email to <to> and 2 more: <subject>` (with ` (refused: 1)` when the server refused one), `Filed <subject> under Receipts, out of the inbox`. No message body is in any of them.
  - New dependencies of `@parcha/agentrun-serve`: `imapflow` (IMAP), `mailparser` (parsing a message) and `nodemailer` (composing one and sending it over SMTP). They load only when the account is tested, a trigger checks the mailbox or a run is given an email tool, never when the server starts.
- A template eval case can set its runs' clock: `now: 2026-11-14T09:00:00Z` in its `case.yaml` (a date and time with its offset, checked before any run) is each run's current date and time. The run's environment line says that day, as does claude-agent's turn date, and each `llm` grader is told the clock the run ran on, so a rubric can say "the run's date". A dated fixture case no longer drifts a day each day it is run. Without `now`, nothing changes.
  - Only the eval's own in-process server honours `now`; no package field, API field, setting or environment variable sets a run's clock, and a case with `now` refuses to run with `--server`.
  - A shell's `date`, a browser's page and Codex's own date still read the machine's clock.
- A template eval case can say `email: fixtures/mailbox.json`, and its runs read a fake mailbox seeded from that file, never real mail. Each run on each of the fixture's `layouts` (`gmail`, `folders`; default `folders`) gets a fresh fake account, saved as the eval's own server's email account and closed after the run, and the case reports per layout.
  - A run starts as the package's trigger would: the mailboxes are seeded, the package applied (its email trigger takes its start), the fixture's `message` delivered, and the trigger's next poll fires on it, so the run reads only that message's thread. A fixture with no `message` starts the package's schedule's run, which reads the whole account.
  - Graders see each email call with its arguments, a refused one too, and `<mailbox-after>`: the drafts and other messages the run added, what it moved or labelled, and what it sent. A `mailbox` grader checks where one message is after the run (`message_id`, `in`, `not_in`). Any grader of an email case may say `layouts`, and grades only the runs of those layouts.
  - On the gmail layout a label's mailbox lists every message carrying the label, as Gmail's does: searching `Ignored` finds the messages labelled `Ignored`, a label added or taken off shows at once, and a flag set through any mailbox shows in all of them.
  - The fixture is checked when the case is read; the run's clock is the case's `now`, and so is the trigger's: each run of a schedule case fires on the case's date, never the schedule's next time after the run before. The apply checks a trigger's date by that same clock, as POST /triggers does, so a one-time `at` on a past case's date is applied, not refused as passed. Only the eval's own server honours `email`, so a case with it refuses `--server`.
  - The eval runner's per-run fakes (`web`, `monid`, `now`, and now `email`) are one map per agent, read in one place by the runner beside the eval's server.
  - The eval's grader agent runs with no computer: it only reads, and on a server with no sandbox its runs failed at the start.
- A template eval's llm grader of a run that searched or fetched reads a link check beside the calls (`<link-check untrusted>`): one line per distinct http(s) link the answer cites, in its text or any string of its JSON, saying `matches call N` or `no matching call`. The match is done in code against every url the run's web calls answered: a web_search's results, a web_fetch's asked url, final url and page links. A fragment, a trailing slash, the query's order and the case of scheme and host are ignored. The query's keys must be the same, and a value the timeline elided to "…" matches any value for its key, so a cited link with a query string can match at last. A link that matches nothing names any fetched page whose links were cut (`(call N's links were cut)`). Cited links are shown with their query values, fragment and userinfo elided, as call urls are. A run with no web call is graded on the same prompt as before. A rubric can now say "every cited link must match a call; read the link check" instead of spelling out URL equality.
- A template eval case can take monid down: `monid: unavailable` in its `case.yaml` answers every call of the package's monid endpoints as monid unreachable does (`<endpoint> was not sent: monid's price for it could not be read before the call (monid could not be reached: fetch failed).`), through the runner's own monid path with a fetch that never connects. No call is sent, nothing is held or charged, and the calls show in the timeline under their monid names, so `tool_used` counts them. It holds on pi, claude-agent and codex, wherever the run's monid endpoints are bound.
  - Only the eval's own in-process runner honours it, by the agent it made for the run: no package field, API field, setting or environment variable turns it on, and a case with `monid` refuses `--server`. The package must grant a monid endpoint.
  - The apply still pins the endpoints from monid's listing (a free read, no run), so the agent's tools are the ones it has live.
- `agentrun-serve eval-template --on-data DIR` runs the eval's own server on DIR, a stopped server's data folder, in place of a temp one. The runs use what that server keeps, so a package's cases are measured on the owner's ChatGPT plan, and every case's fakes still bind (`now`, `email`, `web`, `monid`), which `--server` refuses. The agents the eval made are archived there and the folder stays, with its tool settings, MCP servers and saved API token (`.token`) as they were; the report says `server: {kind: "in_process", data: DIR}`. It is refused with `--server`, while another server holds DIR, when DIR's server has enabled triggers, runs not ended (its built-in learning runs included) or a learning batch running (the eval's server and runner would take them up), and for an email case when DIR's server keeps an email account, which the case's fake mailbox would replace. `EvalOptions.data` is the same in the API.
- A template eval case can fake the web: `web: unavailable` in its `case.yaml` fails every `web_search` with the words a rate-limited free search answers with and every `web_fetch` as a page that never answers, and `web: <fixture file>` answers each search from the first answer whose `query` (a regular expression) matches and each page from the answer for its exact URL, else the fixture's default. No call reaches the network, the calls show in the run's timeline and the graders' tool calls, so `tool_used` counts them, and the fixture is checked whole before any run.
  - The same fake holds on pi, claude-agent and codex: on claude-agent and codex a faked case's runs are never offered the harness's own web search, so the run's `web_search` is the one that answers.
  - Only the eval's own in-process server honours `web`; no package field, API field, setting or environment variable turns it on, and a case with `web` refuses to run with `--server`.
  - Fix: a guarded public fetch of a 2xx answer with no body (204, 205) reads as an empty page instead of failing with "Cannot read properties of null".
- Free OpenRouter models are runnable at $0 and marked Free in the console's Model picker. `openrouter/baidu/ernie-5.5-flash-preview:free` and `openrouter/inclusionai/ling-3.2-flash:free` take tools but are not in pi-ai's catalog, so serve now lists them itself at $0, with OpenRouter's context window and output ceiling. Each one was checked live with a tool call. Capabilities' harness entries carry `free_models` (new, required, `harness/5`): the models in `models` whose catalog price is all zeros, each with its `context_window`. On pi with OpenRouter's key, that is pi-ai's own free models plus these two. A router that picks a model per request (`openrouter/auto`, `openrouter/free`) is not counted as free. The picker tags each free model "Free · <context> context", and a "Free models only" switch narrows the list to them. A template whose `model.prefer` names a model this server does not know now says so in a warning on apply, as it already did for a gateway server, instead of silently taking the tier's model.
  - Breaking: a client that validates capabilities against `harness/4` refuses the new `free_models` field.
- A run on a free model now stops at 60 requests on free models. A free model's catalog price is all zeros (an OpenRouter `:free` model and the like), so no spend cap could stop one stuck in a loop: a run on a free model made 520 web searches before it ended, burning its provider's shared daily quota. The request after the 60th is not sent, and the run ends `failed`, as one its cap ends, with error `spend_cap_reached`: "Not sent: this run reached its 60-request limit for free models." The limit holds capped or not, on every harness, and no raise lifts it. A server that needs more sets `AGENTRUN_FREE_MODEL_REQUESTS` (a whole number above 0; anything else refuses the start). ChatGPT-plan requests don't count.
  - What counts: each request on a free model the run makes, its subagents' and side calls' included, and one a crash cut. A paid request, a paid tool call and a workflow's decision never count.
  - A free request a crash cut, booked by the next process, is now a known $0 marked `free`, as a free request that ends in its own process already is; it was booked as unknown.
  - Capabilities report the limit as `limits.free_model_requests` (marked `freerequests/1`), and the console says "free model: up to 60 requests" beside the spend cap of an agent on a free model.
  - Kernel: `runCap` takes `freeRequests`, and `kernel/cap` exports `freeModel` and `freeRequest` (one rule for what the cap books at $0 and what the limit counts), `planCapModel`, `freeModelRequestsOf` and `freeCeilingEnd`. A runner's `runner.request` record says `freeRequest: true` for a request the limit counts.
- A run on a free model is now told when its free-model request limit is near. The request that has 3 requests left (itself included; the limit is 60, or `AGENTRUN_FREE_MODEL_REQUESTS`) carries one note, "AgentRun server note: 3 free-model requests left in this run, this one included: finish now with your answer.", labelled and placed the way the spend cap's wrap-up note is, once per run and shown as the server's row in the timeline. Before, the request past the limit was refused with no warning. A paid model's or a ChatGPT plan's requests never count or carry it. When the dollar cap's note is due on the same request, that one goes first.
- The Learning tab says "About 7x cheaper at the same accuracy" only when it can back both halves: the ratio, and the replay the serving workflow was promoted on clearing the accuracy bar. Under it, one line: "Replay: workflow 95% vs agent 94% on 40 inputs · served 59 runs, handed back 3". With no replay yet, or one below the bar, it says "7x cheaper" and why accuracy is not claimed.
  `GET /agents/{id}/learning/cost` no longer averages around runs whose cost isn't known. While any run the ratio reads (the agent's runs before the takeover, every run after) has an unknown cost, or a cost known only as an upper bound, `summary.times_cheaper` is null and `summary.withheld` names the counts ("3 runs' cost unknown, 1 known only as at most"). The summary also carries `replay` (the serving promotion's `n`, `workflow_pct`, `agent_pct`, `cleared`), and each run carries `cost_upper_bound` (true when its row stores only a bound, `costAtMostUsd`, with a null cost; `withheld.at_most` counts such runs, `unknown` counts null costs with no bound). `agentrun learning cost` and the CSV read the same rule; the CSV gains a `cost_upper_bound` column after `cost_usd`.
  Upgrading: a script that reads the cost CSV by column position shifts every column after `cost_usd` by one.
- A template package can offer up to three named model choices (`model.choices`), each a model on one of its harnesses with an optional warning and setup note, and the owner picks one at install. `POST /v2/templates/{id}/apply` takes `overrides.choice: <id>` and runs the agent on exactly that model and harness, or refuses: an unknown id, or a choice sent with `overrides.model`, is `422 overrides.choice`; a choice's missing key is `409 agent_not_runnable`, as a package's is; a model this server can't run on that harness is `409` naming the model, never the tier's model in its place. `GET /v2/templates` lists the choices under `model.choices`.
  - A package's `model.prefer` follows the same rule: where this server can't run it on the chosen harness (no key for its provider, no catalog here lists it, or the harness does not run it), apply is `409 agent_not_runnable` under `model`, naming the model and the fix (save the provider's key in Settings → Model keys, or apply with `overrides.model` or a model choice), and makes nothing. It used to take the tier's model in its place without saying so (or, for an unlisted model, with only a warning). The bundled code-review package no longer has a `prefer`, which would have refused its install on a server with the ChatGPT sign-in and no OpenRouter key. It runs on the server's fast model, and `openrouter/particle-ai/particle-1` is now its model choice `particle`, "Particle 1 (OpenRouter)", whose note says it is the model the package was tuned and measured on, at about 18 cents a review. A server behind a gateway still skips `prefer` with a warning, as before.
  - The console's install form shows one Model group when a package offers choices: its default first, then each choice by label, each warning and note shown word for word under it, and sends the pick as `overrides.choice`. A package with no choices shows no group.
- Receive polling and native OpenTelemetry observations from independently running Claude Code and Codex sessions using the existing AgentRun CLI protocol. Scoped credentials, selection fences, durable deduplication and bounded retention preserve activity and token accounting across reconnects and restarts. Observation is read-only and does not enable self-improvement or take over execution.

  Reconnecting a revoked source can adopt its newly approved polling or telemetry mode without losing accepted history. Fresh credentials and selection revisions fence old uploads, and each mode's source clock remains independent. Missing cache usage stays unknown, and receipt capacity is counted once per batch.
  Observation reads and retention scans select their own settings namespace before loading values, avoiding unrelated remote command history.

  Concurrent enrollments share an atomic store capacity check, keeping the connector namespace at its limit across server handles without replacing an existing installation or blocking revoked-source re-enrollment. Every raw connector key counts conservatively, without decoding unrelated settings.

  Native OTLP uploads accept the configured Collector's 100-record batches under a separate 1 MiB limit for both wire and decompressed bodies. Polling and owner requests retain their 64 KiB limit; authentication, consent, record-count and retention checks remain in force.
- A workflow can check in code that the quotes its answer gives are in the pages it fetched: the new `quote_missing` predicate. A compiled workflow whose answer quotes fetched pages must use it as its quote check, never a judge.
  - `{"predicate": "quote_missing", "path": "answer.evidence", "field": "quote", "pages": ["page"]}` holds when a quote at `path` (a string or a list of them; with `field`, records each holding its quote at `field`) is in no string under `pages`, the state paths this run's call steps wrote, each string read alone. Both sides are compared lowercased, with curly quotes straight, en and em dashes as `-` and whitespace runs as one space, then once more as letters and digits alone. A quote under 8 characters is not checked. On an `escalate`, the `escalate.evaluated` event carries `quotes_checked` and `quotes_missed`, counts only, never quote or page text. It is a mechanical predicate, so `not` takes it. Validation refuses an empty `path` or `pages`, a page path that overlaps the quotes' path, a page no input key or earlier node produces, and in a `poll` a page outside the call's declared result.
  - The learning checks refuse a workflow draft whose output schema has a `quote` or `quotes` property and which fetches pages with a call step, unless each place in the answer holding quotes is read by an escalate on `quote_missing` (a quote key whose schema is a union of shapes is a place per shape; quotes no one `path` and `field` read, such as under two lists, are refused), a step of the top-level chain after the answer is written, whose `pages` hold pages as fetched (never a model's summary). The refusal names the predicate to write. The compile prompt says the same: a judge, an `ask` or a guard is never the quote check.
- An agent's owner can replay a learned workflow's revision on the agent's graded inputs: `POST /v2/agents/{id}/learning/workflows/{name}/revisions/{digest}/replays` starts it, and `GET` the same path plus `/{replay_id}` reads it (`agentrun learning replay`). Before, only a run's claim started a replay, for a new revision only, so a held revision could not be checked again and an edited one waited for a run that fit it.
  - `inputs`: `held` (the default), the graded runs the revision's last replay or hold was decided on, else the agent's newest 20; or a number from 1 to 500, that many of the agent's newest graded runs. 202 with the replay's id and how many inputs it replays.
  - It is the claim's replay: the same reservation and replay runs (handed no per-run MCP credentials), the same records (`source: replay`, now with `replay_id`), promoted within 2 points of the agent or held, then refit, as a claim-started one is. The read decides it once its runs ended, so a revision no run lays is decided too.
  - 404 for an unknown agent, workflow or revision; 409 `replay_conflict` while it replays, while another revision of it replays, once it is promoted, or with no graded input it fits; 400 for any other `inputs`. Only the owner's password session starts one; a token is 403.
  - Fix: a graded run a learned workflow answered alone (path `workflow`) is now a replay input, beside the agent's (`agent`, `handed_back`). It has a recorded answer and a grade, which is all a replay scores against.
  - A revision held on runs it served that were graded wrong keeps them (`held_on`, at most 20). Every replay of it covers them, and it is promoted again only once it answered on each. Promoted again, it is checked only on the runs that promotion served (`since` names it, and each run it serves keeps it), never on the ones it was held on, nor on a run served before it and graded after. A check that read an earlier promotion writes nothing over the new one.
  - A replay none of whose runs started by its deadline (its launch was interrupted) reads `failed` (held), and its owner starts it again with POST. A GET never starts runs: before the deadline such a replay reads `running`.
- A run's opening message is saved in its folder as `inputs/message.md`, its `content` byte for byte, beside the files it was given, on every harness. An agent can name that file to a subagent instead of copying a long message into the call. A run with no text `content` gets no file, an upload at that path takes `message-2.md`, and the first message's files line never names it. The bundled code-review package uses it: for a pasted diff, each reviewer's prompt names `inputs/message.md` and the reviewer reads the diff there, so the parent no longer writes the diff out eight times (on a 1,000-line diff that copy alone ran into the model's output ceiling).
- Record tasks executed by existing Claude Agent SDK and Codex SDK backends through scoped, idempotent run receipts. Keep execution and cancellation in the application while the server records bounded evidence, independently checks opt-in notes and skills, pins accepted context for later tasks, and accounts for SDK and reflection usage without inventing unknown counters.

  Keep completed, failed and cancelled SDK runs in the learning cost series by persisting their canonical execution path with terminal usage. A failed or stalled terminal read leaves cost and metrics unknown, and a stop received during that read is taken with the end rather than lost.

  When the backend marks its evidence incomplete, retain valid cost and token aggregates but leave its execution path unknown, so the learning cost series counts and excludes that partial trace.

  Failed or cancelled SDK runs record why learning stopped alongside their final state, without asking a reflection model or leaving learning shown as seeded.

  Keep the task's original cost and answer time with the first reflection prompt. Recovery reuses that snapshot and the paid answer, preserving the task/reflection breakdown and unknown costs when the run's terminal commit was interrupted.

  Keep each workflow compilation attempt under its own durable request ID, distinct from reflection and retry attempts. Recover the first task-cost snapshot within the same learning round, including compile-only rounds, without borrowing another round's figures or resending an answered request.

  SDK callback tools never list or pin tools from AgentRun's managed MCP registry, including when an inline managed launch is refused. Backend starts and evidence recording remain independent of a missing or unavailable managed server.

  SDK reflection repairs carry their original format instructions and bounded, redacted rejected answer from the same durable learning round. A reclaimed run reuses both answers without another paid dispatch; compiler retries retain their separate context and request IDs.

  Keep grades of completed SDK runs as evidence without reopening application-owned execution onto managed feedback rounds. Their scoped completion receipts and existing learning remain terminal.

  Arbitrate SDK completion and deadline/error closure on the same durable evidence inbox, fenced by the runner's current claim. Acknowledged completion keeps its answer and usage for processing or recovery; a closed inbox refuses new evidence while exact retries remain idempotent. Initial read failures settle unknown cost and unasked dropped learning only when closure and the terminal journal can be saved; otherwise the run remains recoverable without replaying the backend task.
- Let checked backend SDK workflows reuse existing application tool callbacks through an explicit local MCP bridge. The host supplies its workflow engine, tools and live permission policy; run-scoped capabilities, schema checks and cancellation bound execution. Capability-aware reflection and grading propose only runnable workflows, and the cookbook compares fresh-input workflow reuse with a learning-Off control.
  Keep each bridge callback and result under its validated workflow invocation in the run timeline, so successful workflow-only work retains its workflow cost path while failed callbacks and extra agent work remain handed back.
  An explicit `nativeMcpServerName` also correlates duplicate native MCP envelopes against one-use bridge completion receipts with the same session capability, arguments, status and result. Unconfigured or unmatched native calls remain ordinary tool evidence.
  SDK workflow checks and selection refuse automatic tool retries the bridge cannot execute, and evidence cannot close a workflow while one of its nested callbacks is unfinished.
  The SDK callback catalog’s advertised schema uses the runtime MCP tool-name grammar: leading dashes are valid, dots and tools longer than 64 characters are refused.
  Workflow admission and SDK delivery reject repeated scoped step labels while preserving declared backend callbacks and the bridge's retry limits.
  SDK proposal checks and approved workflow delivery honor the bridge’s 128-node static limit, including nested chains and composed workflows, without restricting managed workflows.
  SDK jobs use the ordinary note/run compilation thresholds and a separate compiler turn. Its host contract, examples and checks use only explicitly registered backend callbacks, without hosted workflow-first, model or step-guard authority. Each independent SDK retry carries the bounded, redacted original compiler context and its previous failed answer; durable attempt IDs preserve paid-once recovery and the task-versus-learning cost breakdown.

  Revised SDK workflows keep the first compiler ask's main commit as their file conflict base across recovery, alongside the original task-cost snapshot and declared callback capabilities.
- `softEscalates(doc)` in `@parcha/agentrun-dsl` names the escalates of a workflow document that read a judge's output, by label as a run names its step (`parent/child` in a child workflow): the ones a host that measures a check may pass to `WorkflowDeps.softEscalate`. What each node kind writes to the state is one table beside the interpreter's node runner, keyed by every kind, so a new kind says what it writes. An escalate whose `ask` predicate reads only a judge's fields (every `{path}` its `state` and `images` interpolate) is now one of them; an `ask` with no `state` reads the whole state and is not. AgentRun's replay uses it in place of its own copy of the walk.
- Connect existing Claude Code and Codex setups on this server or another machine, select live jobs or approved history imports, and inspect native readiness. Refresh remote readiness on the agent page while it is open and after verification or disconnect, keeping unavailable workers from enabling run or learning controls. Keep SDK execution controls and retries in the original backend, including on Mission Control, and guide onboarding without requiring a model key to connect. Keep reserved agent ids addressable across console links, and show an owner-disconnected target as unavailable even while its worker stays online. Separate native Codex cache reads and writes from uncached input, keeping unreported counters unknown. Show small positive native task and reflection prices without rounding them to zero, while leaving unreported prices unknown. Keep CSV learning batches available only for server-managed agents; native and SDK agents retain notes and skills review with guidance to start tasks in their source runtime or backend. Managed model setup stays behind the explicit run-here choice and preserves a started sign-in across collapse.

  Server-issued links for agents named `new` or `connect` open that agent's Runs tab.
- Build agents from a brief or the full template catalog using a remembered coding-agent dropdown or the API playground. Handoffs preserve complete template settings and prepared requests, and the server serves its matching setup skill. Imported GitHub templates retain their full package identity and reviewed commit across configuration, prompts and prepared requests, alongside publisher trust, pinned installation and visible provenance.
  Setup, build, edit and run prompts read that skill from the selected server, so its instructions match the deployed build.
  Development handoffs reach the same server's setup skill through Vite, and successful skill-file edits disable identical repeat saves while preserving later edits and revision guards.
  Deleting learning or an agent's spend cap from an edit sends the API's explicit reset, including after switching between JSON and Form.

  Template handoffs retain the owner-selected MCP server for each source and toolkit, including prepared API requests. Unread or ambiguous accounts wait for selection; a removed prepared account requires a fresh request instead of switching accounts. Agent edits preserve explicit model and tool-setting resets when switching between JSON and Form before saving.

  Keep unfinished Playground requests, selected options, uploaded attachments and displayed responses when setup import refreshes the agent list, including a failed refresh that can be retried. Replacing the authenticated client resets cached console state immediately; signing out also discards the previous session's request. A selected agent removed or archived during refresh requires a fresh choice.
  Template handoffs use the server's compiled parameter schema and shared input fields, retaining false, zero, scalar arrays, defaults and reviewed consent while rejecting unknown or lossy prepared values.
  Complete JSON definition edits preserve removed fields through JSON/Form switches: deleting an unattended approval policy sends no override and restores the server’s asking default. Confirmed default resets become clean without allowing a duplicate revision request; failed edits keep their unsaved-change guard.

  Editor tool, skill and workflow groups retain their accessible names and linked help, refusal and warning text.

  Edit and run handoffs follow the loaded agent’s native or SDK binding. They direct changes to the original source or backend, without appending a managed-definition request; editable JSON cannot change that handoff identity. Managed requests keep their full prepared JSON and revision precondition. Prepared template requests retain the selected package model and reject choices no longer offered.

  Copy confirmation and manual-copy fallback stay associated with the current prompt and coding-agent selection, including when clipboard responses arrive out of order.

  After clearing an agent's default spend cap, the request is considered saved when the server omits the cleared cap. Repeated sends stay disabled until another setting changes.

  Complete JSON edits now use supported reset values and explain settings that cannot be removed through this API. Saved-response comparison preserves real computer changes and blocks unchanged repeat saves after canonical readback.

  Workflow and agentic edits now normalize fields from the requested definition, so changing a workflow into an agentic agent preserves its new instructions and model settings.
- Inspect an agent's configuration beside its runs and versions, query filtered runs through the shared coding-agent action, and see Mission Control activity and analytics without a model-key gate. Refresh external work when returning to the console. Preserve archived-run scope in coding-agent queries, and keep focused daily analytics readable inside narrow cards. Let slow Mission Control reads finish before automatic refresh, while preserving explicit refresh and scope changes. Keep the server's save warnings visible beside the inspected configuration.

  Keep a visible Detailed editor action for managed agents, including archived agents, so the existing revision history and Make current controls remain reachable. Native and SDK agents retain their original-source editing handoffs; inspecting Versions remains read-only.

  Disable Load more while the agent's run history or refresh metadata is still being read, then allow pagination again after the refresh settles. Preserve loaded rows and the existing retry guidance when a refresh fails.

  Keep the last successfully loaded Mission Control counts, analytics and run links visible beside a refresh error. Preserve the initial error state when no data has loaded, and let retry replace the saved view after a successful read.
- Add Learning Dojo to inspect retained knowledge and reviews across agents, and show each run's recorded learning outcome and grader decisions. Refresh learning safely without replacing in-progress edits, confirmations, or paginated results. Keep workflow agents with reserved ids addressable from Dojo, and distinguish approved remote-history uploads from maintenance of a local store. Show workflow draft errors alongside recorded validation problems, including runs with no parsed reflection result.
  Manual refresh replies preserve a note opened for editing while the read was pending; a completed write still refreshes its own note list.
