  Keep the last successful learning snapshot visible during Dojo refreshes and transient failures, with explicit last-read counts instead of misleading current minimums. Refresh agent metadata, discard removed or unsupported histories, and replace cached learning after a successful read.
- Show independently running Claude Code and Codex sessions in Connected agents, Runs, and Mission Control with reported model and token/cache usage. Keep observed sessions read-only, preserve their data through temporary refresh failures, and offer existing-application setup through the shared handoff. Keep observed sessions visible through unrelated registered-run loading or failures, label retained session counters separately from range totals, and document confirmed owner-authorized unattended disconnection. Observation reads time out after 30 seconds, cancel when their scope closes, and recover through polling or manual refresh without hiding retained session cards.

  Show the complete environment-credential disconnect command, including its required destination origin, in the connector guide and served onboarding skill.

  Keep saved registered-run counts, analytics, and run links visible beside refresh errors and independently loaded observations. Initial registered-run loading or failure still leaves observations visible, and retrying does not discard the saved registered view.
- Connect local Claude Code and Codex setups without copying their configuration or credentials. Native jobs preserve source permissions, uncertain dispatch and exact UTF-8 output, and can use checked notes and skills when learning is explicitly enabled. They honor typed input and output schemas, ask once more when the final JSON misses its schema, and can be cancelled while another job holds their source project. A stop or cancel received while recording final usage still owns the run's end. Native learning jobs record their agent execution path in the cost series while unknown dollar, token and request counts remain unknown in the API and console analytics. A failed or stalled terminal metrics read leaves cost and path unknown within the shared end-read bound, preserves the actual task outcome or person’s stop, and releases the source project without replaying the task. Native tool inputs and results (including credential-shaped property names and numbers), and final answers are redacted before entering the durable journal, including credentials already opened from the server’s sealed store. Codex uncached input excludes both reported cache components, and remains unknown when either split is missing. Preserve unmetered tool coverage alongside unknown native request counts. Already-admitted trigger messages wait for the person’s answer before delivery, and database fixtures release their connections and yield while removing injected write faults. Claude Desktop-only tools remain advisory and do not change a Code project’s launch fingerprint. Task usage remains unknown when a dispatched retry reports no counters, without mixing in separate reflection usage. Workflow node cleanup preserves the original stop after its owning invocation ends, including late attempts. Restart tests distinguish server recovery from a cut paid request whose charge remains unknown, and independent webhook fixtures keep their secret lifetimes isolated. Webhook test waiters recheck committed state when filesystem notifications arrive before a commit or are coalesced. Native prompts keep text and all typed input fields together, using the same fenced input formatter as managed runs. Native definitions reject removed tool-call settings, and old saved or queued revisions that still record a limit fail before dispatch until saved without that setting. Saved native instructions are passed as additive context from the run’s pinned revision, without rewriting native source policy or permissions. Learning uses the last bounded, redacted combined policy recorded before durable task dispatch; abandoned preparations cannot supply or hide the executed task’s policy. Native connections reject AgentRun model and thinking overrides at registration, save, restore and dispatch, with directions to configure the source CLI. Existing queued overrides fail before execution; explicit native connection management clears only obsolete ignored AgentRun fields without changing source configuration or silently deleting managed-agent settings.

  Native connections also refuse managed tool permissions, tool or skill grants, unattended approval overrides, model tiers, different harnesses, computers or sandbox locations, pull-request checkouts and spending controls that their source CLI cannot honor. Empty grants and settings, asking by default, the source harness, runner location, no computer or checkout, zero cap and expected cap pricing remain compatible. Source-discovered models, skills and MCP servers remain source metadata. Legacy execution restrictions block restore and queued dispatch, stay intact on disconnect, and must be explicitly removed before reconnecting or verifying. Reconnecting a legacy binding with no stored harness restores its source harness for ordinary definition round trips.

  Postgres deployment and data-root ownership tests stop their server and runner processes before dropping schemas, keeping teardown DDL from racing live background reads.

  Native source MCP metadata never lists or pins tools from AgentRun's managed MCP registry, including when a legacy managed grant is refused. Runners require the server to install revision MCP and Monid metadata before opening an older store of the same schema version; only the server upgrades it.

  Grades on completed native source runs remain recorded without reopening them into managed feedback rounds that the native runner cannot consume. Their CLI fixture's runtime-name selection is reviewed by the entry-point guard without changing symlinked Claude and Codex protocol selection.

  Codex keeps intermediate messages visible as progress while only its last completed message supplies the final answer, output-schema check and reflection proposal, avoiding an extra task when the final JSON already meets its schema.

  Native stops kill the source immediately and drain already reported tool and usage events before returning the original stop. Recording has a five-second bound; after it expires no later queued event starts, while any in-flight write remains subject to its claim fence.

  Learning task snapshots retain unknown booking charges across a runner restart, so a priced retry cannot turn the interrupted task’s subtotal into a known cost. An already recorded task charge stays known when only its later learning request is cut.

  Codex configurations that select custom model or developer instructions now mark learning evidence incomplete, including quoted TOML keys in user, project and selected profile files. Invalid, changed or unreadable configuration evidence also refuses automatic promotion before grading. Verification makes that limitation visible without disabling ordinary native tasks or changing their source configuration; saved instructions cannot clear the refusal. System Codex configuration is fingerprinted alongside user and project configuration. Older Codex snapshots without configuration inspection remain readable but cannot authorize new automatic learning; a new source run must capture the policy evidence.

  Claude main-agent policy preserves user and current-directory settings precedence even when `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` is deeper than or inside the project. Unrelated ancestor shared settings and user-global `settings.local.json` do not select the agent or change the launch fingerprint. Agent definitions are scoped by read-only repository-root metadata; project definitions override same-name global definitions and explicit selectors remain selected. Potential ancestor-local settings, worktree policy sources, or agent definitions whose scope or nested contents cannot be fully captured make automatic learning explicitly unavailable and the effective model unknown while ordinary native tasks remain available. Older Claude snapshots that did not preserve source precedence remain readable but cannot authorize new automatic learning.

  Claude instruction snapshots detect potential imports before redaction and refuse automatic learning when imported policy was not captured. Known additional sources, including active AGENTS.md fallback, user instruction-file selectors, rules directories and managed policy, also refuse learning when their effective policy cannot be captured. Ambiguous multiline code examples and directories exceeding the bounded metadata inspection also refuse learning conservatively. Ordinary native tasks retain their source configuration and remain available. Older snapshots without the new source-coverage check, or without a recorded dispatch runtime, remain readable but cannot authorize new grading or promotion.

  Normal server shutdown cancels a pending ChatGPT sign-in and releases its loopback callback listener without signing out or changing the saved credential.

  Stop-withdrawal tests advance their store and runner retry clocks together, so a delayed observer cannot miss the first backoff. Wall-clock test deadlines and the production retry policy remain unchanged.
- Run explicitly selected native setups on another machine through an outbound Python worker. One-use owner enrollment becomes a connector-scoped credential; leased commands preserve stable event and completion retries, cancel source work on lost leases, and never redispatch an uncertain model call. Source paths, configuration, credentials and permissions remain controlled by the source operator. Opens are pinned to each run’s reviewed configuration fingerprint and cancelled opens release late sessions, files and locks. Independent polling and delivery keep source lease expiry responsive during stalled uploads. Remote seeds omit unsupported skill and resource counts with a visible reason. Scoped command-owner metadata avoids parsing another connector’s retained payloads and preserves escaped NUL in native content. PostgreSQL applies an additive column/index migration; existing SQLite stores install it and backfill on server reopen. Start this build’s server before its runners; a runner refuses an older SQLite store whose metadata is not yet prepared. Remote Codex grading separates uncached input from both cache components, while unknown cache usage keeps grading tokens unknown. An upload rejected after cancellation waits for a newer heartbeat before classifying a missing cancellation, keeping that source stopped without interrupting other commands.

  An oversized or malformed source bridge response, a stopped event reader or stdout EOF closes the bridge and fails its pending operations. Later commands cannot execute without a reader; the existing four-megabyte frame limit stays unchanged and uncertain native work is never replayed automatically.

  Authenticated command completions accept the source worker's four-megabyte UTF-8 envelope, including its lease token; other request limits are unchanged. A result that exceeds that envelope becomes a small durable command failure before upload, so acknowledgement retries and worker restarts preserve the same outcome without stopping unrelated jobs or repeating native execution.

  A command that exhausts the destination's cumulative event capacity stops only its own native source and records a small durable failure. Unrelated jobs continue; late output is discarded, and retries or restarts reuse the recorded failure without executing the command again.

  PostgreSQL command metadata is migration 0013, after the released 0011 revision-MCP-pin and 0012 revision-Monid-pin migrations. Upgrades preserve existing pins, agent revisions and command payloads. An experimental store that already applied the unpublished native-command migration as 0011 or 0012 refuses startup with a migration-text mismatch; this build does not rewrite that history or reset data. Keep its previous build until a separate preserving migration is available. SQLite stores missing MCP, Monid or native command-owner metadata are upgraded only by the server before runners can open them.

  Remote preparation retains policy omission reasons and current coverage markers; incomplete or older source evidence disables automatic learning while ordinary native jobs remain available.

  Final native tool and usage events are acknowledged before command completion. A cancellation that cannot acquire or flush the bridge writer within 250 milliseconds closes the shared bridge through its bounded child cleanup; pending operations fail without automatic replay instead of blocking the lease loop. Healthy per-command cancellation keeps its ordered frame and other sessions.

  When source preparation withdraws notes and skills or the final source-plus-saved policy evidence is incomplete or truncated, the native run records why automatic learning was skipped before sending a reflection or queuing a grade. Ordinary tasks retain their saved and learned context; complete policy evidence keeps the checked reflection and grading flow.
- Preview and explicitly import ended sessions for one source project and runtime, with separate owner and source consent for history-only or combined connections. Transfers redact and bound selected content, preserve stable source identities for deduplication, and lock authorization guards inside each run import transaction so acknowledged revocation or disconnection prevents later writes.
  Export the exact approved inventory; changed selections require a fresh preview and consent. Resumed conversations retain their first imported snapshot while later sessions continue importing. Disconnected targets cannot advertise live launch readiness even while their source worker remains online.
  Recheck the approved source identity before and after reading each exported session, including archive replacements that preserve file size and modification time.
  Read complete opening metadata records when discovering remote sessions, so large valid Claude Code prompts are included; report sessions whose project cannot be checked within the bounded read.
  Reject oversized selected transcripts before parsing them during previews and export pages, while still using a bounded metadata probe to identify their project.
  Accept valid history pages through the authenticated route's 2 MB raw-body limit; other JSON requests keep their 1 MiB limit, and oversized history is refused before importing any session.
  Prevent new remote history writes after an agent archive commits, while preserving earlier imported history and ordinary local imports. Project-history previews and pages use bounded session metadata, parsing transcript contents for the requested page and retaining approved-file, source-identity and child-session checks.
- A template eval's `tool_used` grader takes `at_least: <n>` beside `count`: it passes on n or more matching calls (its `args` filter first, as `count`'s do), so "web_search called at least 4 times" holds for a run that searches 5 times. `count` stays exact; a grader gives one of the two, and one that gives both, an `at_least` under 1, or `at_least` with `expect: not_called` is refused in words.
- monid endpoints priced by usage (per result, per unit, metered, or a matrix or tier with a usage part) can be granted again, by name and through `monid:<provider>/*`. A run's spend cap is a hard stop for everything except the charge of one such call, which can pass its estimate; when it does, the run stops at once.
  - They are pinned at the save like fixed-price endpoints, and the save's `warnings` name each one (`reason` `priced_by_usage`): "monid:<provider>/<endpoint> is priced by usage: monid can't cap what it charges, so a call can cost more than its estimate and more than the run's cap allows." A wildcard no longer leaves them out, and a provider priced only by usage no longer refuses the save.
  - The approval card reads "Priced by usage: monid estimates the cost when the call runs, and can charge more." The run's `pending.price` is `"priced by usage"`. Nothing is sent to monid while the call waits, and nothing at all when it is denied.
  - Each call is held at monid's estimate for its own input, read once the call may run: after the allow, or at once when it needs no ask. AgentRun reads the estimate by sending the call with `maxCost` 0, which monid refuses unrun and uncharged, naming the estimate. It then sends the call with that estimate as `maxCost`. The read is marked at $0 on the run's ledger before it is sent, so a crash while monid holds it leaves the run's cost unknown rather than missing a charge; a read monid refused unrun is given back with no charge row. A call monid estimates at $0 is run by that read (`maxCost` 0 lets a free run through), and its charge is booked under the call. Under a cap, a read that ends with its charge unknown (no answer, or `FAILED` with no cost) stops the run: "monid may have charged for <name> and did not say how much, so this run's cap can't be kept; the run stopped".
  - A charge above the estimate is booked as charged, and the run ends failed with "monid charged $X, more than the $Y held; the run stopped".
  - An endpoint monid has moved to usage pricing since the save is no longer refused per call. It is held at its pinned price and sent with that as `maxCost`, so monid runs it only at an estimate within the price its card showed. A charge above it stops the run as above. A fixed-price call that does not fit the cap is refused before anything is sent to monid, as before.
  - The controls are which endpoints an agent may call: named grants, `monid:<provider>/*`, and deny or ask per tool.
- A pi run with a desktop or a phone has the host's one `codemode`, as every other run and harness has. A script calls the computer's actions as ordinary tools (`await tools.computer_observe({app})`, `tools.computer_act({app, steps})`), and each is a call of its own: held to the kind's setting, with its own timeline row and its own `computer_calls`. pi's own computer code mode, with its `computer` global, is gone.
  - A script on the host's `codemode` has no `computer` global. The only state that handle kept was the last observed state, and `computer_act` already defaults to it. `computer_script` still binds `computer` for a multi-step script on the computer, on every harness.
  - pi on a desktop or phone whose `surface` is `code` is now offered `computer_script` beside the hand-over, as claude-agent, codex and opencode are. Before, pi's own code mode stood in for it. With `surface` unset or `tools`, pi is offered the same names as before.
  - A deny on `desktop` or `phone` now refuses the computer call a script meets and ends the script there; the calls before it ran. Before, it refused pi's whole script before anything ran.
  - A template eval grades a `codemode` script's call as `codemode` on every harness, beside the calls the script made. Before, it was graded as `desktop`.
  - When a script stops at a call that is waiting, its answer lists each earlier result as the script read it: a JSON object or array as itself, not as an escaped string, and a string value as that string.
  - A tool's image reaches a `codemode` script with its pixels. `image(shot)` shows a screenshot to the model, and a screenshot the script returns is its answer's image. Before, the script got the screenshot without its data, so neither could show the screen. The answer's text never carries the data.
  - A pi desktop run's first request is offered `codemode` beside the computer's tools. Through a gateway its byte bound grows to 11,496 tokens ($0.058 at the cache-write price, was $0.054). The documented minimums stay at $0.12 through a gateway and $0.09 straight to Anthropic. A run a cent under the gateway minimum now parks before its last step, as it does straight to Anthropic, instead of being told to answer without its last screenshot.
- A template package's trigger can be on or off by a parameter: `enabled: "${parameters.<name>}"`, one placeholder alone naming a boolean parameter with a default. Apply fills it and makes the trigger enabled or disabled by the owner's answer (the default when it is left out), so a package can ship a second schedule the owner opts into, such as a weekly brief behind `weekly: false`. The owner can switch it later as any trigger. Validate refuses any other text in `enabled`, a parameter that is not a boolean, and one with no default, each in its own words.
- A capped Claude Agent run on a Claude model reached through a gateway (Sonnet 5.5 through OpenRouter) no longer stops at its second step with most of its cap left. The provider's count is asked for only at Anthropic, and no local tokenizer counts Claude, so each request was bounded by its bytes: about four times its tokens. An inbox agent's second request read as about 32,000 tokens, so at a $0.10 cap the step after one that cost $0.01-0.02 "needs at least $0.10" and the run paused, where a real step costs about $0.03. The model proxy now keeps each model's last request whose answer reported its whole input, and bounds a later request that carries it unchanged by that billed input plus the bytes of the messages it adds, when that is lower. That request must match the earlier one in everything that bills input apart from the added messages (system, tools, thinking, effort, model); a moved cache marker (a `cache_control` key on a tool, a system or message content block, or a block of a tool result's content) does not count as a change, and a `cache_control` key anywhere else is compared as text. The wrap-up note is asked for on that bound. A first request, a request that changes its tools or prompt, one that adds a document, or one that offers the hosted search keeps its byte bound, and a step that does not fit is still refused.

  pi on a Claude model takes the same bound, through the same policy. Through a gateway, the smallest cap that takes a pi desktop run on Sonnet through its four screenshots to its answer goes from $0.12 to $0.09, the same as straight to Anthropic: the run needs $0.082, where it needed $0.110 on its bytes. Its first request keeps its byte bound ($0.052).
- A capped run on a model whose tokenizer is o200k_base, reached over Messages without Anthropic's count (pi on GPT-6.1 Sol through OpenRouter, sent through serve's translation), bounds each request's input by a local count with its stated margin, as a Responses request to a gateway already does. Before, its bytes were the bound: after a few long pages the body passed 272,000 bytes, every rate was priced at Sol's long-context tier, and a $1.50 run stopped at $0.10-0.27 because the cap refused to send a step it could pay for. A Claude model, a body with a document, or one that offers the hosted search keeps the provider count or the byte bound.
  When a run's cap is below what its model needs for one more step and an answer, the wrap-up's words now say so with both amounts, and the effort the model's request asked for when it named one ("This run's cap of $0.25 is below what gpt-6.1-sol at medium effort needs for one more step and an answer, about $0.32."), so a run that stopped its tools at its first call shows the cap was the cause. The rule that decides when a run wraps up has not changed.
  Saving an agent with a cap below that figure (POST /agents, an edit of its definition, or a package install with a per-run budget) now saves with a warning on `definition.max_cost_usd` ("This agent's cap of $0.25 is below what gpt-6.1-sol at medium effort needs for one more step and an answer, about $0.32: a run will wrap up at its first tool call."). It is never refused. The figure is priced on the first request the agent's harness sends: the harness's own input before the agent's prompt (Codex about 12,200 tokens, from billing; Claude Agent, OpenCode and pi measured on their pinned builds, each stated beside its pin), the agent's prompt where the model's tokenizer is o200k_base, and the least output at the agent's effort, its thinking included: a pi agent on a Claude model that thinks with a budget is priced with Claude's 1,024-token thinking minimum, as its first request asks for it.
- Signing out of ChatGPT leaves no token alive behind it.
  - `DELETE /settings/chatgpt` answers 200 `{"revoked": boolean}` instead of 204. `revoked` is true when OpenAI confirmed the revocation, or when nothing was signed in (cancelling a waiting sign-in). When it is false, `message` says "Signed out here. OpenAI didn't confirm the revocation: remove AgentRun in your ChatGPT settings."
  - Sign-out removes the row only while it still holds what it read (`SealedKeys.removeIf`), so a renewal that wrote back meanwhile is removed and revoked too. A renewal that finishes after a sign-out, or loses its write back to a new sign-in, revokes the pair it got and never hands it out. Signing in again revokes the sign-in it replaces.
  - The renewal lease is stamped and judged on the store's clock (`SealedKeys.clock`: the database's on Postgres), not each process's own.
  - A claim gets the plan's reader only when its run can reach a `chatgpt/` model: an agent pinned to a key's model runs on the key while signed in and never holds the sign-in.
  - A runner's redaction lists the sign-in's access and refresh tokens each alone, as renewed by any process. The reader prints its state alone (`util.inspect`, JSON), and the revocation goes only to auth.openai.com.
- A run's pull request checkout is removed from its folder before the run's end is committed, so a run that reads completed never still holds the pull request's code in its folder. Before, the removal ran at the claim's release, after the end, and for that window a finished run's folder kept the checkout. The run's background commands are stopped first, so one still writing under repo/ cannot race the removal, and a removal that fails is tried again at the release instead of being kept as done.
- The bundled code-review package's per-run cap is $2.00, up from $0.50. On its default model where the fast tier is GPT-6.1 Sol (an OpenRouter key alone), the eight reviewers' first requests, each held at its worst case, filled the $0.50 cap within seconds and parked even a five-line review waiting for a higher cap. Measured on that model, a review of a pull request up to about 400 lines cost $0.16 to $0.90, and $2.00 is about twice the dearest. A run on particle-1 (the `particle` choice) still costs a few cents.
- A `codemode` script's calls read as part of that script on the run's timeline, and a script can test for a tool with `typeof`.
  - Each call a script or `tools_call` made now names the outer call in `parent_tool_use_id`, on its `tool_use` and `tool_result` rows. Before, only its `<callId>/s<n>` id tied it to the script.
  - In the default timeline view, a `computer_observe` or `computer_act` row previews the app it names, top-level or nested. What an act types is still never shown there, and neither is a script, which can hold it.
  - A learned workflow or a skill read that a script or `tools_call` made still counts as the model's own call in a run's learning path and cost.
  - In a `codemode` script, `tools.missing` now reads `undefined` for a tool the run doesn't have, so `typeof tools.missing` gives `"undefined"` and `"missing" in tools` gives `false`. Before, the read threw. When the script then fails with a TypeError (calling it, say) or with an error naming it, the error gets one more line: "The script read tools.missing, which this run doesn't have. Its tools are: …".
  - On a computer with no `ui` group, a `computer_act` that names an app still brings it to the front first (one `apps.launch`, then the input). Raw input goes to the focused window, and the focus can change without the run seeing it. An act that names no app makes the one input call.
- Two fixes to how a Codex code-mode `exec` reads on the timeline, and one line in the desktop and phone skills. An exec that ends ok after its call parked on a person's approval and then ran shows its calls' outcomes alone, without "The exec was cut short after these calls (the session stopped)" or a resumed wait's "that cell's script was cut off". The model is still told those words, and an exec that failed still shows them. An exec the run's end closes, because nothing else ended it (the run stopped while its call waited for approval, or a crash whose next claim never resumed Codex's thread), now reads "Using tool: exec interrupted" with no status (`tool_status` null), never failed: a park or a stop failed nothing. A call a crash cut off still reads failed. The skills' "On Codex" paragraph now says Codex's exec has no top-level `return`, so a script's output goes through `text(...)`.
- Two fixes to how a Codex code-mode `exec` reads after a park or a crash, and one to pi's wording. A Codex exec's end row now sorts after the rows of the calls its script made: a crash leaves the exec open on the run's record, and Codex's recovered answer to it ends it after the resume. An exec whose call parked on a person's approval and then ran reads ok, with the stopped-and-resumed text, as a codemode script that parked reads on pi and claude-agent, never failed. An exec cut off mid-call still reads failed, after its cut call's row. The same holds for an exec that yielded and was finished by the model's pending `wait` on its cell: it reads ok when its parked call was allowed and ran, and failed when that call was refused or the wait was told the script was cut off. A recovered exec's outcome is saved in the session's log before Codex is answered, so a second crash before its end is recorded still ends it as that outcome says. An exec that no answer of Codex's ends (its run stopped while its call waited for approval, or a crash whose next drive never resumed Codex's thread) is closed with the run, "interrupted", after its calls' rows, never left open or shown failed ahead of them. A computer_op refused before it ran is named on the timeline by its op ("Refused: files.write"), never by "computer_op" or by its arguments, on every harness. On pi, a script's call a crash cut off now reads "interrupted: the process running it stopped before it reported an outcome; it may or may not have taken effect", the words claude-agent, opencode and Codex already give it. On Codex, a computer_op answer stays text, because Codex 0.164.0's code mode hands a script one string and never throws on a tool's reply. The desktop and phone kind skills now say how to read it: an op that ran answers JSON to parse, and a refused op answers the gate's words, which open with `Permission denied:` or `The user denied this`, or give the tool's name then `is read-only for this agent, so this call was refused:` or `can't be called:`.
- Three fixes to codemode's computer calls. A script call a person allowed carries its computer calls on its own result row only, not on its approval and "ran once you allowed it" rows too, so summing a run's rows counts each computer call once. A script rerun after a crash tells a recorded call whose answer has no value (a file write) by its answer's words, as it was answered live, not as `completed: null`. On Codex, a code-mode `exec` has its own rows, and each host tool call its script makes sits under it (`parent_tool_use_id`, the exec's call id), as a codemode script's calls do on pi, claude-agent and opencode; a host lends this through the new optional `SessionIO.ownCalls`. A Codex script that failed reads failed on its exec's row, never `exec: ok`.
- The 422 for allowing a destructive MCP call without `confirm_destructive` now reads as one sentence that says what to send: "The tool call <id> is one its MCP server marks destructive. To allow it, confirm a second time and send the allow again with confirm_destructive: true." Before, a generated ", e.g. true" was tacked on after the sentence ended. The field's issue still carries `example: true`.
- A run whose every model request went to a free model (one whose known price is $0 for every token, such as an OpenRouter `:free` model) now costs a known $0 and says why: its usage row reads "Cost: $0 · free model over N model requests", its `cost` and the usage row carry `free: true` (`x-agentrun-serve: "freemodel/1"`), and the console shows "$0 · free model". A request on such a model that failed once it left, was retried or was cut is booked at $0, where it used to make the run's cost unknown ("not priced"). The booking decides it from the model's known price, so a model with no known price still reads unknown and a paid model is unchanged. OpenRouter's routers (`openrouter/auto` and its kin), which its catalog lists at $0 but which bill the routed model, are never free.
- An email trigger no longer skips mail when its filter or `every_s` is edited while its start is still being taken. The start (made, moved to another mailbox, or turned on again) forgets the old cursor and then waits on the mail server; an edit that landed meanwhile dropped the start's result if it changed any field of the source, so the trigger was left with no cursor, and its first poll started watching from then. Now only an edit of where it reads (`account`, `mailbox`) or turning it off drops that start, and such an edit takes its own; an edit of `accept` or `every_s` keeps it, and the mail after it starts runs.
- A run's environment line now tells the date in the run's time zone, by weekday, day, month and year, and names the zone (`Today is Sunday 15 November 2026 (America/Los_Angeles).`), where it told the UTC date, a day ahead of the person's in an evening west of UTC. A run a schedule trigger started takes that trigger's zone; every other run takes the server's zone (`TZ`), and a zone the server does not know reads as UTC. The line carries no hour, so it changes once a day and the prompt cache holds within the day. A template eval's clock line to its graders says its date the same way.
- A template eval's `llm` grader sees each tool call's arguments and the first 8,000 characters of its result, not a 500-character preview: a rubric can check which URL `web_fetch` read (its query included), what a `web_search` or monid call asked for, or the fifth row of a result. Both go through the run's redaction, so a held value or a key-shaped string reads `[redacted]` in the grader's prompt and the report.
  - `GET /runs/{run_id}/timeline?calls=whole` adds `tool_input` (the call's arguments, each string cut at 2,000 characters) to each `tool_use` row and `tool_result_text` (the output's head, to 8,000 characters) to each `tool_result` row. The eval reads its runs this way, and the report's `runs[].calls` carry `arguments` and the longer `result`.
  - The grader's prompt stays under 120,000 characters: past that, the longest results lose their middle first, then the middle calls, and the list says what was cut. The rubric, task and answer are never cut.
  - A `tool_used` grader's `args` now match any tool's calls, not only a faked MCP tool's.
- A local eval whose shared harness install is already in place still goes through the server's own installer for it, under its hold. What an eval killed part way through that install left beside it is now swept by the next eval, as a server sweeps what is left beside its own install.
- A local `eval-template` (no `--server`) installs Claude Code and Codex once, not once per eval. The first local eval that needs one installs its pinned version into `$TMPDIR/agentrun-eval-harnesses/harnesses/<harness>@<version>-<platform>` the way a server's first use does (npm into a fresh directory, checked whole, renamed into place, read-only, one installer at a time across processes), and each eval's scratch data directory gets a link to it instead of a copy. A server's own data directory, its first-use install and its "Installing … (first use)" words are unchanged.
- A template eval's `tool_used` grader can name a monid endpoint (`monid:<provider>/<endpoint>`) that the package's `tools` grants by name, and counts its calls under that name. A monid name the package does not grant by name is refused when the cases are read, and so is one granted only by its provider's wildcard (`monid:<provider>/*`): the wildcard is filled from monid's listing when the agent is saved, so the eval cannot check the name before the run.
- A run whose runner was lost, and whose next claim then ended before its own computer started, no longer leaves the lost runner's computer running until its deadline. Before, the earlier claim's sandbox (and a Docker computer's egress volume) ran on for up to a day on Docker, or the vendor's lifetime elsewhere, whenever the next claim's image failed, its computer was refused on that runner, a person stopped or cancelled the run, the claim was refused before its computer, or that claim was lost too. Now, when a run is over, the runner deletes every computer any of its claims made, by the run's label. The computer janitor also ends a finished run's computers on its next sweep, without waiting for their deadline. A persistent computer and a paired computer are never deleted.
- A web_fetch page's `links` now hold the absolute URLs written out in its text, not only its markdown link targets. A page fetched directly that is not HTML lists the URLs in its body; it listed none before. That covers a JSON API, a plain-text file and an XML feed:
  - a JSON body's URLs are read from its string values, so a Statuspage incident's `shortlink` or a search API hit's `url` counts
  - any other body is read with its entities undone once, so an Atom entry's `<link href>` counts, and so does the escaped `&lt;a href=&quot;…&quot;&gt;` in its content, instead of a garbage link running to the next space
  - a feed's namespace name (`xmlns`) is not a link

  A page read through Parallel lists the URLs its markdown writes out as well as its link targets. A template eval's web fake gives a faked page the same links. An HTML page fetched directly keeps its link targets alone, as before. The same dedup, fragment removal, caps and `links_cut` count apply.

  The eval link check matches a cited link from any of those bodies. Two more fixes there:
  - A URL now ends at `|`, so a Slack-style `<https://x|text>` link is cited as `https://x`. A markdown link's target still runs to its `)`, so `[route](https://maps.example/?markers=a|b)` is cited whole, as a page's links read it.
  - A call that is not a web call counts too: its urls are the URLs its result holds, a JSON string that is a URL whole counted whole (a calendar event's `htmlLink`). The check now shows when the answer cites a link and some call returned URLs, not only when the run made a web call. A grader reads only the head of such a result, so a link that matches nothing names a call whose result was cut, as it names a page whose links were cut.

  Where a URL in text ends, which trailing punctuation is not its own, and where a markdown link's target ends are now one module, `text-urls.ts`. The link check, a page's links and the timeline's scrub all read through it. The scrub keeps going through a `|`, so a query value holding one is still elided whole.
- A finished look-back or revise round keeps its outcome sentence after a reload. A run's grade now keeps the feedback round it opened: `GET /runs/{id}/learning`'s `graded` is the grade as `PUT /runs/{id}/grade` answered it, without `expected` (`run_id`, `correct`, `source`, `graded_at`, `path`, `workflow`, `workflow_digest`, `feedback`), plus `feedback_status`, how that round stands as the run's journal and the round's steer row say it (never the server's `graded_at` against the runner's `ended_at`): `running`, `ended`, or `not_run` when the reopened run ended before it took the grade's words (its claim refused, say); null for a grade that opened none. The console's Grade control says what came of a grade from the read alone, stays "Reviewing" until the round ended and its learning settled, says "The review could not run." with Grade again for a round that never ran, and reads the learning again on a backoff when a read fails while the round is unsettled. The round is written on the grade only once the run opened again on it: a reopen that fails leaves a grade with `feedback: null`.
  Upgrading: a client reading `graded` gets the PUT's fields; `correct`, `source` and `graded_at` are unchanged.
- A wrong grade with no words no longer tells the model the verdict twice in each ask. The round's steer carries only the words, else "A right answer holds: {…}", else "(no words)" (the Timeline's "Your grade" row reads the same); the look-back and revise asks each say the verdict once.
- A server restarted after a crash during a harness install no longer fails the install. A first-use install removes what an earlier install left beside it only when it can: a leftover the crashed server's orphaned npm still writes into (`ENOTEMPTY`), or one with a folder that can't be read, stays while the new install goes on in its own directory. The same holds for the install it replaces, and a failed install whose staging can't be removed reports why npm failed instead of why the staging stayed. What stays is swept later: a server that finds a harness installed (at its start, or when an agent's save or a run looks) removes what earlier installs left beside it, under the install's hold and never while another process installs, so a leftover doesn't stay on the disk once its npm has finished. That npm is never killed by its process id.
- Hosted computers (Agent37, E2B, Modal, Daytona) take network `open` and an allowlist, so a hosted desktop's browser and a hosted sandbox's `pip`, `npm` and `git` reach the web. Before, every hosted descriptor declared `none` alone: the server's list was narrowed to `none`, and a provider asked for `open` refused it.
  - The tools' network namespace stays loopback alone. Their one way out is an egress proxy that `computerd init` starts before it leaves the machine's network (`--network open` or `--network allow:<list>`). It runs as `nobody`, listens on a Unix socket only root and the tool user's group reach, and init relays `127.0.0.1:3128` to it and sets the proxy variables.
  - The proxy follows the Docker egress proxy's table: public addresses only. It refuses metadata (169.254.169.254 and the other clouds'), private and link-local ranges, loopback (so the vendor's agent on the machine), and the machine's own addresses, with 403 and an `x-egress-refused` header. A list is checked before any lookup, on ports 80 and 443.
  - The machine gets the vendor's egress for it: Agent37 `allow-all`, E2B `allowInternetAccess`, Modal without `blockNetwork`, Daytona without `networkBlockAll`. Under `none`, nothing changes.
  - A descriptor declares only the network forms its computer enforces. A form it doesn't declare is refused in words naming the provider and the choices, such as "Orgo can't limit the network to a list; choose none". Orgo still declares `none` alone: its adapter starts no proxy.
  - Create and `network()` read the network back from inside: nothing answers directly, init's relay answers, and the policy file beside the proxy's socket holds the form the label records.
  - An Archil computer takes `open` or a list too. Its root still mounts the folder outside the tools' network.
  - `places.boxes` lists a Daytona or Modal box as `allowlist` under a host list, not `none`.
  - Breaking: desktops now reach the public web by default; set none or a list to narrow it. This holds for Docker and hosted desktops alike. Under the default `AGENTRUN_BOX_ALLOW` (a sandbox's package-install list, not a browsing policy), a desktop is `open`: public internet only, through its egress proxy. The operator's or the launch's list is its allowlist, and `none` stays none. A sandbox keeps the default list, Orgo stays `none`, and Settings says what a desktop gets.
  - Breaking: a Docker computer on network `open` now reaches public addresses only, through its egress proxy. It no longer reaches the host's LAN, private ranges or metadata. The computer is `--network none`, and its one way out is its own egress proxy container, started with `--open public`. It gets the same refusals as an allowlist: private, loopback, link-local, metadata and the Docker host's own addresses. A computer on Docker's bridge reads back as `other`. `open` is refused where an allowlist is: on a Docker host that remaps user ids, or one this provider doesn't run on, unless `egress.hostAddresses` is given.
  - A host or LAN service isn't reachable from a computer on any network setting, Docker or hosted. An allowlist can't name one. A private address such as `10.0.0.1` isn't a list entry, and a private CIDR such as `10.0.0.0/24` or `192.168.1.0/24` is refused at check. A listed LAN name that resolves to a private address is refused by the proxy.
- The model picker's free mark (`harnesses[].free_models` in `GET /capabilities`) now uses the kernel's free-model rule, the same one that decides what a run books at $0, so the two cannot disagree. A catalog price tier that leaves out its input or output price is no longer read as $0.
- A desktop or phone run gets its kind's skill again. The claim read the computer kind from the run's launch, which never carries it, so no run since the store cutover had `.agents/skills/desktop-computer/` or `.agents/skills/phone-computer/`, and a read of either answered ENOENT. Now the kind comes from the agent's computer setting, the one the claim starts the computer from. The skill is laid beside the revision's own skills and named the same way: pi's system prompt lists it, and Codex, Claude Code and OpenCode get it as one of their own skills (or in the prompt, where the harness refuses it).

  A phone run's refusal and ask now say phone. A computer tool is still held to the stricter of the desktop and phone settings, and the words name the setting that decided the call, which is the run's own kind when both say the same. Before, a phone run with phone set to deny was refused with "Permission denied: desktop is set to deny for this agent.", and its approval was asked as desktop.

  Naming the skill makes a desktop run's first request larger. Through a gateway, the smallest cap that takes a pi desktop run on Sonnet through five steps goes from $0.11 to $0.12 (the run needs $0.110), and its first request from $0.05 to $0.06. Straight to Anthropic it stays at $0.09. At $0.11 through a gateway the run still answers, but the wrap-up refuses its last screenshot. The serve README's table says so.

  The phone skill's scroll is now a point scroll on a call with `foreground: true`, because a swipe is the phone's own input and the phone refuses it otherwise. Its script scrolls Settings until About phone shows, then expects "Device name", which is on screen after the press. The old expect, "Android version", is below the fold, so it never showed.
- A run that answered and lost its runner's claim while looking back (its end-of-run learning turn) now ends completed with its answer. The claim that takes it over no longer runs the open learning turn as the job's turn: that turn is never told the cap's "finish now" note, and a cap refusal of its requests drops the learning as `no_budget` instead of parking the answered run for a raise. The runner beside a server now logs a lost claim and a failed renew in the runner's name, as the `runner` subcommand does.
  A run's status is now how its job's own turn ended: learning spend that takes the run past its cap (its cut requests booked at their worst case included) drops that learning as `no_budget`, the spend still booked, and never fails the run; a compile turn the cap refuses is dropped the same way.
  A run whose job failed (a tool call that faulted on every restart, an answer cut at the model's limit) and that lost its claim during its end-of-run learning now ends failed in the same words after the takeover, never completed: the job's end is kept before the learning starts and the takeover reads it.
  Upgrading: a run that is in its end-of-run learning while its runner is upgraded, and loses its claim there, ends failed ("the end-of-run turn is open, but the job's end was never kept before it"), because the older runner never kept the job's end. Let running learning settle before upgrading a runner.
- A replay run's learned_workflow call that was rerun after a park and refused before any node ran no longer drops its earlier attempt's guard rows from the run's `metrics.guards`, which threshold refit and promotion replay read, and its timeline row keeps showing the earlier attempt's `learned_nodes` instead of none.
- A run its learned workflow answered keeps the path `workflow` when the agent restates the workflow's JSON inside prose (a fenced `json` block with words around it), the same as when it restates it bare.
- The eval link check now treats a host and the same host with `www.` in front as the same, whether the `www.` is on the cited link or on the call's URL. A citation of `https://www.cpsc.gov/x` now matches a call that returned `https://cpsc.gov/x`, and the reverse. Before, it read "no matching call". No other subdomain is dropped, so `m.`, `amp.` and the rest still have to match exactly.
- The analytics page's top tools name an MCP tool whose `mcp__<server>__<tool>` is longer than 52 characters by its catalog name (`slack · SLACK_FETCH_MESSAGE_THREAD_FROM_A_CONVERSATION`), as its timeline does, not by the hashed name the harness called it. Runs on claude-agent, codex and opencode now count their tool calls there too; their metrics counted none. Runs that ended before this change keep the metrics they stored.
- An MCP tool whose `mcp__<server>__<tool>` is longer than 52 characters can be granted. Composio's Slack tool for a thread's replies (`mcp:slack/SLACK_FETCH_MESSAGE_THREAD_FROM_A_CONVERSATION`, 58 characters) was refused at the save, so the templates that need it could not be applied. Every harness now calls such a tool by its name cut to 52 characters with a hash of its catalog name, and its timeline rows, settings and approvals still name it `mcp:<server>/<tool>`. Two grants that would be called by one such name are refused, naming both.
- Learning: a replay, a threshold refit and a serving revision's graded check score their rows with one function (`scoreRows` over refit rows), so the numbers a refit promotes on are the ones a replay would give its new revision. A refit record's `agree` now counts the revision as it serves, its new guard fit included. No API shape changed.
- OpenRouter runs book what OpenRouter charged; routers need no cap or a read-back cost; a provider's error inside a stream is booked by what it reported.
  - A request on an OpenRouter model is booked at the cost OpenRouter states in the answer's usage (with your own provider key, its fee plus the provider's charge). The price table's figure is kept beside it (`tableUsd`). A cap still holds each request at list price before it leaves. A stated cost that is missing, not a number, or above that hold is not used: the table's figure is booked instead.
  - OpenRouter's routers (`openrouter/auto`, `openrouter/free` and the others) have no price here, because the model they pick is not known in advance. A run with a spend cap is refused before it starts. A run without one is booked at the cost OpenRouter reports, else unknown, never $0.
  - A provider's error inside a successful (200) stream (Anthropic's `overloaded_error`, `api_error` or `rate_limit_error`, OpenRouter's mid-stream errors, a Responses `response.failed`) is booked by one rule. If the stream reported tokens before the error, they are booked at list price, or at the cost OpenRouter stated, and the run's cost stays known: before, such a request was booked at the cap's hold and made the run's cost unknown. If it reported no tokens, it is booked as refused at $0, and the run's record keeps the provider's message (`refusal`, or `providerError` beside a booked figure). That holds only while the model generated nothing: once the stream shows the model began its output (a content block, a Responses output item, hidden reasoning included, or a text-tools model's reply the runner had not sent yet), an error with no usage is booked at an unknown cost, never $0.
  - Kernel: `startModelProxy` books a cost stated in the answer's usage when its origin is OpenRouter's or serve's translation route's (`statesUsageCost`, `ROUTE_ORIGIN`), on every harness: claude-agent, codex and opencode runs on OpenRouter book what OpenRouter charged too. `Ended` gains `tableUsd` on an answer, `{ end: "answered", label: "error", reason }` and `{ end: "nothing", label: "refused", reason }`. `bookRequest` books the table's figure (rule `answered:over_hold`) when a reported figure is above the hold. The claude-agent policy's usage reads a stream that ends in an `error` event as whole. Routers and in-stream errors are handled on those harnesses too.
- A desktop or phone run that parks for a person (a tool's approval, a cap raise, a question to a person, a learned workflow's park) keeps its computer for 10 minutes. Before, every park let the computer go, so the run resumed on a new machine and lost what the agent had open on the old one. Now the timeline says "The desktop is kept for 10 minutes while you decide.", and an answer within that time resumes the run on the same machine, with its screen, files and programs as they were. After 10 minutes the kept computer is ended, and a later resume gets a new one that says "The desktop wasn't kept: 10 minutes passed." before the usual replaced-computer words. A stop or cancel while parked lets the kept computer go at once. The end at 10 minutes survives a server restart: the computer janitor reads the kept computers and ends each one at its time. An agent's own computer and a paired computer are unchanged; a sandbox is kept the same way (see park-view-sandbox). The desktop and phone skills now say that app ids come from `apps.list`, so the agent calls it before `apps.open`.
- While a run is parked, its desktop's or phone's live view says what the run waits for and that the computer is kept, never that it ended. Before, a park closed the viewer page with "This computer's session has ended.", and the console's Screen tab said "This desktop has been released.", though the computer was kept for the resume. Now the viewer page says, for example, "Waiting for your approval. The desktop is kept for 10 minutes, until 14:05.", and the console says "Waiting for your approval. The desktop is kept until 14:05." (or "Waiting for your answer.", "Waiting for you to raise the spend cap."), its time from the park's timeline row. After the 10 minutes both say "The desktop wasn't kept: 10 minutes passed. A new one starts when the run goes on." GET /v2/runs/{run_id}/computer answers a parked run's kept desktop or phone as `none` with `session: "closed"`, then `ended` with the timeout's words once that time passes. Take over stays off while parked. A sandbox run's GET /v2/runs/{run_id}/computer now says "A sandbox has no screen: what the agent runs in it is on the timeline.", where it said "this run's agent has no computer".

  A sandbox run that parks now keeps its sandbox for 10 minutes too, as a desktop's is kept: the timeline says "The sandbox is kept for 10 minutes while you decide.", an answer within that time goes on on the same sandbox ("It's the same sandbox, as the wait left it."), with its files outside the run folder as they were, and one after it gets a new sandbox that says "The sandbox wasn't kept: 10 minutes passed." The computer janitor ends a kept sandbox at its time across a server restart.
- On pi, a tool call that is already running beside a call waiting for approval now finishes and keeps its result. Before, when one answer from the model made two MCP calls, a read that runs on its own and a write that asks, the run paused on the write at once and cut the read before it reached its server. Once the write was answered, the model was told the read was interrupted and may have partly run, so it ran the read again.
  - The pause now waits up to 30 seconds for the calls already running beside it to end, so their results are kept and the model gets them with the answer to the waiting call. Nothing runs twice.
  - A call that is still running after 30 seconds is cut, as before, and the model is told it was interrupted.
  - No new call starts while the pause waits. One the model made in the same answer is asked about again when the run goes on, and runs then.
  - A cancel or stop while the pause waits ends the run at once.
  - Claude Code, Codex and OpenCode are unchanged: their pause lets the run go at once, and their resume keeps a finished call's result.
- Learning: a replay scores a graded run graded wrong against its grade, never as a tie. The workflow's answer is right only when it is the grade's expected answer; with none expected, on a run a learned workflow served, at least not the answer graded wrong, and on a run the agent answered, never (both sides wrong). The agent's side is its own grade when it answered the run, and right on a run a learned workflow answered alone. So a revision held on runs it served wrong is promoted again only once its replay answers them right (or hands them back), never by answering them as wrongly again, and never on gains elsewhere: the runs it was held on are also scored alone and must be within the bar. One expected field that is no text (a number, say) now also reads a bare answer.
- A run that resumes on a new computer says so. After a lost runner or a crash (any kind), or a server stop (a desktop or a phone), the claim that starts a fresh computer for the run adds to its ready line that it's a new one and what was on the old one is gone (in Mode 2, that the run folder is kept). The model's next request carries one server message saying its computer was replaced, once, and a `computer_act` that names a ref or a state the new computer never gave, or a point before the model looked again, is refused in words and never reaches the computer. An agent's own (persistent) computer and a paired one get neither.
- A sandbox run resumed after a server stop, and any run resumed after a park, is now told its computer is new. Before, only a desktop or a phone was told after a server stop, and a parked run's resume never was. The ready line says "It's a new <kind>: the one before is gone, with what was on it." The model's note names no cause, and it reads by kind: a desktop or phone is told to look at the screen again, and a sandbox to check its files. The note and the cap's wrap-up note now start with "AgentRun server note:". The timeline row still reads "AgentRun: …" with the label only once. The run's journal now records each computer a claim makes, and a later claim reads that record. A run that made its computer before this upgrade has no record, so if it resumes after the upgrade on a new computer, it isn't told.
- An ended run's cost is one figure, read from its booking, and no run reads as ended without it. `GET /runs/{id}`, the runs list and the stored `cost_usd` of an ended run now read the same sum of its booked requests, paid tool calls and decisions (each request counted once), where the view used to read pi's own price for an answer whose booking had not landed yet. A run's end waits for every booking whose write has begun (bounded at 30 s, with a warning when it gives up) before it writes the end, so the final request's booking is never left behind. The end's cost is read apart from its metrics, so metrics that time out no longer drop the cost.
  A model request cut with no answer and no usage (its runner lost mid-request) under a cap is booked at what the cap held for it, the most it can have cost (`runner.turn` `rule: "cut"`, `atMost: true`), so the run's cost stays known instead of turning unknown. A cost that counts one says so: the run's `cost` and the timeline's usage row carry `upper_bound: true`, the usage row reads "Cost: at most $0.97 over 2 model requests", and the console shows "at most $0.97". A cut with no hold (no cap) or a paid tool call that was cut stays unknown, as before: a paid call's `runner.request` now says `paid: true`, so a later process that books it cut never reads its fee as a bound. A hold is never counted as spend: when another charge leaves the total unknown, `so_far_usd` sums the exact charges only and each request booked at its hold counts in `unpriced`, and `upper_bound` is set only on a known figure. The usage row of a CLI or workflow run, and a pi run's with side requests, now carries `upper_bound` and "at most" the same way. The run row stores the bound beside its cost: a new `cost_upper_bound` column (SQLite: added when the server opens a store, and a runner refuses a store until then; Postgres: migration 0014), which `GET /runs/{id}` and the runs list read as `cost.upper_bound`, so the view, the list and the column always agree on the figure, the bound and an unknown. A stored bound is never read as spend: `GET /usage` counts a run whose stored cost is a bound as a run of unknown cost (in `unpriced_runs`, with only its exact charges in `total_usd` and its lines, by every grouping and meter), and the runner's `run_ended` log line says `cost_usd=unknown` with `cost_usd_at_most` beside it. An end whose cost read fails reads it again (three tries within its 30 s bound) before it stores the cost unknown, and `GET /runs/{id}` of an ended run reads the stored cost, so it never shows a figure the list and the column do not. Learning's figures say no "at most", so they read a bounded run's cost as unknown: a look-back's `look_back_usd` and `job_cost_usd`, a learning batch row's `cost_usd` and `total_usd` (a batch stops `cost_unknown` on one, as before), the cost series, the money rule's all-in cost, and an agent's learning impact (`median_cost_usd`, `cost_runs`).
  A cost marked `upper_bound` (the run's `cost` and the timeline's usage row) now also carries `so_far_usd`, what it is known to have spent with no hold in it, and `unpriced`, how many requests it counts at their hold, so every reader that adds more charges to it keeps the hold apart: a workflow's usage row joined with its decisions, its `GET /runs/{id}` cost while it runs, and its graph's `totals.cost_usd` (which says no "at most", so a sum with a hold in it reads null there). A charged $0.01 beside a $0.25 hold and a decision of unknown cost reads "$0.01 known, 2 not priced", no longer "$0.26 known". The over-cap row says "Spent" of the known spend only; a bound past the cap reads "At most $0.26 spent, at most $0.06 over the run's cap". Breaking: `so_far_usd` and `unpriced` are no longer absent whenever `usd` is known; a client that took their presence to mean an unknown cost checks `usd === null` instead.
  A request billed to a ChatGPT plan costs the run $0 however it ended: one cut by a crash or stopped is booked `rule: "cut"` (or its stop's rule) at $0 with `billing: "plan"`, never unknown, so a plan run's cost no longer blanks when a request is cut. Its `runner.request` says `plan: true`. The stored `cost_usd` and the runs list of a plan run now read the known figure the view already showed.
  A workflow run's stored `cost_usd` is read from its booking by the same rule (`GET /runs/{id}` of an ended workflow run reads it too), no longer from its cap's figures. Breaking: a workflow request stopped while it streamed now leaves the cost unknown, as on an agent run, where it used to store the cap's estimate; a decision cut by a crash counts at its hold as an upper bound.
- A URL in a timeline row's text (a tool's result and its preview, a page's title, a decision's sources, a note) never shows a query value after an apostrophe. An apostrophe inside a URL (`https://books.example/O'Reilly?token=…`, a query's `q='rust'`) is now part of the URL, so its whole query is scrubbed; one that closes a quote around a URL stays outside it, as a sentence's punctuation does.
- A server note (the replaced computer's, the spend cap's wrap-up, the free-model limit's wrap-up) now counts as told only once a request carrying it is answered. Before, it counted as told when the request was admitted, so a request that then failed (an upstream 429, an error status, a lost or cut stream, a runner stopped before the answer) took the note with it, and the harness's retry or the resumed run went out without it: the model never saw it. On a route serve translates (OpenRouter's), a provider's error status counts as a failure too: the model proxy now ends a stream that closes on an error event in words with `label: "error"` and the words as its reason (the session record's `providerError`), booked as before. The failed request gives the note back, the retry carries it, and the timeline row is written once, when the note is answered. One request at a time still carries it.
- Use consistent rounded action controls and a single translucent primary action, and paste clipboard values into the selected secret field while retaining manual entry when clipboard access is unavailable.
- A run whose turn a person stopped now says so to an API reader: `GET /v2/runs/{run_id}` and its item in `GET /v2/runs` carry `pending: {kind: "stopped"}` beside status `input_required` and state `idle`, so a stopped run no longer reads like one that is stuck. The `run.needs_input` webhook tells that stop with the same kind, once, across a restart too.
  - A person's stop used to reach the webhook as `run.ended` with status `input_required`. It is a wait the run stands at, so it is now `run.needs_input`; `run.ended` comes when the run ends.
  - A turn its harness ended on its own reads the same status and state with `pending` null, and its `run.needs_input` carries no `pending`. It was told as `stopped` before. The webhook's kind is always the run read's `pending.kind`, `computer` included.
  - `agentrun runs wait` says a stopped run was stopped, and says of a run whose turn ended on its own that it ended its turn.
  - Breaking: a reader that took `pending` null with input_required and idle as stopped reads `pending.kind` `stopped`; a webhook receiver that took `run.ended` with status input_required as a stop gets `run.needs_input` with `pending.kind` `stopped`. The generated TypeScript and Python clients gain the kind.
- A stop that reaches a run while it parks on a tool approval, and whose end the journal refuses, now waits out its retry backoff. The run was released still parked, and a parked run with an untaken stop is claimed at once whatever its backoff, so the end was tried a second time with no wait and the give-up came one try early. The refused end now releases the run running, as every other refused end does: the next claim comes after the backoff, and the tries count one per step (5 s doubling to the 5 min cap).
- A tool row on a run's timeline carries the call's catalog name (`mcp:notes5/write_note`, `monid:faux/person/enrich`), not the wire name the harness called it by (`mcp__notes5__write_note`). Runs recorded before this show the same names now: the rename is made when the timeline is read.
  - Each harness's facts state their own map from the model's name for a host tool to the host's (`AdapterFacts.hostName`, replacing OpenCode's `toolAlias`), and the tool gate and the meta tools read it instead of stripping prefixes.
  - One conversion turns a host tool into the tool bridge's (`bridgeTool`, from `@parcha/agentrun-kernel/process`); the Claude Agent, Codex and OpenCode adapters each add only what is theirs.
- A web_fetch or web_search answer now keeps its `links` and still parses after the run's redactor cuts it. The redactor treats any stretch of more than 8,192 characters with no whitespace as `[redacted]`, and it used to run over the answer's whole JSON line. Escaped newlines in that line are not whitespace, so the end of the page text and the whole links array formed one such stretch, and redacting it broke the line's JSON. The grader's link check then found no links in the stored answer and read a cited link from it (a release from a feed) as "no matching call". This happened on both the pi and the CLI harnesses. Each string inside a web call's JSON is now redacted on its own, along with the lines after the JSON, so a held value is still cut. Any other tool's answer is redacted as one text, as before.
- web_search stops asking a provider that has said no, for as long as the provider asked. If a run's search provider says the run is out of quota (Parallel's or a model provider's 402, Anthropic's billing_error, OpenAI's insufficient_quota), every later web_search call in that run answers "search is unavailable for the rest of this run; answer from what you have", and the provider isn't called again. If it says the run is rate-limited (keyless Exa's free limit, a 429, rate_limit_error, rate_limit_exceeded, or the hosted search's own too_many_requests, even after another search in the same request found results), each call answers "search is busy; try again in N s, or answer from what you have" without calling the provider, until the wait the provider named has passed. That wait comes from Retry-After, in seconds or as a date, is 60 s when the provider names none, and is capped at 15 minutes. When two calls in flight are both rate-limited, the longer wait holds: a shorter one never shrinks it. After it, the next call goes to the provider again. Keyless Exa answers its daily count running out with the same rate limit and no wait, so for keyless Exa alone a second such limit naming no wait, after a wait has passed, in the same run, is read as quota (a 429 with Retry-After is a timed limit and only waits): that call and every later one answer that search is unavailable for the rest of the run. One that comes while the wait is still open (two calls in flight) doesn't count, and a search that succeeds in between resets the count, since a spent daily count limits every call. A quota answer holds even after a wait passes. The timeline shows each held call as a failed search in those words. One run had kept searching 520 times against Exa's limit. The breaker belongs to the run, so another run on the same server searches as before. Other failures leave it closed: a 5xx, a timeout, or Exa refusing the connection.
- A capped run's wrap-up note now comes due on the same input count its request is admitted by. The model proxy counts a request (the provider's count, or the local count for a model whose tokenizer is o200k_base) before it asks for the note, so the note's least, its step-0 figure and the reserve it is checked against are priced on that count, never on the body's bytes. Before, the note was priced on the bytes while admission read the count: a $2 code review on pi with GPT-6.1 Sol through OpenRouter, whose script call was cut at the output ceiling, sent an answer request past 272,000 bytes that was told to "finish now" with $1.56 left (its least read as about $1.45 at the long-context rate, $0.25 on its count), and it answered with no review; a $1 run was told its budget was "enough for little work" on its first request. The noted request is bounded by that count plus the note's own bytes, and a client that goes while its request is counted no longer takes the note.
- Every way to run AgentRun (`npx`, Render, Docker, Compose) starts with no model key and ends the same way: Continue with ChatGPT (Settings → Model keys, or the first screen), then run your first agent. A model key stays the other way, beside it.
  - The deployment guide has one copy-paste `docker run` line: the server and a runner on a named volume, a seal key made once in a file beside it, the port on this machine's loopback, no model key.
  - Where Render and Docker are introduced, the docs say that a ChatGPT sign-in is for the person who runs the server, with OpenAI's words on usage, and how to finish it on a server elsewhere: copy the sign-in tab's whole address into the console.
  - The harness table says which harnesses run on a ChatGPT plan (pi and Codex); Claude Code, OpenCode, Jev decisions and paid tools need their own keys. The server's README documents `/v2/settings/chatgpt` and `models.source: "chatgpt"`, what capabilities say of codex and pi with no key (the sign-in, `needs: ["key", "chatgpt"]`), and that a curl call with the owner's session sends the server's `origin` and `content-type: application/json`, a DELETE too (else 401).
  - The setup skill offers "Continue with ChatGPT" or a model key, and leaves the sign-in to the person.
- A one-page guide for template authors on giving a template tools (`templates/TOOLS.md`): how to declare built-in tools, a Composio toolkit and monid endpoints (`monid:<provider>/<endpoint>`), how to pin a tool's arguments to the owner's parameters, what asks the owner and what runs unasked (Allow reads, a destructive call's second click), and which toolkits are proven live. The templates README's `tools` row says a package grants monid endpoints there.
  The serve README's "Finding and calling the run's tools" now says that a deny of `tools_search` or `tools_call` turns Claude Code's ToolSearch off and lists every tool, that Settings → Tools lists the three, and that a `codemode` script leaves a harness's prefix off a tool's name.

## 0.1.0-beta.38 (2026-11-14)

- Daytona no longer takes an Archil mount: Archil's client hangs on its sandboxes (its FUSE session never answers a `statx` of the mountpoint), so a create that asks for one waited out its 120 s mount bound. Breaking: Daytona's descriptor declares `mounts: []` and its `capabilities().mount` is `[]`; `check()` and `create()` refuse an Archil mount up front, code `refused`, in the words "Archil mounts don't work on Daytona yet: Archil's client hangs on its sandboxes", before anything is asked of Daytona. `DAYTONA_ARCHIL_EGRESS` is no longer a Daytona key, and `DaytonaProvider` refuses the `archilEgress` option at construction; drop both. In serve, a Mode 2 agent whose computer is a Daytona sandbox, with GPUs or without, is refused at its save and its run's start with those words: pick a Modal or E2B sandbox instead.
  A descriptor may now say why it takes none of a mount kind, `unmounted: { <kind>: "<one sentence>" }` (`Unmounted`, also a `HostFacts` field and `checkMount`'s third parameter); `check()` refuses a mount of that kind in those words, and `defineProvider` refuses an `unmounted` that names a kind `mounts` declares.
- A template's `parameters` are read, compiled and checked as its `inputs` are: one grammar, one compiler, one required rule. Breaking: a parameter is required unless it says `required: false`, a `default` is allowed only beside `required: false`, and GET /v2/templates serves `parameters` as a closed JSON Schema object (`type`, `additionalProperties: false`, `required`, `properties`) where it served a map of descriptors. A package that left a parameter optional by omitting `required` adds `required: false`; a client that read `parameters.<name>.required` reads `parameters.required` and `parameters.properties.<name>`.
  - Apply fills a blank parameter (absent, or `""`) with its default, then checks the parameters with the run input check, so a refusal reads as a run's: `parameters.topic is required`, `parameters keeps no field tone`, the validator's own words for a bound or a pattern.
  - A parameter takes the `inputs` keys (`title`, `examples`, `minimum`, `maxLength`, …); `cron` and `timezone` are in the one format list. The console's Apply form is the run form: a parameter's `title` is its label.
- Template packages lose three parts that repeated what the server already does. A package that uses one must drop it.
  - The `schema` grader is gone. Every completed graded run of a package that declares `output` is now held to its output schema by an `output` verdict, so a case no longer needs a `graders/schema.md`. A case that still has one is refused: "type is one of llm, regex, tool_used, file_exists".
  - The `examples/` folder is refused ("a package's folders are skills/, rules/ and evals/"), and GET /v2/templates no longer serves `examples`.
  - The `checks` field in agent.md is refused ("no field checks").
  - The run read (GET /v2/runs/{run_id}) now serves `input`, the run's input as it was started (null when withheld), and `file_ids`, its files. The console's "Run again" resends both, so a run whose message is over 2,000 characters, has typed fields or was given files now starts again whole instead of being refused.
- A template's `mcp` needs name where their tools come from, `{source: composio | github | url, toolkit, tools, required?, reason?, allow?, pin?}`, never a saved server's name: `server:` is removed, and a package that still has it is refused with the new shape in the message. To upgrade a package, replace `server: <name>` with its `source` and `toolkit` (`source: github, toolkit: github` for GitHub; `source: composio, toolkit: <slug>` for a Composio toolkit, its tools by their action slugs; else `source: url` with the toolkit you will set on the saved server). Inside the package its tools are `mcp:<toolkit>/<tool>`, and an apply's `grants` name them that way.
  - Apply maps each need to the saved MCP server whose recorded source and toolkit are the need's; where several are, the owner picks one with the apply's new `servers` (`{<toolkit>: <server>}`), and an apply with no pick is `422` naming them: a server is never picked for the owner. When the server's name is not the toolkit, apply renames the package's tool names (`mcp:<toolkit>/<tool>` and `mcp:<toolkit>/*`) to `mcp:<server>/...` in the instructions, the skills, the tool settings and the grants. The answer's `servers` says which server each need used, or null. A need with none is not set up here: its warning (or a required one's `409`) says how to add one, for Composio the preset with the toolkit and actions filled in.
  - Each saved MCP server records `source` and `toolkit`, shown by `GET /v2/settings/mcp-servers`, when it is saved and from what made it: the Composio preset records `composio` and its toolkit, a `github_app` server is `github`, any other is `url` with the toolkit its owner sets (`toolkit` in the `PUT`, or Settings → MCP servers). `POST .../oauth/start` takes `toolkit` too, for the server its sign-in saves.
  - A template eval's fake MCP server stands in for the need it fakes: the eval's own server records it as the need's source and toolkit. With `--server`, a case that fakes a `composio` or `github` need fails, saying to run it on the eval's own server.
  - New display fields: `category` (one of engineering, security, sales, marketing, research, finance, operations, compliance, personal) and `tags` (at most 8).
  - The shipped packages say where their tools come from, with a reason each: code-review and release-notes from GitHub, market-monitor's sends and inbound-lead's HubSpot and Slack tools from Composio by their action slugs (`SLACK_SEND_MESSAGE` pinned to the channel; `GMAIL_SEND_EMAIL` to the one address, `cc`, `bcc`, `extra_recipients` and `from_email` held absent). An alias neither listing declares (Slack's `channel_id`, Gmail's `to`) needs no pin: the gate refuses an undeclared argument of a pinned tool.
  - Security: code-review and release-notes pin every GitHub tool, reads too, to the one repository, so a hostile pull request or release body can't have the agent read another repository the GitHub App reaches. Their `repo` parameter is now `owner` and `repo`, and their trigger is held to `<owner>/<repo>`.
