The free-text searches that can't be pinned are dropped: code-review's `search_code`, release-notes' `search_issues` and `search_pull_requests` (it lists with `list_pull_requests` and `list_issues` instead). Each has an eval case where the body asks for another repository's file.
  - Security: inbound-lead reads nothing from HubSpot. It runs unattended on a form anyone can submit and holds `web_fetch`, so a CRM read could be sent out in a fetched URL. Its one HubSpot tool is `HUBSPOT_CREATE_NOTE`, optional: one note, the fit score in its text, on the contact a HubSpot CRM event's own payload names (with none, it answers with the brief and says why). The contact update and the `crm_score_property` parameter are dropped too, since a pin can't limit which fields an update sets. A package that holds `web_fetch` now lists no MCP read.
  - The console's apply screen shows each need's source, reason and the saved server it will use, a choice where several match, and a link to add one where none does; Settings → MCP servers shows and edits each server's source and toolkit.
- A tool-call budget is removed: `max_tool_calls` on an agent definition and `budget.tool_calls` in a template manifest are refused as unknown fields, and the `subagent` tool no longer takes `max_tool_calls`. The count only ever held on pi; the run's spend cap and its wrap-up stop a runaway loop on every harness. Put a call count in the instructions and set `per_run_usd` (a template's `budget` is now `{per_run_usd}`, required when `budget` is given).
- A run's MCP tools are host tools on every harness: each call passes the run's one tool gate before anything is sent, and the runner calls the server with the credential, books the call and records it, as it does any host tool. opencode now runs MCP tools (`features.mcp_client.harnesses` lists it, and an opencode agent granted `mcp:<server>/<tool>` saves and runs). claude-agent offers a granted tool as `mcp__hands__mcp__<server>__<tool>` and codex as `mcp_<server>__<tool>` (Codex refuses a dynamic tool named `mcp__*`); the Timeline, tool settings and approvals still name it `mcp:<server>/<tool>`. A call set to ask on claude-agent, codex or opencode holds the CLI's call while the run waits (no "waits for a person's approval" result row while it is parked); on the person's allow the resumed session gets the call's own result, no `[tool approval]` message. A codex run no longer fails at its start when a granted server can't be reached: the server's error shows at the first call, as on pi. On a code-mode Codex model, a script's tool call held for a person's approval runs once on their allow, under its own call id, and the script's cut-off `exec` reads its result (or, when the `exec` had yielded, the model's `wait` on its cell); before, the resume told the model the call may have run, and the call the model made again asked again, so the allow never reached a call.

  Who breaks: a run parked on an MCP call at the MCP door before this version does not resume its call: cancel it and start it again. A Codex thread started before this version loses its MCP tools when it resumes (Codex resumes a thread with the dynamic tools it started with): start a new run. Code built on the kernel's MCP door breaks too. Removed: `SessionSpec.mcp`, `SessionMcp`, `McpClient`, `AdapterCapabilities` and `AgentAdapter.capabilities()`, `AdapterFacts.mcp`, `ModelProxyOptions.mcp`, `mcpRoute`, `McpHandler` and `McpRouteOptions` (`@parcha/agentrun-kernel/host`), and `McpCallResult.parked`. Hand a session its MCP tools as host tools in `SessionSpec.tools` instead.
- An MCP tool's name is held to one rule wherever it is taken: `mcp:<server>/<tool>`, the server's name in lowercase letters, digits and `-` (at most 32, starting with a letter), the tool's in letters, digits, `_` and `-` (at most 64). The tool settings (`PUT /settings/tools`, an agent's `tool_settings`), a learned workflow's call nodes, a template's `mcp` tools and its eval fixtures now refuse a name the grant always refused (a `.` in a tool's name, a tool's name over 64 characters, a server's name with capitals, `_` or `.`), where before they took it and the agent could never be granted it. Who breaks: a settings key or template naming such a tool, which now gets 422 `not_allowed`; rename it to the server's listed name, or drop it, since no run could call it. Composio actions (`GITHUB_CREATE_AN_ISSUE`) are unaffected.
- A provider-native web search's fee is one constant, `NATIVE_SEARCH_USD` ($0.01, $10 per 1,000), instead of three copies. The price does not change.
  - Kernel: `@parcha/agentrun-kernel/host` exports `NATIVE_SEARCH_USD`. The Claude and Codex proxy policies and the runner's hosted search all read it.
  - `@parcha/agentrun-harness-claude` no longer exports `CLAUDE_WEB_SEARCH_USD`; read `NATIVE_SEARCH_USD` from `@parcha/agentrun-kernel/host`.
- An agent's desktop or phone can be driven by code alone or by tools alone, and can have no shell: `definition.computer` takes `surface` ("code" or "tools") and `exec` (false).
  - `surface: "code"`: the run gets its harness's script tool (pi's `codemode`, else `computer_script`) and the hand-over, and no `computer_observe`, `computer_act` or `computer_screenshot`. On pi, the `codemode` tool's description declares `computer` then, since no `computer_script` is listed to declare it.
  - `surface: "tools"`: the per-step tools and the hand-over, and no `computer_script` and no pi `codemode`. Absent, both, as before.
  - `exec: false`: the agent's card has no `exec` or `processes` group, so no tool or script has `computer.shell` or `computer.processes` (a script that reaches for one is refused in words), no folder is mounted in the computer, and the run has no `bash` or background tool anywhere, Archil's exec included. The run's own computer channel (`POST /runs/{run_id}/computer/call`) keeps every group.
  - Both are a desktop's or a phone's alone: on another kind, 422 `not_allowed`. GET /agents/{agent_id} shows them.
- A template parameter may be a list of a scalar, so a scheduled agent's scope (the companies it watches) is set once at apply and reaches each run as typed input.
  - `parameters.<name>` takes `type: array` with `items`, a scalar in the `inputs` vocabulary. Apply checks each item as an input's are, and the console asks one item a line.
  - A trigger's `target.input` value that is one placeholder alone (`"${parameters.companies}"`) takes the parameter's value with its type: a list stays a list, an integer an integer. One whose parameter was given no value, and has no default, is dropped, so the input schema sees the field absent. Before, every placeholder filled as text.
  - In text (instructions, display name, `content`) a list fills as its items joined by `, `, an empty one as `""`. Apply checks the filled `target.input` against the agent's input schema.
  - A pin value that is a list parameter's placeholder alone pins the list as a one-of.
  - An eval case whose `prompt.md` body holds its own `Input:` block is refused: the server writes that block from the case's `input:`.
- ask_person runs on Claude Code and Codex. A `claude-agent` or `codex` agent granted `ask_person` is no longer refused as pi's (`409 agent_not_runnable` with `details.unbound`, and the save's warning on the tool): the tool is bound as a host tool, its call passes the run's gate like any host tool's, and the run waits on the person as a pi run does. Its turn ends at the question, the run parks `input_required` with the question pending and the row saying "Waiting for your reply", and the person's answer resumes it as its next turn. A stop while it waits ends it stopped. `GET /v2/capabilities` lists every harness for `ask_person`.
- A learning agent now writes its whole job as a learned workflow in a compile turn, which replaces the ask that came after a skill had served 3 runs. The turn runs at the end of a completed run when the agent has 3 or more active notes or 5 or more completed runs, has no learned workflow active or waiting, and compiled nothing in its last 4 runs. It also runs when a workflow handed the run back, when the money rule stopped one, or when its promotion holds it (its replay on the agent's graded inputs, or its graded runs, fell under the bar); then it asks for that workflow's next version, and a held one's ask carries the replay's numbers. A held workflow is asked once per hold. The model gets the DSL's own author contract with this server's rules, one worked example (an extract step, a judge step when the run has a decision provider, a decide step, and an escalate step for a case the policy does not cover), the agent's notes, and the last 5 runs' tool calls, answers and follow-up messages. Every step gets a guard that starts at threshold 0.7. When the run can call Jev, judgment steps (decide, agent, judge, pick, sift) get `{"signal": "both"}` and extract and call steps get `{"signal": "jev"}`. Otherwise judgment steps get `{"signal": "self"}` and the others get no guard. For an agent with an output schema, the turn shows the schema whole as the shape the workflow's final output must have, and the dry run holds the draft's answer to it the same way a serving run shapes it, so a draft that answers one field where the schema asks for more fails its dry run in the schema's words. The draft goes through the static checks and then a dry run. Whatever they refuse goes back to the model, up to 3 more times.
  Every attempt is recorded. `GET /runs/{id}/learning` now always has `compiled` (the workflow, the notes it absorbed in `from_notes`, `attempts` with each one's `ok` and `errors`, the kept draft's `digest`, and `promoted`: true once its promotion record promotes it or a refit of it, false while held, null until decided; or null) and `draft_errors`, which holds the errors of a draft that never passed. A draft that fails also goes into the run's `problems`. When a compiled workflow merges, each note it absorbed gets `compiled_into: <workflow>` in its front matter and is still served to runs the agent does by hand. A run's own note may not set `compiled_into`. The end-of-run look-back no longer asks for a workflow draft. The DSL's `dryRunWorkflow` takes `onOutput`, handed the workflow's output when the dry run passed.
- computer-bench has a Linux desktop suite, `suites/linux-desktop`: ten tasks (five dev, five held out) in Mousepad, xfce4-terminal, Thunar and Firefox, two of them across two apps. Every task denies the agent `exec`; checks read the files, git config and server logs the work leaves, and every oracle is keyboard input only. All ten are verified live on E2B Desktop for seeds 1, 2 and 3 (untouched fails, solved passes), and the eight without Thunar on Agent37. Teardown stops only the apps its run started, by the pids setup kept. Setup places the windows with xdotool, puts the pointer on the one that takes the keys and activates it, so the tasks run with a window manager or without one.
  - serve's `--faux` desktop answers `ping`. computer-bench pings the computer after the agent's turn, so every bench run on a faux desktop was scored infra.
- A pi code-mode script's computer calls are on its `codemode` tool call's result row, as a direct computer tool call's are: one `computer_calls` record per call, each with its own `started_at`.
  - Each record also names the call's `app`, and each `ui.act` step the element it acted on (`on`: its role, and its name as the last observe read it, at most 60 characters), the chord it pressed (`keys`, only a chord with ⌘, ⌃ or ⌥, or named keys alone) and a `nav` place. A typed or set value is never kept. An element's name goes through the run's redaction.
  - Console: a step with computer calls shows how many it made and how many failed; open, each call in words ("select all (⌘A); type into the text box “Pears: 41”"), when it started after the first, and how long it took. `@timeline/computer`'s `callWords` gives the same words to any reader.
  - Breaking: a `computer_calls` record now always carries `started_at`; a reader of the old shape that built its own start time from the row's timestamp reads it from the record instead.
- An agent can open an app on a Linux desktop. Before, every app an agent started there closed right away, so a person watching the Screen tab on E2B or Agent37 saw a black desktop for the whole run. `computer.shell.run` passes no `DISPLAY`, and its command's guard ends everything the command started, `setsid` and `&` included. Two changes fix this:
  - `computer.processes.start(command, { cwd, env })` (on a computer with the processes group) starts a program that keeps running after the call. That program, and any app a launcher forks, runs until it exits or the computer ends. It answers `{ pid }`. In a run it is held to bash's setting, as `bash_background` is, so a read-only bash policy refuses it.
  - On a desktop whose hello names a display, the surface adds `DISPLAY` to the env of `shell.run` and `processes.start`, under the call's own variables. An app opens where the screen is, and a tool such as `xdotool` finds it.
  - The desktop-computer skill's Linux section says how to open an app.
- A Linux desktop has the `apps` group, as a Mac does: `computer.apps.open("mousepad")` and `computer.apps.list()` read the same on both.
  - computerd answers `apps.list`, `apps.launch` and `apps.terminate` on its X display. `apps.list` reads the desktop's `.desktop` files. `apps.launch` takes an id, a name or a program, starts the app with `DISPLAY` so it runs on after the call, and answers `{}` once the app's window shows, raised and focused. It answers `timeout` ("no window within 10 s") when none does. `apps.terminate` ends the app and waits until its windows are gone.
  - E2B's and Agent37's desktops start xfwm4 once the display is up (the host fact `HostFacts.windowManager`; Docker's desktops run none), so the apps an agent opens are framed and focused.
  - A desktop's init names its user (`agentrun-tool`) when the image has no passwd entry for it, as E2B Desktop has none, so the session bus xfwm4 needs and a terminal's shell work. A window manager that ends within a second of its start fails create in its own words.
  - The Agent37 box image (`agentrun-box`) adds xfwm4, Xfce's terminal, Mousepad, Firefox ESR and xdotool.
  - The conformance case `apps.launch-terminate` runs on any Linux desktop that lists Mousepad, Xfce's terminal or xterm.
- A computer step reads in one voice wherever a person sees it: a computer tool call's Timeline row, the step's computer call list in the console, and a Mac movie's caption all come from `@timeline/computer`'s `callWords`, in the plain past tense ("Opened TextEdit", "Selected all (⌘A), typed into the text box “Pears”", "Pressed “Save”", "Could not press “Save”"), the same on a phone, a Linux desktop and a Mac.
  - An app is named as a person knows it: "org.xfce.mousepad" is Mousepad.
  - The console's call list shows a failed call's code beside its words.
  - A `ui.observe` call that names no app is recorded with the app its answer showed, so its row and its call both read "Looked at Settings".
  - A step refused after an act's first three is still said ("…, +1 more, could not press “Save”"), not counted away.
  - Breaking: `computer_act` and `computer_observe` rows no longer show a typed or set text, a click's point or a scroll's direction, and `computer_observe` no longer names the window ("Looked at Settings", not "Looked at Display in Settings"): a row says what the call's record says. `callWords` and `stepWords` answer the past tense ("Opened TextEdit", was "open TextEdit"), and a failed call no longer carries its code in its words.
- A run on a desktop or a phone reads plainly to the person watching it.
  - The timeline says what the agent did on the computer: "Pressed “Display”", "Typed “dark”", "Went back", "Looked at Display in Settings", "Took a screenshot", a script's title. These replace "Using tool: computer_act". A finished act says only the steps that ran; a refused step reads "Could not press “Save”", and the act reads failed with the step and the reason. Typed or set text shows whole or not at all, and only for a step that names its field when that field is not a secure field; a type with no field of its own reads "Typed text".
  - An act's answer names each step's element as the outline does (`2. press @e31 generic "Display": semantic, verified`), `[secure]` by the element's own flag. An element with no name of its own, such as an Android settings row, takes the name of the first named element inside it. A type with no element names none.
  - While a new computer boots, the timeline says so ("Starting a phone from Phone harness…") instead of staying blank until "The phone is ready".
  - The console's Screen tab sizes a phone to the page's visible height, so the whole phone shows without scrolling. The live view says a hand-back once, in words that name the phone.
- The console's Learning tab now walks through the self-learning loop. A strip at the top shows five stages: the notes learned, the workflow they compiled into, the run where it took over, how much cheaper runs got, and where it is unsure. Each stage has a state and says what happens next ("1 of 3 notes, 0 of 5 runs: a workflow compiles at 3 notes or 5 runs"). The cost chart marks each promotion record on the run it first affected, with a lettered flag for a new revision, a promotion, a hold or a refit; the flags have a key, a hover and table rows. Replay runs are drawn as hollow rings and left out of the rolling mean. Runs with an unknown path or cost are counted in a chip. The headline gives the server's own before and after with the hand-back rate since the takeover. The learned workflow card says whether each revision is serving, served, refit, held or replaying, with the replay's numbers in one line, and how many replayed inputs were skipped because they need a write the recording doesn't have. It shows each step's guard on the step in the graph ("jev ≥0.70") and lists the guarded steps: how often each handed back, and each run's p split into right, wrong and not graded. A learning feed lists compile turns (the notes that went in, each attempt, and the checks' own words when a draft was refused) next to the promotion records. A note compiled into a workflow says so. New: `GET /agents/{id}/learning/loop` (the agent's compile turns and guarded steps, `agentrun agents get-learning-loop`), and each workflow revision now has a `digest`. Every count is over every run, never only the newest a read lists: the cost summary's `hand_backs` (since the takeover), and each guarded step's `right` and `wrong`; a replay run (its guards read at a record-only threshold) is counted apart in `replays`, never as a served run, and a step only replays ran has a null `threshold`. Each round a follow-up opened lists its own compile turn (`round`), and the cost per run counts every round's look-back and grade. A compile in the feed says Serving only for the revision that serves now, and Stopped when the money rule stopped it running first. A guarded step inside a composed child workflow reads its runs by the runner's `parent/child` name. A step's `grades_past` counts runs whose grade is no longer kept (the agent keeps its newest 500 grades), so an old revision never reads "none graded". An agent that learns notes only is promised no workflow.
- A saved MCP server's read says why a tool can't be granted, and a failed MCP save says it in the one credential word.
  - Each tool of GET /v2/settings/mcp-servers/{name} (and the save's answer) may carry `grant_problems`: why a grant of it is refused where it would run, in the words the save's 422 says. `*` is a refusal on every harness (its wire name `mcp__<server>__<tool>` is past the 52 characters every harness's tool names share); a harness id is that harness alone, whose own MCP client would drop or retype the tool's schema (claude-agent drops a tool whose schema's root has `anyOf`, `allOf` or `oneOf`). The console renders these words and keeps no rule of its own; it also disables a known meta tool (`grantable: false`) in the picker, with the server's reason.
  - A preview, save or refresh that fails now cuts every credential value and its bare token, of any header scheme (`Basic`, `Token`, `Bearer`), from the server's words, as a run's call already did; before, only a `Bearer` token was cut, and any other scheme's bare token a server echoed was shown. The cut text reads `[redacted]`, where the preview used to say `[credential]`. A credential value of any length is cut (a run's call used to leave one under 8 characters in the server's words).
  - One credential scrubber, one 4 MiB cap on an upstream answer and one SDK client setup now serve the probe and the run's gateway (packages/serve/src/mcp-wire.ts); every MCP read of the registry from the runner and the server goes through the sealed layer (mcp-store.ts).
- An agent's MCP tools are pinned when the agent is saved, not when a run starts.
  - Saving an agent (POST /agents, PUT /agents/{agent_id}/definition, an inline agent's first run of a version, a template's apply) lists each MCP server it grants a tool of, once, and keeps the granted tools on the new revision as the server listed them: name, title, description, input schema, annotations, and the prices set for them. Every run of that revision calls those tools, whatever the server lists by then. A call the server no longer takes as pinned is the server's to refuse, as before.
  - A save is refused (422, on the tool's field) when a granted server can't be listed right now (`The MCP server <name> could not be listed to pin its tools: ...`), or no longer lists a granted tool (`The MCP server <name> has no tool <tool>; ...`). Nothing is saved: save again once the server answers. Applying a template with a GitHub tool ticked, whose GitHub MCP server runs on the GitHub App's tokens, on a server with no GitHub App connected, is refused this way too (`... This server has no GitHub App: Connect GitHub in Settings.`), and nothing is made; it used to make an agent whose every run was refused when it started. Connect GitHub and apply again. An edit that grants nothing new from a server that can't be listed (its instructions, say) saves, keeping the agent's current pin for that server; only a tool new to that pin, or an agent with no pin yet, is refused. A server that keeps no credential of its own (`per_run`), or an OAuth server whose access token only a run refreshes, and that refuses the listing for its credential, is pinned as its last save or refresh listed it.
  - Saving the agent again re-pins: an unchanged definition saved after a server changed a granted tool is a new revision with the new tools; saved again with nothing changed, no revision.
  - GET /agents/{agent_id} and GET /agents/{agent_id}/revisions show the pin as `mcp_pin`: per server, the pinned tools and their prices (never the server's URL); null when the revision grants no MCP tool.
  - A run no longer lists an MCP server at its first claim. A run of a revision that grants an MCP tool its pin does not hold is refused before it starts (409 agent_not_runnable), and at its claim, saying to save the agent again.
  - A revision saved before this release that grants an MCP tool has no pin yet. Its first run pins it, once, as a save would (two first runs at once agree on one pin), and every later run uses that pin. This holds for an inline agent's (POST /runs) version stored before this release too. Nothing needs saving again. That first pin covers every server the revision grants a tool of, or none: if one of them can't be listed, or is no longer saved here, nothing is pinned, the run is refused (409 agent_not_runnable at its start; a run picked up at its claim fails) and the next run tries again, so saving that server again lets the revision run. A run picked up at its claim lists a GitHub MCP server that runs on the GitHub App's tokens with a token of the run's repository that can only read its metadata, revoked at GitHub once the listing is done.
  - The store upgrades itself in place. On SQLite the server's start adds the revision's pin column and drops the per-run pin table (the schema stays version 11, so the previous release's data directory still opens). Postgres migrates itself (migration 0011). A run that already existed (queued, or followed up later) pins its revision the same way at its next claim; its old per-run pin is not carried over, so it runs on the revision's pin.
- An agent with an `output_schema` is told the schema, and asked once more when its answer misses it, on every harness (pi, claude-agent, codex, opencode).
  - The runner appends the schema to the run's instructions: "End your final answer with exactly one ```json block that matches this JSON Schema:", then the schema.
  - When the final answer has no json block meeting the schema, the run gets one more turn in the same session, under the same cap: "Your final JSON did not match the output schema: <why>. Reply again, ending with the corrected json block." It is booked like any other turn and shows on the timeline as a server message. There is never a second retry, and a run that is parked or at its cap ends without one.
  - A completed agentic run whose answer still misses the schema serves `result.output: null` with `result.output_error`, why it missed. The TypeScript and Python clients carry the field.
  - The console's Report reads an agentic run's `result.output` with its revision's schema, not the answer's text: a string property marked `contentMediaType: "text/markdown"` renders as a Markdown section, at any depth, and a property's `title` names its field. A run that missed says why above the answer as written.
  - Templates: applying one no longer copies its answer schema beside a skill's SKILL.md, since the runner now gives the agent the schema itself. A template whose skill reads the schema as a file keeps it inside that skill's folder (code-review's `findings.schema.json` is now `skills/review/findings.schema.json`). The bundled templates' report fields (kyb's `report_markdown`, release-notes' `draft_markdown`, code-review's `summary`) are marked `text/markdown`.
- A pinned call now carries only what it may: a pin can fence an MCP tool's object argument to named keys, and a pinned tool takes only the arguments its listing declares.

  Object keys. `{"keys": ["hs_lead_score"]}` on a CRM update's `properties` lets an unattended write set that one field and nothing else.
  - The argument, when given, must be an object whose keys are all in the list. Any values are allowed. Leaving it out, or passing `null`, also holds.
  - A call that sets another key is refused before it is sent or asked about, under approvals `never` too, and the model reads `properties keys in (hs_lead_score)`.
  - When the agent's settings and the server's settings both pin the same argument to keys, only the keys in both are allowed. If no key is in both, every call is refused.
  - Templates can fill the keys from parameters (`{keys: ["${parameters.crm_score_property}"]}`). A key whose parameter is not given sets the tool to deny, as an empty pin does today. A key that is a list parameter alone adds each of its items.
  - Tool settings and template packages refuse a malformed keys pin with a message. The console shows a keys pin as "properties may hold only the key hs_lead_score (any value)".

  Undeclared arguments. Some servers take an alias for an argument their listing never declares: Slack's `channel_id` for `channel`, Gmail's `to` for `recipient_email`. A pin on the declared name could be walked around through the alias.
  - A call of a tool with a pin in either layer may carry only the top-level arguments its listing declares under `properties`, plus its pinned ones. The listing is the one the run pinned when it started, the same one its model is offered.
  - Any other argument is refused before it is sent or asked about, directly, through `tools_call` and from a codemode script, and the model reads "`to` is not an argument of GMAIL_SEND_EMAIL; a pinned tool takes only its listed arguments (recipient_email is pinned)." Templates no longer need to pin aliases to `null` by hand.
  - A listing with no `properties` object closes nothing. Tools with no pin are unchanged.
- A learned workflow's new draft or revision now serves first only after it is replayed on the agent's last 20 graded inputs and its accuracy there is within 2 points of the agent's on the same inputs. Grade a finished run with `PUT /runs/{id}/grade` (`{"correct": true | false, "expected"?: {...}, "source"?: "feedback" | "eval"}`); the grades the agent's runs carry are the inputs a replay uses. A replay starts one run per graded input the workflow fits, with `metrics.path` `replay` and `metrics.replay: {of, outcome}`, at the workflow's cost, and meanwhile the revision promoted last (the champion) keeps serving, or the agent when none was promoted yet. A replayed input the workflow hands back (it escalated: an escalate node or a guard) counts as the agent's recorded answer for it, never as a failure; one it failed on (a step failed) is no evidence and is left out of the score, and a replay with fewer than 5 inputs answered or handed back holds the revision. A replay run has the agent's tool credentials as a served run does: an MCP server's `per_run` credential is the one the claimed run was handed, sealed for the replay alone. A replay never sends a write: each tool is a read or a write (an MCP tool by its server's annotations, read only when `readOnlyHint` is true and `destructiveHint` is not; the built-ins `web_fetch`, `web_search`, `pdf_pages` and `llm` read; anything else writes). A read runs live once a replay, through a cache seeded from the graded run's recorded calls on the same tool and arguments. A write is answered from the graded run's recording when a call there has the same tool and arguments, else that input is skipped (`metrics.replay.outcome` `skipped_write`, with `skipped: {tool, step}`), neither right, wrong nor failed; a replay whose every input was skipped holds the revision, its reason saying it needs a write the recording doesn't have. A replay run runs only while its revision replays: a superseded, promoted or held revision's replay run, or one whose claim cannot lay its revision, ends failed without asking the agent. A replay's answer is right when it matches the grade's `expected` fields, or when it says what the graded answer said and that answer was right. With fewer than 5 graded inputs it fits, the workflow serves on its passing dry run, as before, and its record says so.
  `GET /agents/{id}/learning/promotions` lists each decision as `{workflow, digest, at, decided: "promote" | "hold" | "replaying" | "superseded", source: "replay" | "dry_run" | "refit" | "graded", reason, replay?: {of, n, agree, agent_acc, wf_acc, delta, handed_back, skipped_write}, runs?, refit?: {from, guards: [{node, was, threshold, fit?}]}, commit?, superseded_by?}` (`commit`: the learning commit holding that revision's workflow.json), and `serving: [{workflow, digest, replaying}]`: which revision serves and which one replays. A held revision never serves; the champion keeps serving, also on inputs the folder's revision no longer takes (a new required field). One revision replays at a time: the newest revision (the one the learning folder's main holds; a run pinned to an older commit never counts as newer) supersedes the one replaying, whose replay runs are cancelled (what they spent stays on them) and whose record says `superseded` with `superseded_by`. A wrong served grade asks for a revision and never stops the champion. Escalation never holds a workflow. Two things do: the money rule, and graded runs it served more than 2 points under the agent's graded runs by hand, checked once per 20 new graded runs it served (each grade carries a sequence number the check counts from, so the check keeps coming once the 500 kept grades are full).
  At that check, and when a replay holds, each guarded step's threshold is refit to the cheapest one that keeps the replay's accuracy within the bar (a hand-back its guard made, whose answer nobody read, counts wrong at a threshold that would have let it through, so a threshold never comes down on no evidence), and a `both` guard's `fit` is refit (a logistic over its self and Jev reads) when it has 30 graded rows with 5 wrong. A refit that moves a threshold commits the workflow as a new revision, promoted on the rows it was fit on; its money-rule count starts over.
  A run its learned workflow answered alone, on a CLI-shaped record, now reads its booked cost on `GET /runs/{id}` (it read `null`).
  Breaking: a learned workflow draft that gives two steps one label (a child workflow's step read `parent/child`) is refused at learn time and before a call, as a saved workflow already was (`DUPLICATE_LABEL`): a label names one step, its guard's threshold, replay score and refit included.
- A workflow step can carry a guard: `"guard": {"signal": "self" | "jev" | "both", "threshold": 0.7, "question"?: "...", "fit"?: {"w": [...], "b": 0, "n": 0, "fitted_at": "..."}}` on an agent, decide, extract, code, call, workflow, judge, pick or sift node. After the step runs, the host puts p, the chance the step is right, against the threshold. Below it, the run escalates at that step with kind `guard`. `self` reads the step's own confidence: an agent or decide node submits a `confidence` between 0 and 1 beside its record, kept at `<as>$confidence` and never in its value, and a judge, pick or sift node uses its weakest answer's (a sift's, over every item). `jev` asks Jev once about what the step was asked to do (`GuardStepParams.task`: its instructions, a judge or sift's questions, the schema of its `out`, a code node's code, a call's tool or command), its input and its output, each cut to a bounded length; a pick's input is what its judge chose among (its state, the candidates), a sift's its state and the items. `both` puts the two through the guard's fitted logistic, or takes the lower of the two when it has no fit. `validateWorkflow` refuses a bad signal, threshold, question or fit, and refuses `self` on a node that reports no confidence, with a message that says what to write. A host that runs guarded workflows passes `WorkflowDeps.guardStep`; a run without it refuses a guarded workflow before any node runs.
  In a learned workflow's call, a guard below its threshold hands the job back to the agent in the same run. The agent's input carries the trace and one line per guard: its signal, what it read, p and the threshold. Jev runs on the pinned model `jev-1.14.0` as a decision of the run, the way a decision node's is: the run gets the Jev key for a workflow whose guard reads Jev, the gate's setting for `jev` applies, and the call is admitted on the run's cap and counts toward the run's cost. A guard with no signal to read (no Jev key, `jev` set to deny, or a failed Jev call) hands back and never passes. A learning run's `metrics.guards` lists every check as `{node, signal, self?, jev?, p, threshold, escalated}`, including those of a map over more items than the call's trace keeps.
- A template package can be installed from GitHub: `POST /v2/templates/import {source, dry_run?, trust_publisher?}` reads `github:<owner>/<repo>[/<path>][@<ref>]` (or a `https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/tree/<ref>/<path>` address), resolves the ref to a full commit SHA first, downloads that commit's tarball from GitHub's hosts alone, and checks the package with the same checker the bundled ones pass. Nothing in it runs.
  - A dry run answers the package whole (its instructions and every skill file) and stores nothing. A stored import is listed by `GET /v2/templates` beside the bundled packages under its own id, `github:<owner>/<repo>[/<path>]`; importing the id again replaces it, and `DELETE /v2/templates/{id}` removes it.
  - The first package from a publisher (the GitHub owner) is stored only with `trust_publisher: true`; the server remembers the trust.
  - A link, a special file, an oversized package or archive, a redirect off GitHub, or a source on another host is refused, storing nothing. The server reads GitHub with its GitHub App's token when it has one, else anonymously, and its rate-limit error says which.
  - Each template in `GET /v2/templates` now has `id`, `bundled`, `source`, `sha` and `publisher`; `POST /v2/templates/{id}/apply` takes the id (a bundled package's id is its name, as before). An agent applied from a template carries `template: {id, version, sha}` (`sha` null for a bundled one).
  - CLI: `agentrun template install <source> [--dry-run] [--trust]` imports one and prints the console page that applies it.
  - Console: an "Add from URL" box on Templates and a `#/templates/install?src=` page that shows the publisher, the commit, the instructions and every skill file before anything is stored, with an "I trust <owner>" tick for a new publisher.
  - The store keeps imported packages in a new `imported_templates` table: on SQLite a server adds it at its open, with no schema version change; on Postgres it is migration 0010.
- One discovery system. A run lists every tool until its catalog tools (MCP and monid) pass 20; then they are deferred, found with `tools_search` and run with `tools_call`. Under 20 there is no search or call, and Claude Code's own tool search follows the same threshold and gets neither of ours. `codemode`, `tools_search` and `tools_call` each have a tool-settings key (allow by default); a tool set to deny is not offered at all.
- Every harness (pi, Claude Code, OpenCode and Codex) now offers three host tools over the run's own tools: `tools_search`, `tools_call` and `codemode`. Codex gets the first two and keeps its own code mode. With MCP servers on a Claude Code run, the CLI's own tool search is on.
  - `tools_search {query, limit?}` ranks the run's tools by what they do (BM25 over each tool's description and argument words) and answers each match's name, description and input schema. It lists only tools the run may call: never one set to deny, and never the three tools themselves.
  - `tools_call {name, args}` calls one of the run's tools by name. The call is asked about, recorded and booked as that tool's own call, under `<callId>/call`. An ask parks the run, and once approved the call runs once. A deny refuses it in the gate's words. A call of an unknown name, of `tools_call` itself, of `tools_search` or of `codemode` is refused in words, and nothing runs.
  - `codemode {script}` runs a JavaScript script in a QuickJS sandbox. Its `await tools.<name>(args)` calls are each the run's own call, gated, recorded and booked under `<callId>/s<n>`. The sandbox has the tools and nothing else of the run: no environment, keys, files, network or timers.
  - A call inside a script that needs approval follows Codex's rule. The run parks. Once a person answers, the script runs again: recorded calls answer from their records, the parked call runs once (or is refused), its outcome is the script's answer, and the rest of the script does not run.
  - A call made through `tools_call` or a script answers what a direct call answers: its text and images to the model, and in a script its value (a tool's structured result, else its text). On pi the harness's own tools (an extension's, the browser's) are found and called the same way as the host's.
  - A refused call inside a script ends the script with the refusal's words.
  - After a crash, a call that was cut off is told as possibly done, and it is not run again.
  - A paid call made through `tools_call` or a script books exactly as a direct call does: held before it is sent, under the cap, and settled once. The cap's wrap-up still refuses the model's own next call.
  - The three tools' definitions ride on every model request: about 2,000 bytes, 639 tokens on Sonnet. So the smallest caps the README measures rise. A pi desktop run on Sonnet through a gateway now needs $0.07 for its first request and $0.13 for five steps in `strict` mode, or $0.07 in `expected` mode (it was $0.06, $0.12 and $0.06). Straight to Anthropic, it needs $0.04 for its first request, and five steps still need $0.09 in `strict` mode and $0.06 in `expected` mode.
  - Claude Code: with an MCP server's tools on the run, the CLI runs with `ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH=true` and its ToolSearch. The run's MCP tools reach the model through `hands` only once ToolSearch finds them, and every other tool of the session loads as before. The session's proxy admits the tool search's beta (`advanced-tool-use-2025-11-20`), ToolSearch and its placeholder. It also admits a `tool_reference` block, inside a tool result only, that names one of the session's own tools. Without MCP tools, all of these stay refused.
  - A server started by `agentrun-serve` (and so by `npx agentrun`) can start a worker thread from a file. The launcher no longer passes Node `--input-type`, which a worker inherits and Node refuses. Before this, a `codemode` script there failed with "--input-type can only be used with string input via --eval, --print, or STDIN", and so did pi's code mode on a desktop or a phone.
- An agentic agent can take typed run input: `definition.input_schema`, a JSON Schema object, and every run's `input` is checked against it with the full compiler before the run starts.
  - Every path that starts a run checks it the same way: `POST /v2/agents/{id}/runs`, the CLI, the clients, the MCP `runs_start` tool, a trigger (when it is saved and when it fires), a template's trigger at apply, and the console. An input the schema refuses is `422 input_invalid`, one issue per field, by path (`input.country`, `input.topics.1`) and reason (`missing`, `wrong_type`, `not_allowed`, `not_an_option`, `bad_format`, `too_short`, `too_long`, `too_few`, `too_many`, `duplicate`, `invalid`).
  - `content` is always a string. It is required when the schema requires nothing else. An edit that leaves `input_schema` out keeps it. A workflow agent refuses it (its workflow's own input schema is the one in force).
  - The model is sent the input's `content`, then the other fields as one fenced `json` block under the line `Input:`, on pi, claude-agent and codex alike. A value holding backticks gets a longer fence, so no value ends the block.
  - Templates: a package's `inputs:` (the parameter vocabulary plus `title`, `examples`, bounds and lists of a scalar) compile into the agent's `input_schema`, shown on `GET /v2/templates` as `input_schema`. A template's trigger input and each eval case's `input:` front matter are checked against it.
  - The `kyb` template takes its subject as typed input (`company`, and optionally `website`, `country`, `registration_number`, `reason`), matching its report's `subject.input`. An agent applied from it before keeps its own definition. A newly applied one refuses a run without `company`.
  - Console: an agent with an `input_schema` gets a run form drawn from it, with the same field renderer as the template parameter form, and its issues shown on the fields.
- A template's webhook trigger may filter its deliveries by a parameter, as a github trigger already could.
  - A `${parameters.<name>}` may go in the `in` values of a webhook trigger's `accept` where conditions, and apply fills it. The parameter must be required or have a default, so the filter never fills empty.
  - A provider that sends every trigger of a project to one URL (Composio) then starts a run only for the repository the owner set: `{pointer: /data/repository_name, in: ["${parameters.repo}"]}`. A delivery for another repository is answered `200 {"ok": "ignored"}` and starts nothing.
- A learning agent now starts a run on its learned workflow before its own model takes a turn, when exactly one active learned workflow fits the run's input. A workflow fits when its input schema has a required field and the run's input passes that schema. If the workflow answers, its answer is the run's answer and the agent's model is never asked. For an agent with an output schema, the answer is shaped to it first: an object output as it is, a one-field output (a bare code or a line of text) as the schema's object with that field, fenced as the answer's json block so `result.output` meets the schema; an output that cannot meet the schema goes back to the agent with the schema's complaint. If it hands back (an `escalate` node holds, a node fails, or its output fails its schema), the same run goes on to the agent, whose first input says which step handed back and why, what the workflow had, and then the job. The run's `metrics` say which path it took: `path` is `workflow`, `handed_back` or `agent`, with `learned_revision`, `workflow` and `workflow_digest`. Its cost includes the workflow's model nodes. A handed-back run's end-of-run turn asks for the workflow's next revision by its name. The reflect prompt asks that a workflow take the run's input as the run is given it, and that its model nodes name tier `fast` unless a step needs the agent's own judgment.
  A handback is an escalation, not a failure, and never stops a workflow from serving. One money rule does: a workflow runs first while its mean all-in cost over its last 10 runs served at its current version (its `workflow_digest`) stays under the agent's cost by hand, the mean all-in cost of the agent's `agent`-path runs (with none, of its runs before the workflow first ran). All-in is the run's `total_usd` on the cost page: its own cost plus every learning round booked for it (look-backs and grades). A run whose all-in cost is unknown is left out of the mean and counted (`unknown_cost_runs` on each workflow), never read as 0. Fewer than 10 such runs, or no by-hand cost at all (said in the log), and it serves. At or over the line it no longer runs first: the agent takes the run, the run's journal keeps why with the two numbers, its end-of-run turn asks for a new version of the workflow, and `GET /agents/{id}/learning/cost` lists it under `workflows` with `state: "needs_revision"` and both means (the console's Cost per run says so). A new version serves again from zero. The rule does not catch a workflow that answers wrong with confidence. The run's `metrics.path` is the one path the agent's cost per run (`GET /agents/{id}/learning/cost`) shows, including for a run whose agent called the learned workflow itself. `learned_workflow` set to ask still parks the run before any node runs. Set `workflow_first: false` on a run to send it to the agent from its first turn.
  A follow-up to a run its workflow answered goes to the agent with the job, the workflow's answer and then the message, and the run's `path` becomes `handed_back`. A follow-up to a served or handed-back run looks back as a learning round of its own, as on any run that learns.
  A learned workflow with a name only a workflow may have (such as `sort_invoice`) gets its revision ask like any other.
  A message sent while the learned workflow runs first waits for it without holding up the run's other commands: a later stop or cancel cuts the workflow at once, and a raise or hand-back reaches the run while it runs. As with any stop, a message sent before it is the run's next turn; a cancel refuses it.
- A capped run no longer prices a request as if nothing were cached after an approval, a deny, a raise or a smaller request of its own, and a Codex or Claude Code run no longer has a tool call refused with "Budget nearly spent" while the request that asked for it is still streaming and the cap has room for both.
  - The recent requests: the cap keeps the session's answered requests of the last 4 minutes and prices each request from the one on its model with the biggest body no bigger than its own. A smaller request between two of the conversation's own (Codex sends one while a tool runs; a summary, a child's) no longer resets the history, so the conversation's next request stays warm. Before, a $0.50 Codex run's next request after one was priced all fresh, held all that was left, and was told "About $0.43 left of this run's budget: finish now" on a $0.08 job.
  - Resume: the recent requests are kept with the run, so the first request after a new claim is priced from them, warm when they ended under 4 minutes ago and uncached after that, the same rule as inside one claim, on every harness. Before, a $0.15 Codex run paused after a deny with "needs at least $0.22": its next request was priced all fresh.
  - In flight: a CLI harness's request is now sent with the most output whose worst case still leaves the run's wrap-up reserve (one typical step and one least answer) free, so a call it makes mid-response finds room. A $0.50 Codex request that held $0.36 and a $0.12 bound at its whole 32,000-token ask is now sent with fewer tokens, and its call passes. When the request's least and the reserve do not both fit, it is admitted as before, with the most what is left buys, and a call it makes is refused for the reserve as before. pi starts a tool only once its response is complete, so its requests are sized as before.
  - The cap's guarantees are unchanged: no request is held past what is left, a warm price that guesses wrong costs at most the request's bound beyond its hold (as any cache miss under `expected`), every hold settles to what the request cost, and turns sum to the run's cost.
  - Kernel cap (private, not in the package's index): `ModelCapRequest.previous` is `recent` (a list of `RecentRequest`, was `Previous`), `previousOf` on `beforeRequestOf` and `runCap` is `recentOf`, and `previousAfter` is `recentAfter`, with `warmFrom` picking the request a price reads. `JudgeState.keepUsd`, and `keepBackUsd` on `beforeRequestOf` and `runCap`, tell the rule what the host keeps back beside a request.
- A learning run on a CLI harness (claude-agent, codex, opencode) whose runner died or lost its claim during the end-of-run look-back no longer pays for that look-back twice on the next claim. The next claim settled nothing: it resumed the open look-back as if it were the job's turn, threw its answer away, and then asked the CLI again. Now the open look-back is settled and asked again once, under the run's cap, and a request the earlier attempt sent is booked once at an unknown price. The run's learning also keeps the job's cost and answer time from the first attempt, so the earlier attempt's spend counts as look-back spend instead of job spend.
  A look-back the next claim skips (its spend unknown under a cap, or the cap reached) keeps the job's cost and answer time from the first attempt, its look-back spend unknown rather than missing. A look-back a person stopped no longer makes a later claim settle the follow-up after it: that follow-up's turn is recovered and answered.
- A computer's `process.start` call reads "Started a process" in the console's call list and a movie's caption, not the raw method name.
- The live view's bar wraps on a frame as narrow as a phone's on the Screen tab, so who drives ("the agent has the phone") is never clipped at the frame's edge, and Take over stays on one line.
- The console's Screen tab shows who drives and the first frame when they happen. It used to show them up to 3 s late. It read the run's computer every 3 s, so the header kept saying "Yours after the agent's step" for up to 3 s after the viewer said "you have the computer". A hand-back's answer, read before the run applies it, kept "You drive" up as well. Measured live on E2B and Agent37, the header followed the viewer by 1.6 to 3.3 s. The tab now reads again every 400 ms while a change is on its way: while the screen is being opened, while a take-over waits for the agent's step, and for 4 s after the page's own take-over or hand-back. Otherwise it keeps reading every 3 s. A take-over's or hand-back's answer reaches the tab when it comes, no longer after the run's re-read that follows it. An ask's Done and Cancel stay off once the answer is taken, until that re-read takes the card away.
- An agent's cost per run (`GET /agents/{id}/learning/cost`, `agentrun learning cost`, the console's Cost per run) now counts only the agent's own runs, and no longer shows a run as the agent's at $0 when its cost and path are not known. A follow-up's end no longer queues a learning run beside a kept learning that names none, so a `<run>-learning` row never shows up in the series as an agent run. A grade's spend stays booked as its run's `learning_usd`, inside the run's all-in cost. A run's end now waits up to 30 s for its cost and path, not 2 s: with eight runs ending at once, some ends were written without them. An end that still gets neither within that bound writes both as unknown (null) and never keeps what an earlier end stored. The series leaves out a run that learns but has no path on its record, and counts it in the new `unknown_path_runs` field. The console says "N runs' path and cost are not known: left out."
- A desktop with no ui group (E2B's, Agent37's) can be driven by the tools alone, and its first screen no longer reads as broken.
  - `computer_observe` and `computer_act` with `app` open that app, or bring it in front, before the screenshot or the input (apps.launch, as a script's `computer.apps.open` does). A screenshot with no app in front lists the app ids to name. Before, a tools-only agent had no way to open an app there. Such an observe counts as an app opening. While the person holds the desktop it waits, then is not done. After a crash it is not run again.
  - The desktop's background is one slate colour (xsetroot, run before xfwm4), not black. Agent37's desktop recipe (`box/build-agent37.mjs`) adds x11-xserver-utils for it; rebuild `agentrun-box` once.
  - `computer_act` offers no `expect` on a desktop with no ui group, which can't check one: its schema there has none, so a model is no longer offered a wait that is then refused.
  - `GET /v2/runs/{run_id}/computer` on an ended run says `session: "closed"` for its desktop or phone, and for a browser step the run ended under, not `opening`.
  - A provider's label takes its article: "an E2B sandbox", not "a E2B sandbox".
- A run starts sooner: a runner in the server's process claims a new run as soon as it is queued (it waited up to a second for its next poll), and a run's first claim makes its desktop, phone, sandbox or browser without first asking the vendor to list older computers of the run (there can be none). On a fake desktop the time from the run's start to the vendor's create went from 0.78-0.93 s to 0.07-0.11 s; on a vendor's desktop it also saves that vendor's list round trip.
- Behind serve's gateway (`AGENT_MODEL_BASE_URL`), pi sends a Claude model on Anthropic's Messages API (`<base>/v1/messages`) instead of OpenAI's Responses API, so its prompt cache works: the second turn of a run reads the prompt from cache, where every turn used to pay full input. Every other model stays on the Responses API.
  - A model is Claude's when its id names Anthropic as its vendor (`anthropic/claude-sonnet-5.5`, or a revision's `anthropic/...` with bare gateway ids), or names no vendor and pi-ai's catalog lists it under Anthropic (`claude-opus-5-5`). The gateway must serve `/v1/messages` beside `/v1/responses`, as LiteLLM's proxy and OpenRouter do; its key goes as a bearer token, as on Responses.
  - Cache reads and writes are booked at the model's own rates (the catalog's, or the 3rd and 4th numbers of `AGENT_MODEL_PRICE`), so the run's cost is the sum of its turns. With `AGENT_MODEL_PRICE` set for a Claude model, give its cache write price (Anthropic's is 1.25 times input): left out, a write is booked at the input price.
  - The same route serves a learned workflow's model nodes and the learning grader on a Claude gateway model. Claude Code, Codex and opencode send as before.
- The console's template install and Apply screens say what a package does before you take it: each typed run input (its label and name, what it takes, Required or Optional, its description, in the run form's words), its eval cases by name, and on the install screen each MCP need with the reason the template gives and the tools it asks for. A required text field sent empty (`""` where `minLength` asks for more) is now refused as missing (`input.company is required`, reason `missing`), so the run form says "Company is required"; an optional field or a list item keeps its length issue. A source path with a `%` that starts no escape (`github:…/k%ZZb`) is refused by a sentence that names it; a `github:` source takes no percent escape (each is named), since its source is stored and linked as written. An install refusal shows its sentence once.
- The kyb template's report uses one set of names for its subject: `subject.input` is the run's typed input as the run received it.
  - `subject.input` holds `company`, `website`, `country`, `registration_number` and `reason`, the names of kyb's inputs, with their values as given; a field the run did not get is left out. It held `name` and `domain`, with nulls and a `reason` of `unspecified` filled in by the skill.
  - The kyb skill copies the input block whole; its field-by-field mapping is gone. An agent applied from the earlier kyb keeps the output schema it was applied with.
- A saved MCP server's credential is sent only to the address it was saved with. Listing a saved server (preview by name, refresh, a first run's pin listing, a save or a sign-in that keeps the saved credential) reads the server, then checks its address and waits for the listing. If the owner saved the server at another address with a new credential during that wait, the new credential could be sent to the old address. Each of these now opens the credential of the server as it read it.
- In Mode 2 (run folders on an Archil disk), a Modal, E2B or Agent37 sandbox is no longer shown as ready. It needs Archil's image in your own vendor account, which this server can't put there yet, so it failed at its start. Settings → Computers says so, `capabilities.computers` leaves the sandbox out in Mode 2, an agent's save warns in the same words, and a run's start refuses it (409 `agent_not_runnable`) before any computer is made.
- On Postgres, the store's pool connections are named for their schema in `pg_stat_activity` (`application_name` `agentrun-store:<schema>`), as its lease (`agentrun-store-lease:<schema>`) and owner lock (`agentrun-store-owner:<schema>`) connections are, so an operator can tell which store holds each connection. Before, every pool connection was `agentrun-store`.
- A learned workflow held because its replay could not run an MCP tool now says which tools and why. Replay runs an MCP tool live only when its server marks it `readOnlyHint: true`; a tool listed with no annotations was treated as a write the graded run's recording lacked, so every input was skipped and the hold read like a data problem ("needs a write the recording doesn't have"). The hold now names those tools: "nothing was replayed on its 20 graded inputs: browse, fetch_page and 2 more have no readOnlyHint, so replay can't run them: if they only read, mark them read-only in the MCP server". A destructive tool or a built-in write keeps the old words. A promotion record's `replay.skipped_tools` lists each tool that stopped an input, how many it stopped, and `no_read_only_hint`. The console's Learning tab says what a promoted workflow was decided on beside its standing ("Serving · replayed 18/20", "Serving · not replayed" for a dry-run promote, which is no longer shown green, "Held · 0 replays answered"), and a replay line names the tools with no readOnlyHint.
- A capped Codex, OpenCode or pi (on OpenAI's Responses) run's next-step estimate is closer to its real input, so it pauses for a raise later and less often: the input bound counts the text the model reads (a tool's output, a message, a call's arguments) at its own bytes instead of its JSON-escaped ones, some 4 to 6% less on a code-mode body full of fetched pages, which keeps more requests under the 272k-token long-context tier where every rate doubles. On a route straight to OpenAI the input is counted exactly by OpenAI's `POST /v1/responses/input_tokens`, asked with only the credential and account headers and never through a gateway; a count that fails or takes over 3 seconds leaves the byte bound. The cap still never spends past itself: tool definitions and encrypted reasoning keep every byte.
- The console's Screen tab and run badge read right at a desktop's or a phone's start and end, and a script's refused shell call on a phone says what to do instead.
  - A desktop or phone that was live and is let go at the run's end reads "This desktop has been released." until the run reads as ended, never "Waiting for the desktop".
  - A queued run whose desktop or phone is starting reads Starting, not Queued.
  - The Screen tab has one Take over (and Hand back): the one in its header. The viewer framed there (its fragment says `hands=page`) shows neither, nor a second line of who drives; a phone's bar keeps its back, home and recents buttons. Opened on its own, the viewer keeps its bar.
  - A script's computer call that the agent's settings refuse starts with what could not be done and where ("could not run a shell command on the phone: …"), says why in a person's words, and what to do instead. On a phone that is the phone's screen (`computer.observe`, `computer.act`), never the bash tool, which does not run on a phone.
- Applying a template grants only the MCP tools the owner ticks. A tool left unticked is not given to the agent at all, so no harness offers it and a call of it is refused before it reaches the MCP server.
  - Before, an apply gave the agent every tool of each saved MCP server the template uses and set only the ticked ones to allow. Under approvals `never`, which four of the five bundled templates default to, the unticked tools then ran unasked too.
  - `never` only skips asking for a tool the agent was granted. To use a tool left unticked, grant it later in the agent's tools.
  - A template's pin on a tool is still written when the tool is unticked, so it holds if the owner grants the tool later.
  - The apply's GitHub App permission warnings name only the tools the owner ticked.
  - The console's apply screen says that an unticked tool is not given to the agent.
  - Under approvals `ask` too, an unticked tool is no longer offered and asked about on each call: it is not granted.
  - An agent applied from a template before this release may still hold every tool of its MCP servers. Review its tools (or apply the template again) and remove the ones you did not mean to grant, above all on an agent set to `never`.
- A `monid.run` approval card shows its price, on every harness.
  - Before, the card for a `monid.run` call asked for approval with no price, although the call is held at a known figure.
  - The card now shows what the call is held at: the price an `monid.inspect` in the run quoted for that endpoint, else the $1 allowance a run with no quote is held at. It is the same figure the run's cap and ledger count the call at.
  - Other tools' cards are unchanged.
- Four tool-plane fixes found by a QA walk of the tools.
  - Behavior: a call waiting for your approval whose tool you then set to deny is refused, and the run says why. The record keeps your answer: an allow sent after the deny is taken and kept as the answer the setting overrode. The call's rows read "Not run: its tool is now set to deny on this server", its approval row reads "Denied by the tool's setting on this server", and the outcome reads "You allowed <tool>, but it is now set to deny on this server, so it was not run". Before, the rows said the run had ended while the call waited and the ask was withdrawn, and the allow was never recorded. The refused call ends as an error on every harness, as before.
  - Behavior: Settings → Tools lists each saved MCP server's tools, read from the MCP servers list, with the permissions the server offers for each (allow, ask, deny). The owner sets a server-wide permission for a tool, and choosing its default again removes it. A server's `mcp:<server>/*` wildcard shows as its tools' default. Tools the server offers no permission for (the meta tools) are not listed.
  - Behavior: a call you allowed, or one its setting allowed while it waited, shows what it did and its result like any call once it ran, with "(ran once you allowed it)" or "(ran, as its setting allows it)" after its result. It no longer reads "Held for your approval" after it ran. A declined call still reads "Held for your approval".
  - Behavior: on Claude Code and OpenCode, `tools_call` and `codemode` each have their own row ("Using tool: tools_call", "Ran a script") with their result, as on pi, and the calls they make read after it.
- Serve's per-process spend engine in `cap.ts` is gone: the run's one ledger (the kernel cap) holds every model request and paid call, so nothing reads the process-wide spend any more. `cap.ts` keeps what the store readers and the refusal words use: the cap modes, `spentFrom`, `meterFiguresFrom`, `money` and the refusal code. No public export changes.
- A codex or opencode turn cut by a park (a host tool call held for a person's approval) is booked at the usage its provider reported. Before, the park closed the session while that answer was still streaming, its booking was lost, and the next claim booked the turn cut at an unknown price, so the run's cost read `unpriced`. A park now waits for the session's paid requests to be booked before it lets the claim go, as a run's end does (bounded; past the bound the turn is booked cut, and the spend cap counts it at its hold).
- Three follow-ups to the tools_search / tools_call / codemode rule, found in a live walk.
  - Claude Code now follows the same switch as every other harness. With `tools_search` or `tools_call` set to deny, its own tool search is off and every tool is listed; before, it deferred a run's catalog tools behind its own ToolSearch whatever the setting said. The server makes the one decision (`SessionSpec.deferCatalog`) and Claude Code's adapter obeys it.
  - Settings → Tools lists `tools_search`, `tools_call` and `codemode`, each allow or deny, allow by default. They are in `capabilities.tools` with `meta: true` (no grant: the agent editor does not offer them) and a one-line blurb.
  - codemode's description names real functions of the run (`tools.<name>`, the first three) and says to leave off the prefix a harness shows in the model's own tool list (`hands_`, `mcp__hands__`). On OpenCode a script wrote `tools.hands_mcp__hn__…` five times in five runs and failed.
- On pi, a script's or `tools_call`'s nested calls now show in the run's timeline, as they do on every other harness. A script now reads a nested call's JSON result as a value.
  - Behavior: on every harness, `codemode` and `tools_call` each have their own row, and each call they make has its own row with its result after it. A nested call that waits for your approval shows its approval row, as a direct call does. On pi the nested calls were missing from the timeline: only the script's row showed. They are now written to the same call records Claude Code, OpenCode and Codex runs write, and those records do not count toward pi's model requests or cost. A nested call still waiting when you stop the run reads "Not run: the run was stopped while it waited", as on the other harnesses.
  - Behavior: in a `codemode` script, a nested call's value is the tool's structured result when it has one. Otherwise, when its result is one text part that parses as a JSON object or array, the value is the parsed object or array. Otherwise it is the text, as before. What the model sees from the call does not change.
- A paid tool call books on the run's one ledger or is not sent. A `monid.run`, a search or extract through Parallel (`web_search`, `web_fetch`) and a browser call or a person's browser time that find no run's ledger to book their price under are refused unsent, in words that say so (`monid.run was not sent: this call has no run to book its price under.`), as a priced MCP call already was. Before, each of them was sent and booked off the ledger, against a per-process spend count the run's cap never read. Every run the runner drives has a ledger, so its paid calls book and refuse exactly as before.
  A learned workflow's web nodes (`web_search`, `web_fetch`) now book on the run's ledger like the run's own calls: the run's cap holds their price before they are sent and refuses one that would pass it, in the cap's words.
- A tool this server does not register defaults to ask, not allow; the tool list is one table.
  - Before, a name that was neither a table tool nor a catalog tool (`monid.<tool>`, `mcp:<server>/<tool>`) defaulted to allow in `defaultPermission`. Now only a built-in (a row of the tool list, `learned_workflow`, a computer kind's key, a decision provider's) allows by default and anything else asks. No tool of today's table changes: the capabilities and agent-tools views are the same.
  - `replay`, `blurb`, `host`, `askable` and `table` are fields of each tool's row in `tool-list.ts`; `TABLE_TOOLS`, `ASKABLE`, `REPLAY`, `TOOL_BLURBS`, `webToolNames` and `tool-blurbs.ts` are gone.
- A trigger's message that reaches a run just as it comes to wait on a person is now delivered after the person's answer, as a turn of its own, whenever it lands. Before, one that reached the runner between the question's turn end and the park (or while the run waited in its claim) was refused and never ran, while its firing still read `sent`.
- A run's usage row reads the same on every harness, and says what an owner needs to know about its cost.
  - A run that ended says "Cost: …" in the Timeline and the run's view; only a run still going says "Cost so far: …".
  - Claude Code, Codex and OpenCode runs count their tool calls with no price ("; 1 tool call not metered", and `usage.not_metered`), as pi runs did.
  - A model request that failed with no price (a provider's refusal sends none) says on its row that its cost is unknown and the provider may still bill it. Its cost stays unknown, never $0.
- A capped run on a CLI harness (Codex, Claude Code) prices its next request from the cache its previous request left warm, at admission, for the wrap-up note and for the room it keeps back to answer, so it is no longer told to finish, or refused a tool call, while what is left still buys many of its steps.
  - Before, a CLI's request names its model as its provider does (`openai/gpt-6.1-sol`, `claude-sonnet-5-5`) while the cap prices it under the run's model id (`gpt-6.1-sol`, `anthropic/claude-sonnet-5.5`). The session's previous request was filed under the first and looked up under the second, so every request was priced as if nothing were cached. The note and the reserve never read the previous request at all, on any harness.
  - Example: a Codex run under $0.50 was told to finish with $0.45 left, because its next request was priced at $0.23 all fresh; read from the cache, it needed about $0.05.
  - Admission's rule is unchanged: a request whose least does not fit what is left is refused. A request with no previous one in hand (a run's first, or one after a compaction) is priced uncached, as before. A CLI request on a warm cache is now held at its warm price, as pi's already was.
  - Kernel: `capRequestOf` builds a request as the cap prices it (its model, and the session's previous request when it continues the conversation, looked up by the priced model's id). `RunCap.asked(request)` returns it with the run's own pricing. `beforeRequestOf` uses the same function.
- The learning batch restart test no longer ends now and then with the batch `stopped: cost_unknown`. Its in-process runner stopped with no drain, so a stop that landed while a row's model request was out cut it, that request's cost stayed unknown for good, and the batch stopped on the row as its cap rule says. The CLI's runner drains at a stop (`--drain-timeout`, 30 s by default), so a turn in flight finishes and is booked; the test's runner now drains the same way.
- monid is granted per endpoint: `monid:<provider>/<endpoint>` (one endpoint, such as `monid:apollo/people/match`) or `monid:<provider>/*` (every endpoint monid lists for that provider, at most 50). The tools `monid.discover`, `monid.inspect` and `monid.run` are gone: an agent that grants one is refused at its save (422 `not_an_option`), and its owner grants the endpoints it calls instead.
  - Each grant is read against monid's listing when the agent is saved, and pinned on that revision with the endpoint's description, its input schema and its price. A provider or endpoint monid does not list is refused at the save in words, and so is any monid grant saved with no monid key (Settings → Tool keys). An endpoint whose input schema the agent's harness would drop or retype (Codex's `patternProperties` or `not`, for example) is refused at the save as an MCP tool's is, naming the endpoint and the schema's path.
  - Each pinned endpoint is one tool of its own on every harness, under its wire name (`monid:apollo/people/match` is `monid__apollo__people__match`). Its input is `{body, queryParams, pathParams}`, as monid's endpoint takes it.
  - The gate and tool settings key a call by its endpoint (`monid:apollo/people/match`), or by the provider's wildcard (`monid:apollo/*`). A monid endpoint asks by default.
  - A call is held on the run's ledger at the endpoint's pinned price: a per-call price, the dearest variant of a matrix, or a tiered price's default plus every tier. It is sent with that hold as monid's `maxCost`, so an endpoint monid has re-priced above its pin is refused unrun. Its price is read again from monid before each call, and an endpoint monid has re-priced by usage since the save is refused unsent. The approval card shows that hold, and the charge row names the endpoint: "Tool cost: monid charged $0.0260 for monid:apollo/people/match".
  - An endpoint monid prices by usage (per result, per unit, metered) cannot be granted: monid bounds no such call's charge, so no hold could keep a run's cap. A named grant of one is refused at the save, naming the endpoint and why; a provider's wildcard leaves it out and names it in the save's `warnings`.
  - A workflow's nodes do not bind monid endpoints yet: a workflow granting one is refused at its save.
  - Template packages may grant monid endpoints in `tools`, pinned at the apply's save.
- The console's agent editor grants monid endpoints. The Tools step has a monid row: type `monid:<provider>/<endpoint>` for one endpoint, or `monid:<provider>/*` for every endpoint of a provider that monid prices per call, and Grant. The row checks the name's shape as the server does and says what is wrong before a save; the save still reads monid's listing and prices and is the judge of the rest.
  - An agent's monid grants show on the row, each as a card. Untick one to take it away; it stays on the row to tick again. An edit that does not touch them keeps them.
  - After a save, what the server said of a grant (each endpoint a wildcard leaves out, because monid prices it by usage) shows on the row and above the form, in the server's words. These no longer read as things that keep the revision from running.
  - A save refused at a grant (an endpoint priced by usage, a provider monid does not list, no monid key on the server) shows the server's reason on the row, beside the grant.
  - The agent's page that opens after a create shows the create's warnings in the server's words.
- `agentrun-serve eval-template` runs its agents with approvals `never`, whatever the package's own `approvals`, so a template whose tools ask by default (a paid data endpoint, say) is measured instead of stopping at its first ask. The package's default is unchanged. The report says how it was measured: `approvals: {measured: "never", package: "ask" | "never"}` in the JSON, and "Measured with approvals never (the package's own default is ask)." in the markdown.
- A grade is now the way a label reaches a run's learning, and a label never makes the agent answer the job again. `PUT /runs/{id}/grade` takes `label` (the grade's words, up to 4000 characters) and answers `feedback`: a right grade of a run its learned workflow answered alone is kept and nothing more (`null`, no model request, $0); a wrong one opens the run again on a revision ask for that workflow (`revise`): the agent's end-of-run turn alone, told the job, the workflow's answer and the label; a run the agent finished, graded with a `label`, opens again on a look-back on it (`look_back`). Neither round runs a turn of the job's; the label shows on the run's Timeline as the reviewer's message.
  A run's path is who wrote its final answer: a run its learned workflow answered stays `workflow` after a feedback round or a follow-up that ends on the same answer, and turns `handed_back` only when the agent writes a new or changed one.
  The cost per run (`GET /agents/{id}/learning/cost`) counts every round of a run a follow-up or a grade opened again: the job is what the run cost when its first round answered, and everything after it (each later round's turns and every round's look-back) is its `learning_usd`. It read the newest round's look-back alone and counted a follow-up's turn as the job's.
  Upgrading: a client that sent a label as a follow-up message (`POST /runs/{id}/messages`) sends it as the grade's `label` instead.
- Allow reads: one switch on a saved MCP server lets each of its read-only tools run with no one asked, while its writes keep asking and a destructive call takes a second click to allow.
  - A tool's effect comes from its server's annotations: read when `readOnlyHint` is true; else destructive only when `destructiveHint` is true; else write (no annotations included, which still asks). The MCP spec's default reads a tool with no `destructiveHint` as destructive; this does not, since every tool of a server that annotates nothing would then need two clicks. A saved server's read gives each tool's `effect`, `allow_reads: true` on a tool whose allow is its server's Allow reads, and `fallback_allow_reads: true` on a read-only tool that Allow reads would let run once its own setting is removed.
  - `allow_reads: true` on an MCP server's wildcard (`mcp:<server>/*`) in the server's tool settings (`PUT /settings/tools`) turns it on; `false`, or leaving it out, turns it off. An agent's own tool settings, or any other key, refuse it (422). It never lifts a deny (the server's or the agent's), the agent's own ask, a tool's own setting (`mcp:<server>/<tool>`) or a pin's refusal.
  - Turning Allow reads on releases a read-only call already waiting for approval: the save wakes its run, and the call runs, its approval row reading allowed by the setting. A write waiting beside it keeps waiting.
  - The run's gate reads each tool's effect from what the run pinned when it started, never from a later listing, so a server that marks a tool read-only mid-run widens nothing for that run. An agent's read (`GET /agents/{id}`) gives each MCP tool's permission by the same marks, the ones its revision pinned when it was saved, so it says what that revision's runs do after a refresh changes them.
  - A destructive call's approval carries `destructive: true` in the run's `pending`, and allowing it needs `confirm_destructive: true` beside the decision (without it, 422 on `confirm_destructive`, and the call still waits). A learned workflow's call is marked the same way when its card names a destructive MCP tool, since its one allow lets that tool run. A deny needs nothing more.
