  - Console: Settings, MCP servers shows the Allow reads switch on each server, its tools with a read, write or destructive mark and their permission here (an allow by Allow reads reads "allow (allow reads)", never "default"; a read-only tool set to ask there falls back to "allow (allow reads)", so choosing allow removes its own setting instead of saving a permanent allow), and asks a second time before a destructive tool is set to allow, there and in an agent's tool settings. An approval card marks a destructive call, and its Allow once asks again before it sends the allow. Closing either second question (Back, Keep asking or Esc) puts the keyboard back on the control that opened it. A server's tool settings save one change at a time: a destructive tool's allow waits while a save is out, so two saves never write the whole map over each other.
- A learned workflow's replay records an escalate that reads a judge's field instead of obeying it, and its refit may switch that escalate, or any guard, off. A replay that hands back every input is held: it would never answer alone.
  - In a replay, an `escalate` node whose `when` reads a field of a `judge` node's output (`not` included) no longer stops the run: the workflow goes on to its answer, and the run's guard rows carry the escalate (`signal: "escalate"`, `p` 0 when it fired) so the replay scores it as a hand-back where it fired. Every other escalate stays hard in a replay, and serving obeys every escalate.
  - The refit keeps its rule (the cheapest setting within 2 points of the agent) and now has "off" among its settings: an escalate or a guard that stops right drafts is dropped from the new revision, one that stops wrong drafts stays. It runs when a recorded escalate is the workflow's only switch. The refit record's `guards` say what changed: `{node, was, threshold: null}` for a guard switched off, `{node, was: null, threshold: null, escalate: true}` for an escalate.
  - A replay or refit that handed back every one of its inputs is held, with the reason "it handed back every one of its N replayed inputs: it would never answer alone". The console shows how many inputs it answered alone, counted from the record (`n` - `handed_back`): "replayed 20/20 · 9 alone".
  - DSL: `WorkflowDeps.softEscalate(label)` makes the named escalate record its `escalate.evaluated` event (`soft: true`) and go on instead of handing back; a child workflow's escalate is asked by its `parent/child` label.
- Four fixes from the computer milestone's QA: the live view keeps moving while an input batch waits, a script on a vendor desktop may start a process, the linux-desktop bench's count-errors and new-note tasks need their apps, and a computer row on the Timeline says what failed in the same voice as the rest.
  - computerd: a watch's look no longer takes the display's hold. `input.actions` holds the display for its whole batch, waits included, so the live view made no frame for a batch's length (0.3 fps through a batch with waits on E2B). A look's requests all have replies, which go to their own waiter, so it never needed the hold.
  - Serve: a `computer_script`'s calls are decided as on the run's computer. The script guard used the run's host-tool gate, whose `computer` flag says where `bash` runs; on a vendor desktop (shell "none" or "local") that gate denies `bash_background`, so `computer.processes.start` was refused while `shell.run` ran. A script's calls always run on the computer, so they now take the computer's defaults: allowed unless the agent's own settings (`bash: ask`, `bash: deny`) say otherwise. A script's `shell.run` on a vendor desktop under approvals "ask", with no `bash` setting, now runs where it was asked before.
  - Bench: `exec: "deny"` takes programs away, not the files group, so both tasks could pass with `files.write` alone. `linux.terminal.count-errors` (version 2) gzips its log, so counting it takes a program, and its probe asks for gzip and zgrep. `linux.editor.new-note` (version 2) also checks that a Mousepad window is titled with the saved file's name, and its instruction says to leave Mousepad open. The report no longer says an exec-deny task's agent "worked through the UI"; it says the agent kept the files group.
  - Timeline: a failed computer row reads "Could not run the script “…”: …", "Could not take a screenshot: …", not "… failed: …". Firefox ESR and Chrome are named "Firefox" and "Chrome". A no-ui `computer_observe` row names each call it made: "Opened Mousepad, took a screenshot, listed the apps".
- Deleting a Composio preset server in Settings → MCP servers also deletes the MCP server the preset made in your Composio account, using the saved key, so nothing is left behind there. Composio saying it is already gone is fine; if Composio refuses or does not answer, the server is still forgotten here and the answer (`200 {deleted: true, composio: {removed: false, note}}`) and the console say what to remove in Composio yourself. Any other server is deleted as before (204).

  Saving a Composio server whose picked actions Composio serves none of (HACKERNEWS_GET_FRONTPAGE, say) now answers 422 naming those actions, instead of a bare 424 "Method not found", and the server it made on Composio is removed again. Only the server's own "Method not found" answer says that: Composio's MCP server being down, slow or erroring still answers 424. A preset server whose saved key can't be opened here is still forgotten, and the answer says to remove it in Composio yourself. The Composio server is deleted only after our row's checked removal succeeds, and is the one that row named.

  The generated TypeScript and Python clients now type an operation that documents 204 beside a 2xx body as the body or nothing (`X | undefined`, `X | None`).

  Saving a preset server over to another address (an ordinary save with a different URL) makes it that service's server, no longer Composio's: deleting it never sends the key it holds to Composio, whatever the new path looks like, and the delete is an ordinary one (204). The Composio server the preset made stays in your Composio account until you remove it there.
- A desktop or phone deleted under a live run (through the vendor's own API, say) now reads "This desktop has been released." on the run's Screen tab, and Take over goes. Before, the tab kept reading "LIVE The agent drives" with Take over until the run ended, because the run's viewer stayed registered after its computer was gone.
  - When the viewer's watch ends gone, or can't start because its computer is not found, the runner reads the computer's provider's listing under the computer's own labels (`list`: read-only, and it leaves out a machine that is going). If the computer is not listed (or, for a phone, which is never stopped and kept, is listed stopped: its session closing), the view closes "released": its row is dropped, so `GET /v2/runs/{id}/computer` stops answering `live`. Measured live, the tab read released 2.6 s after the delete on E2B and 14.9 s after it on Agent37 (3.4 s after the computer's not_found, which waits on the 15 s SSH keepalive bound).
  - A stream that ends while the provider still has the computer leaves the view as it is, so the tab still shows the run as live.
- The Learning tab no longer says "replayed 20/0" for a promotion record that names no replayed runs; it says "replayed 20".
- In Mode 2, an E2B or Agent37 desktop is no longer shown as ready. Like their sandboxes, it would mount the run's folder and needs Archil's image in your own vendor account, which this server can't put there yet. An E2B desktop failed at its start after a computer was made. Settings → Computers now says so, an agent's save warns in the same words, and a run's start refuses it (409 `agent_not_runnable`) before any computer is made. Orgo's desktop, a phone and a browser mount nothing and run as before.
- market-monitor's digest header names the window's `from` date on every harness: its skill now has a worked example (fired 2026-11-09 with a lookback of 7, the header reads `2026-11-02 to 2026-11-09`). Before it, a Codex run could start the header at the first day that counts.
- A long answer through an OpenAI Responses gateway that writes its JSON with spaces is priced, a request that answered while its runner's claim was lost is booked at its cost when the run resumes, and a run whose spend is unknown never reads as a full cap to its learning.
  - Before, the model proxy read a long answer's usage (its terminal event longer than the 64 KiB it keeps) only when the gateway wrote `"usage":{` with no space. A Python gateway (LiteLLM's `json.dumps`) writes `"usage": {`, so such a request was booked at an unknown cost though the harness counted its tokens: the run's cost read unknown with nothing unmetered. pi on the gateway, Codex and OpenCode read the usage the same way and are all fixed. Kernel: `lastObjectOf(text, key)` reads the last `"<key>": {...}` object of a cut answer, whatever its spacing.
  - Before, a runner that lost a run's claim (its lease lapsed while the box stalled) and took the run again in the same process booked a request that had answered meanwhile as cut, at an unknown cost: the lost claim's write of its cost was refused, so the resumed run read the request unanswered. The run's cost read unknown though the request reported its usage on a priced model. Kernel: `SessionWriter.scope` names a session across claims in one process (serve's `journalSessions` sets the run's id beside the key); a booking whose cost write is refused hands it to the next booking of the same scope, whose `bookCut` waits (at most 10 s) for one still in flight and writes it as it would have been written. A request with no price stays unpriced and counts for the cap at its hold. A process that died hands nothing on: its requests are booked cut, as before. A workflow run's model booking now takes them too: its claim books an earlier claim's requests before the workflow resumes, where before it never did, so a workflow's request that answered under a lost claim stayed counted at its hold.
  - Before, a run cancelled or stopped while its model request was being admitted could still send that request: the proxy forwarded it after its client had left, nothing stopped it, and it was booked only once the provider ended it, after the run had ended, so the run read the request as cut at an unknown cost. The proxy now books such a request at nothing (never left) and never sends it, so a run cancelled before any request reached the model costs $0. A request that reached the model and was cut keeps the cut rule: unpriced, counted for the cap at its hold.
  - Before, a capped run whose shown cost was unknown gave its learning grade a cap of $0 ("Not graded: no room under the cap.") and its look-back a reached cap. The grade's cap and the look-back now read the run's spend as its own cap gates read it: an answer with no price counts at the figure the cap held for it, never $0 and never the whole cap. Only when that figure is unknown too, the grade is not queued and says why: "Not graded: this run's spend is unknown, so its budget can't cover the grade."
- After a grade's feedback round, or a person's follow-up on an ended run, the Timeline shows the round's rows first and then the learning row ("Learned: …"), as it does after a server restart. Before, the live Timeline kept the learning row where it was when the run first ended, above the reviewer's words.
  - The timeline's change log now serves rows in the order the run's rows come in: a row the rows now hold after a row served later than it gets a new `seq`, sent as a change, so a reader from a cursor and a fresh read from `after=0` agree. The usage row still goes last.
- A call that waited for approval now reads in the order it happened, on every harness: the call, then the "Asked your approval" row, then the call's result, then what came of it. The approval row carries the time the approval was asked (the run's `pending.requested_at`), not the time of the call's result. Before, it sat below the result and carried the result's time.
- A monid call that monid charges more than the run held for it now stops the run at once. The charge is booked at what monid charged, never the hold; the run makes no further model request or tool call and ends failed with the error "monid charged $X, more than the $Y held; the run stopped"; and the runner logs one error line naming the run, the endpoint and both amounts. A charge at or under the hold behaves as before. monid's maxCost checks only its estimate, so this can happen when monid re-prices an endpoint between the price check and the call.

## 0.1.0-beta.37 (2026-11-13)

- The `bwrap` box id is removed from the box enum: it was never in a release and always reported itself unavailable. A place of `{ "mode": "sandbox", "box": "bwrap" }` is now a 422 `not_an_option`, and `capabilities.places.boxes` no longer lists it. A client that named `bwrap` picks `docker`, `modal` or `daytona` instead.
- Pair a person's own computer with the server: Settings → Computers → Pair a computer shows a code (`POST /v2/computers/pairings`), the computer's driver, on any OS, trades it for its own token (`POST /v2/computers/pair`, no server token; a driver whose hello serves no kind of computer is refused, naming what it lacks, and so is a browser driver, whose CDP connection the attach path cannot carry yet; `POST /v2/computers/pairings` answers the pairing's `id`, which the computer its code makes carries as `pairing`, so the console tells its own code was used) and attaches over `GET /v2/computers/attach` (a WebSocket, subprotocol `agentrun.computer.0.2`), and an agent whose computer is `{"kind": "desktop", "provider": "<its cmp- id>"}` uses it: a run claims it at its start and releases it at its end or its lifetime. `GET /v2/computers` lists the paired computers under `paired` as their drivers' last hellos say (os, device, screen, groups, features, and `unserved`, why one serves no kind), online or offline, with the run that holds one and when that hold ends, and `DELETE /v2/computers/{computer_id}` removes one, closing its connection. Only the runner beside the server can use a paired computer. `node dist/attach-conformance-cli.js` runs the binding's conformance cases against any driver that pairs with the code it prints.

  Who breaks: the store's schema is version 10 (SQLite) and Postgres gains migration `0008_paired_computers`, so a SQLite store an older build made is refused at the start as a version this build does not know; start on a new data directory. `GET /v2/computers` answers a required `paired` array.
- The phone harness's Android is driven by phoned, a driver that runs on the phone, in place of adb shell commands. Breaking: an `adb` option given as a transport of your own must now offer `open(service, { timeoutMs, transport })` beside `run` and `server`, and a package built from source needs `npm run build:phoned` (a JDK 17 and an Android SDK with `platforms;android-35` and `build-tools;35.0.0`) for `dist/phoned.jar`, or the provider's `phoned` option naming the jar.
  - phoned (`packages/computer/daemon-android/`) is plain Java built with javac and d8, no Gradle, into one dex jar. `connect()` pushes it to `/data/local/tmp` under its sha256 when the phone lacks it, starts it as the shell user through `app_process` (scrcpy's way in, credited in `daemon-android/NOTICE-scrcpy.md`) on adb's `exec:` service, and speaks the protocol to it over that socket. Its hello is its own: protocol 0.2, the screen in points, `device`, and each feature on or off with the reason.
  - On the phone: `ui.observe` straight from UiAutomation (rows named from their texts, zero-size nodes dropped, refs stable while the element lives) and `ui.act` by accessibility actions or injected input, settled on accessibility quiet and a new frame and read back before `expect` is checked; `input.actions` through InputManager, a pinch, key combos and holds included, and Unicode text through the clipboard; `screen.shot` and `screen.watch` scaled on the phone; `apps.launch` with a deep link; `exec.run` as the shell user (the `exec` group). A screen marked secure is refused `denied` in words.
  - `apps.launch` answers once the app's window is on the screen and still (its open animation done), or `timeout` after 10 s in words that name the windows the tree shows. `ui.observe` and `ui.act` never wait: an app with no window is `not_found` in words that name the windows the tree shows. A window's bounds are its root element's, in the space of its elements, the screen and input, which is not always the space the accessibility service reports windows in.
  - One phoned answers every connection to a phone (UiAutomation is one per phone). Closing a connection cancels its own calls; the last close ends phoned, then drops the adb transport.
  - The server image builds phoned after the daemon, with Temurin 17 and the Android SDK's files (zips from Google pinned by sha256) in its build stage alone, so the image's phone provider has `dist/phoned.jar`, and checks it (`npm run check:phoned`: a dex jar stamped with the package version). CI's `phoned` job, outside the verify gate, sets up the same toolchain itself (`.github/actions/android-toolchain`: Temurin 17 and the same pinned zips), builds and checks the jar, and runs `npm run test:phoned`.
  - `npm run test:phoned` runs phoned's JVM tests and the TypeScript client against its real core over a scripted phone, the conformance suite's phone kind and Full ui cases included.
  - The ui fixture as an Android app (`packages/computer/fixture-android/`, `npm run build:ui-fixture` for `dist/ui-fixture.apk`, signed with a debug key made for each build). The provider's new `apks` option installs APKs on each phone before phoned starts; a conformance run installs the fixture when it is built, and its notes say when it is not.
- The computer protocol 0.2's follow-up: create is idempotent by a required request id, a driver whose hello lacks a group its kind needs is refused, `apps.launch` answers once the app has a window, and `ui.act` waits for windows, follows them when one closes, and answers a `set` verified only when its value holds. Breaking: `ComputerProvider.create` takes a required context, `{ requestId }`; `UiActResult.state` is optional, and an act whose app has no window left answers `window: "closed"` with no state.
  - Idempotent create (`CreateContext`, `computerNameFor`): one computer per request id, named `computer-<12 hex of sha256(request id)>`; the same id while it starts or runs answers it, and after it ended is refused `exists`. Serve passes the run's claim (`<run>#<epoch>`). The Full cases `provider.create-retried` and `provider.create-after-release` check it. The providers that make computers keep it through one helper, `CreateRequests` (creates in flight shared, requests ended remembered): the hosted adapter, Docker (a retry whose `docker run` finds the name taken answers that container), the phone harness (its ledger read by name, and an `Idempotency-Key` derived from the request id) and the fake ui provider. The attached provider keeps it for the computer a pairing holds. A fake ui computer's network is fixed at create (a change is `refused`).
  - Breaking: a phone-harness ledger entry (`PhoneLedgerEntry`) carries the computer's `name`, and a phone's ref is `{ id: <session id>, name: computer-… }`.
  - Breaking: a `PhoneLedger` (and serve's store ledger, `ComputerLedger`) has `claim(entry)`, a put only while no entry has its id, in one step: a phone create claims its request before its POST, so a create of the same request with another spec, from another provider on the same ledger, is refused `exists` before it can send the request's key. A Docker computer carries `agentrun.computer.labels` (its spec's label keys) and `agentrun.computer.attempt` (which create made it): a retry that drops a label is `exists`, and a create cut off during `docker run` removes only what it made.
  - phoned answers `expect.window` (the app's main window, a phone's windows all of role `window`).
  - Computerd for macOS keeps the same `ui.act` rules: `expect.window` (which needs no tree), `window: "closed"`, one final view for a set's hold and the expect, and `UiWindow.role` from the window's AX role and subrole (a sheet, dialog or floating panel is `"dialog"`).
  - The refusal kinds are `ComputerErrorCode`, with `vendor` the only open one: `invalid` is a malformed request, `unsupported` a call or feature the provider lacks, `refused` a value or state it does not serve, such as a network change after create on a remote computer.
  - `kindServed(hello)` answers the groups a hello lacks for its kind (a desktop needs `screen`, `input.pointer` and `input.keys`; a phone `screen`, `input.touch` and `apps`). The attach binding closes such a driver `4426` naming them, and the Core case `health.kind-served` fails it.
  - `DAEMON_METHODS` lists every method the daemon answers.
  - `apps.launch` answers once the app shows a window, or fails `timeout` naming the app after `LAUNCH_WINDOW_MS` (10 s); the Core case `apps.launch-window` observes right after the launch. The fake ui driver takes `windowAfterMs`.
  - A node's bounds are clamped to its window (`insideWindow`).
  - A settle compares the window's nodes, and its image only when it has none, so a blinking caret no longer holds every act to `MAX_SETTLE_MS`.
  - A `set` answers `verified: true` only when its value still holds in the act's final view: at least `SET_HOLD_MS` (500 ms) after the settle, and after the expect's last settle. A set's hold, the expect and the answered state all read that one view.
  - `expect.window` (`{title?, role?}`) waits for the act's app's main window to match, from its first look (never the window a target or state aimed at), and answers its state; none in time is `unmet`. `UiWindow` gains `role` (`"dialog"` for a sheet, alert or panel).
  - A step that closes the act's window hands the act to its app's next main window; with none left the act answers `window: "closed"`.
  - The fake ui driver's windows are its own objects: each owns its screen, history, values, switches, focus and pending effects, and closing one cancels its effects.
  - The ui fixture gains "New window", "Close" and a "Code" field that takes its value back, with the Full cases `ui.settle-tree`, `ui.set-holds`, `ui.expect-window`, `ui.window-closed` and `ui.window-follow`. A fixture with one window per app leaves out "New window", and the window cases skip.
- The computer protocol is 0.2: a new `ui` group sees one app's window as named elements (`ui.observe`) and acts on it by short lists of steps that settle before they answer (`ui.act`), and `hello` says the screen's size and what the computer can and cannot do (`hello.screen`, `hello.features`). Breaking: the `apps.ui_tree` group and method are gone, replaced by the `ui` group; read a screen's elements with `ui.observe`, whose nodes are a flat list with refs, ARIA roles and bounds in window points, in place of the nested tree.
  - `ui.act` steps: `press`, `set`, `perform`, `click`, `type`, `key`, `nav`, `scroll` and `drag`, by ref or at a point read from a state, with an optional `expect` checked on the computer. Each step answers the route that ran (`semantic`, `page`, `background`, `foreground`) and whether a readback verified it. A ref whose element is gone, or a point whose window changed under it, is refused with the new error kind `stale`, and a step on a disabled control, a type into a ref that is not a text field, or a type into a field that did not take the focus with the new kind `refused`.
  - `hello.features` names what is on, or off with the reason (`ui.tree`, `ui.image`, `ui.background`, `ui.foreground`, `ui.page`, `ui.nav`, `apps.background`). With `ui.tree` off, `ui.observe` answers the window's image with no nodes and says why in `empty`. `hello.device` names the machine (`maker`, `model`), and a node's `desc` carries what else it says beside its name and value. `apps.launch` takes `url` (a deep link) and `background`.
  - `@parcha/agentrun-computer/fake-ui-driver` answers `hello`, `apps` and `ui` over the wire from scripted apps (the ui fixture by default), in process (`fakeUiConnection`, `fakeUiProvider`) or on stdin and stdout. The conformance suite's new `ui` cases run on the ui fixture: `ui.hello` (Core) and, where the fixture is installed, observe's shape, refs that survive, an expect met and unmet, stale refs and points, the route each step took, a click never verified unless it landed, and each feature on doing what it says and off refused with its own sentence.
  - `UiSession` calls `ui.observe` and `ui.act` with their types on one target and carries the last state to a step at a point; `findNodes` and `refusedStep` read their results.
  - The attach binding is specified as a draft (`spec/computer/attach.md`): a driver dials `wss://<server>/v2/computers/attach` with a token it got by pairing a code from the console, and the same messages travel as WebSocket text frames. A driver of another protocol version, or a hello missing a field the server reads, is closed `4426` with words that say how to update it; any build within the protocol is accepted. A hello not answered in 10 s (`ATTACH_HELLO_MS`) is closed `4408`. `AttachHub` and `attachedProvider` are its server side, written against an `AttachSocket` interface; serve's routes come later. A run's ref names its hold (`<computer id>.<hold>`): its release ends only that hold, and the hold ends at the run's `lifetimeMs`.
  - `UiEngine` implements the group's rules over a `UiSource`; the phone harness's Android answers `ui` through it, over uiautomator and adb's input (foreground only, unverified).
  - agentrun-serve's phone tree tool reads `ui.observe`; its nodes' roles are ARIA names (`button`, `textbox`) in place of Android class names.
- Every harness sees a desktop or a phone through one surface: the tools `computer_observe`, `computer_act`, `computer_screenshot` and `computer_script`, the same answers from a script, an MCP client or a tool call. Breaking: the `desktop_*` and `phone_*` tools are gone, replaced by the `computer_*` tools (a desktop's and a phone's alike, held to the `desktop` or `phone` setting), and the script API's `apps.open(id)` returns nothing; bind the app with `computer.app(id)`.
  - `computer_script` runs JavaScript in an isolate in serve whose only binding is `computer` (no network, no keys, no timers); its types are `spec/computer/computer.d.ts`, generated with the tools' schemas by `scripts/generate-computer-surface.mjs` (`--check` in CI). A model reads them compactly (no comments, one line a declaration); `computer_act`'s schema types its steps with no words, and its description declares them as TypeScript.
  - A script's `computer.shell` and `computer.files` are held to the run's tool settings as the `bash`, `write` and `read` tools are (a deny or a read-only bash policy refuses inside the script; a setting that asks refuses, since a script can't wait for a person), and a refused step throws in the script, so the steps after it never run. Without the ui group a scroll goes as wheel clicks (about 120 pixels each), which every driver takes.
  - pi offers its code mode (`codemode`) beside its tools with a desktop or a phone, `computer` bound in its scripts; the call is held to the computer kind's setting.
  - In Codex's code mode a script's call of a computer tool answers the tool's value as JSON, its images' data in it; any other tool answers its words and a line saying its images were not sent (in code mode an image reaches a script only as text). A call a script repeats after a restart, of a computer tool that completed, gets that same JSON again.
  - agentrun-serve's `computerMcp` serves a run's computer tools to an MCP client, each answer with `structuredContent`.
  - The desktop-computer and phone-computer skills teach the route: observe, act by ref, check, and one script for steps already known.
- Serve's file-era decision and run-database readers are gone: `decisionSpentIn`, `DECISION_COST` and `DECISION_HOLD` (cap.ts), `durableDecisions` (workflow/readers.ts) and all of run-db.ts (`readRunDbSync`, `observeRunDbOpens`, `runDbTestHooks`, `ChangedReadError`, `BehindReadError`, `MonotonicReads`); none was in the package's public entry point, and a workflow decision's spend is read from the runner's journal (`sessionSpendOf`), its receipts with `readDecisions` or `decisionsOverStore`.
- A run's live view (its browser, desktop or phone, watched and taken over) works when its runner is on another host than the server, as in the compose stack's server and runners. Breaking for a SQLite store: its schema version moves to 9, so a server refuses a SQLite store an earlier version made; start it on a fresh data directory. A Postgres store migrates itself (migration 0007). A runner names the host the server reaches it at (`AGENTRUN_RUNNER_LIVE_HOST`, listening there or on `AGENTRUN_RUNNER_LIVE_BIND`), and each viewer's row in the store carries that host (a new nullable `computer_viewers.host`). The server dials a row's host only when it is one of its runners' (`AGENTRUN_RUNNER_HOSTS`), and signs each request it makes of the viewer with an HMAC under a key derived from the seal key; a runner's viewer off loopback refuses, before any WebSocket, a request with no good, fresh proof for its own viewer, and the viewer's token still decides who watches. The hop between server and runner is plain HTTP, for a private network. With neither setting, every viewer stays on loopback as before. `@parcha/pi-browser`'s `createLiveView` takes `listen` (the address its own server listens on and the host its links name) and `admit` (a host's own check of every page request and upgrade).
- Security: an MCP server's credentials stay out of what anyone reads, and its address is held to the private-address rule at every door. Breaking, three ways:
  - An MCP server on loopback (a `127.0.0.1` or `localhost` URL) is taken only by a server started with the new `AGENTRUN_MCP_ALLOW_LOOPBACK=1`, which says this is a local install; it is never inferred from where the server listens. Without it such a URL is refused at the save, the preview and the sign-in, in words naming the variable, and runs never reach one. To upgrade: on a machine you alone use, start AgentRun with `AGENTRUN_MCP_ALLOW_LOOPBACK=1`.
  - An MCP server's URL is shown on every read (the list, a server's read, a save's answer, errors) as its origin and `/…`: its path and query are held as a secret, sent only to the server itself. Sending the shown URL back for a saved server keeps the saved one. A client that read the whole URL back reads its origin now.
  - A saved MCP server whose URL names a credential-like parameter in its query, or sits on a private network the owner hasn't listed, is refused from this release on (its preview, tools refresh, sign-in, and a run's claim). To upgrade: move a query credential into the server's Headers, and add a private host you use to the MCP private-hosts list (PUT /v2/settings/mcp-servers/oauth/private-hosts, which now covers the server's own URL too) over https.

  And:
  - A URL whose query names a credential-like parameter (`token`, `api_key`, `secret`, `signature`, `password` and the like) is refused at the preview, the save and the sign-in's start: "<name> in the URL's query looks like a credential; send it as a header instead (Headers)."
  - The server's own URL goes through the same private-address rule as its sign-in's endpoints, at the preview, the save, the tools refresh, the sign-in and, on the runner, every request, dialled at the address checked: a private-network host only when the owner lists it, over https; link-local and cloud metadata addresses never; a 6to4 address judged by the IPv4 address it carries.
  - A claimed run's calls follow the server's row: a server removed since is refused unsent, a replaced credential is the one sent, a token another run refreshed is the one sent, and an access token near its end is refreshed before the call. Removing an OAuth server revokes its refresh token at its authorization server (RFC 7009, best effort).
  - Every credential value a run's MCP opens, refreshes or mints joins the run's one redactor, so it is cut from its logs and errors as well as from its tool answers.
- Orgo finds its workspace from the saved key: `ORGO_WORKSPACE_ID` is no longer required. With it unset, an Orgo provider reads the key's account's workspaces (`GET /workspaces`, deleted ones skipped) and uses the one there is; with several it refuses in words naming them, and with none it says to make one at orgo.ai. Settings → Computers offers the Orgo workspace as a picker by name once `ORGO_API_KEY` is saved, and saving a pick stores its id under `ORGO_WORKSPACE_ID`, read through the new `GET /v2/computers/{provider}/choices` (`listComputerChoices`). A provider view lists such keys under `picked`.
  Breaking: Orgo's `workspaceId` option is optional (`COMPUTER_ORGO_WORKSPACE` too, for the conformance run), and a server whose Orgo account has several workspaces and no `ORGO_WORKSPACE_ID` saved now has its Orgo runs refused until one is picked in Settings → Computers.
- The outbound webhook (`/v2/settings/webhook`) keeps everything in the one store, on SQLite and Postgres alike, and refuses a private address: the server no longer reads or writes `DIR/webhook.json` or `DIR/webhook-outbox.json`, so a webhook saved before this release is not set and its pending messages are not sent. To upgrade, let pending webhooks drain, then set the webhook again with `PUT /v2/settings/webhook` and give your receiver the new secret it shows once; the two old files can be deleted. A receiver on this machine or a private network is refused unless the operator sets `AGENTRUN_WEBHOOK_PRIVATE_TARGETS=1` where the server starts.
  Its URL is a store setting, its secret is sealed in `trigger_settings` (on a runner's redaction list, as the other sealed settings are, and a secret replaced or removed stays on it across restarts), and its messages, their tries and the run notices it told are in the channel tables (Postgres migration 0006, SQLite schema version 8). The server says once at its start when an earlier build's file is left (`condition=webhook_left_over`).
  The run notices follow the store's run-change feed, so a run that starts and ends between two reads, or whose end cannot be read for a while, is still told once.
  A URL is refused at its `PUT` when it is on a private network or this machine, by address or by what its name resolves to, and each try dials the address it checked. A `PUT` that changes the URL makes a new secret and shows it once (the same URL keeps its secret, and one that no longer opens under the server's key is replaced and shown); the URL and its secret go live together, so a `PUT` the store refuses leaves the webhook as it was. `GET /v2/settings/webhook` and the log show the URL's origin and its last four characters, never the whole URL.
  A run that asked a question sends `run.needs_input` once for it: the answer's take clears the run's waiting summary for a reopened run that parked on a question too, and a wait's `webhook-id` comes from its ask, never from the row the run shows last.
- An owner can drive a run's computer from anywhere, and a run can hold its computer for its owner.
  - POST /runs/{run_id}/computer/call `{ method, params }` sends a running run's sandbox, desktop or phone one computer protocol call and answers what the computer answered, verbatim. The call is a command row the run's runner answers: it waits while a person holds the computer, as the agent's calls do, and a runner beside the server answers in about 10 ms (a runner in another process finds the row at its next command poll). A method outside the computer protocol is refused. The call's params (text it types, say) leave the store once the call settles. The route takes the owner's token or session, never a run's.
  - `hold: true` on POST /agents/{agent_id}/runs (an agent's run, not a workflow's) claims the run's computer and waits, the agent not started, until POST /runs/{run_id}/start; after the agent ends, the run keeps the computer until POST /runs/{run_id}/computer/release, or until `hold_minutes` (default 30, at most 120) pass with no call from the owner. A stop of a held run ends its agent and keeps the computer the same way, and the run ends `stopped` at the release; a cancel ends the run at once and lets the computer go. GET /runs/{run_id} says where the hold is in `computer.held`, and the Timeline says each change. A benchmark sets a task up, starts the agent, checks the computer after, then lets it go.
  - Each tool call's computer protocol calls are on its `tool_result` Timeline row as `computer_calls`: method, outcome, time, error code, and for `ui.act` each step's kind, route and readback. No param value, no screenshot bytes, no typed text.
  - GET /runs/{run_id}'s `computer.state` reads `taken_over` while the owner holds the run's desktop or phone, and `ready` again after the hand-back.
  - **Breaking for a SQLite data directory.** The store's SQLite schema is now version 11 (a command row keeps its answer). A server or runner of this release refuses a data directory an earlier release set up, with `SchemaVersionUnknown`: start this release on a new, empty data directory and add your agents, MCP servers, keys and sign-ins there again, or keep the old directory with the earlier release. A Postgres store migrates itself (migration 0009).
- Settings → MCP servers has a Composio preset: give a Composio API key, a toolkit and the actions to grant, and the server has Composio make a managed MCP server and saves it as an ordinary MCP server with the key sealed as an `x-api-key` header. It is `POST /v2/settings/mcp-servers/composio/tools` (the toolkit's actions) and `PUT /v2/settings/mcp-servers/{name}/composio`, both the owner's session alone; a toolkit that needs the person's account answers `connect_url`, Composio's page to connect it.
- Composio events start runs through a webhook trigger: `signature: "composio"` checks Composio's delivery (its secret as the whole string, not a decoded `whsec_` key), keys each firing by `webhook-id` and takes `accept` rules by the body's `metadata.trigger_slug` (else its `type`, for Composio's account events such as `composio.connected_account.expired`), with `where` pointers into `/data`. Register the trigger's `hook_url` as Composio's webhook subscription and give Composio's secret with `POST /v2/triggers/{id}/secret` and a `{secret}` body (a composio trigger is made with none, none is made for it, and every request is refused until one is set). The console's trigger page has a Set secret button for it. It is sealed and cut like every trigger secret.
- Agent37 serves the desktop setting: `create({ kind: "desktop" })` makes a Linux desktop (`screen`, `input.pointer`, `input.keys` beside the shell) whose Xvfb the adapter starts through the daemon as the tool user. Its default image is `agentrun-box` (`AGENT37_BOX_TEMPLATE`), our box image plus Xvfb as a template of the key's own workspace: `AGENT37_API_KEY=... node packages/computer/box/build-agent37.mjs` builds it once per workspace, and again only when the recipe changes. The conformance module takes `COMPUTER_AGENT37_KIND=desktop`.
- Agent37 is a computer provider (`agent37`, kind `linux` for the sandbox setting), on the shared machine-host adapter: an Agent37 instance on type `vm` (default) or `default` (gVisor), made with no network, auto-sleep off and no public port, and read back. It takes two keys, `AGENT37_API_KEY` and `AGENT37_SSH_KEY` (the private half of an SSH key registered on the same workspace, its contents), and runs every command over SSH through the platform's tunnel with the host's own `ssh2` (pinned 1.17.0 as a root devDependency). The conformance module reads `COMPUTER_AGENT37_*` behind `AGENTRUN_COMPUTER_LIVE_AGENT37=1`, and `dist/conformance/sweep.js --provider agent37` sweeps a live run. Kind `desktop` waits for the box image as an Agent37 template.
- A desktop's or a phone's screen is watched and taken over live, as the browser's is. The runner opens its view as it claims the run's computer: `openComputerView` (computer-live.ts) starts the computer's viewer on loopback and hands it over in the store under the run's claim (`computer_viewers`, the token sealed); a stale claim is refused `fenced`, and an open that fails is refused `failed` in words with nothing left listening. Its WebSocket speaks the browser viewer's protocol: hello, ready with Take over, the screen's frames (JPEG or PNG) each sent once the viewer acked the one before (a frame held back for a slow viewer is replaced by a newer one, and the replaced frame is acked), and Take over and Hand back through the run's hold, the same take-over and hand-back the routes write. Input is mapped by one `createActionMapper` per take and reaches the computer only while the person holds it, as the run's own hold says at that moment, so input stops as soon as a take ends; otherwise it is answered `held` ("Take over to drive."), and what a desktop refuses (ctrl+alt+F1, ctrl+alt+Backspace) comes back in words. The mouse buttons a take holds are let go when the viewer loses focus, before a hand back, and once when a take ends on the run's side or the viewer goes. One viewer per computer; a viewer that goes mid-take hands the take back (`away`). The runner now journals the hold of every run's desktop or phone (computerForClaim hands it to the run's spec), so `GET /v2/runs/{id}/computer` answers live with `kind` `desktop` or `phone` and who drives, and the viewer's own page (Take over and Hand back; a phone's back, home and recents) is served under `/v2/runs/{id}/computer/live/`, its socket proxied to the runner's endpoint with the same checks as the browser's. `@parcha/pi-browser/live-view` exports its WebSocket server and token helpers for it. A desktop or phone run whose screen is not open answers `GET /v2/runs/{id}/computer` `none` with its kind, no longer `off` with "this run's agent has no computer" (#2170). The viewer types from a phone's or tablet's soft keyboard too (its `beforeinput` text, deletes and Enter), with a desktop's keys still sent once. Under `--faux`, a run on the faux desktop starts and is claimed by the runner (its start check and the runner's claim read `--faux`'s computers beside the package's), and its screen is watched and taken over through this same viewer; the faux desktop's old page under `/faux/desktops/` is gone.
- A capped run now wraps up instead of running into its cap with no answer. It keeps back enough to answer: one typical step (its own answers' typical cost) and one final answer at its least, as the cap prices the main model's next request. Once its spend, plus what its requests and paid steps still out are held at, leaves less than that, the run's tool gate refuses every tool call a model makes, in every conversation of the run and on every harness, with one fixed message: "Budget nearly spent: stop calling tools and answer now from what you have." A call that would start a child conversation (a `subagent` spawn) is refused the same way. Children already working are not cut: they get the same refusal and answer. Model requests continue, so the parent's final answer lands, and the cap stays the last line. A fan-out keeps room for each conversation to answer, because its holds count as taken. A simple run uses its cap up to its last step and answer. Its one known miss: a request that writes to its max output can still leave no room for the answer; then the run pauses for a raise rather than overspend. The figure is read from the run's booking records at each call, so a restart or a moved claim holds the same line, and a raise of the cap moves it.
  - Upgrading: this changes how a capped run ends. A run that used to end `spend_cap_reached` (or pause at its cap) after its in-flight reservations filled the cap now stops calling tools once it can afford only a step and an answer, and answers from what it has. A run with no cap is unchanged.
- A learned workflow can hold decision nodes (judge, pick, sift, a route by question, an ask predicate, a verify), under the run's spend cap. Each decision is admitted on the run's cap before it is sent, priced the way a workflow agent's decision is, and booked at what it charged. If the cap has no room, the decision is never sent: the run pauses at the cap, and the `learned_workflow` call says why. A decision node's provider (the one it names, else the default, `jev`) is checked against the run's tool settings: each provider is a settings key of its own (`jev`, `parallel`, `openrouter`), allow by default, allow or deny, and the published tool settings schema names them. Set to deny for the agent or on the server, the workflow is refused before any node runs, in the gate's words. A workflow agent's own decisions read no such setting. A decision's spend is in the run's cost (its row, its view, `/v2/usage`, and the runs list's cost while the run is going or paused), beside its model requests and paid tool calls, and a decision that reports no cost leaves the run's unknown, never the amount the cap held for it. The runner hands the run the keys of the providers its learned workflows name, so a decision node is answered by the run's decision provider under its cap. A denied provider refuses the workflow in the gate's words, and one the server has no key for refuses it as a provider this host does not have; either way nothing is sent. A decision node that sends images reads them through the run's own folder (on a run's disk in Mode 2), as a workflow agent's does. A run's new workflow draft with a decision node is checked against the server's decision providers, so it is proposed and graded like any draft, and a retired one is restored the same way.
  Upgrading: nothing to do. To keep an agent's learned workflows from asking a provider, set that provider's id (`jev`, `parallel`, `openrouter`) to deny in the agent's tool settings.
- An agent that learns can learn from rows: `POST /v2/agents/{id}/learning/batches` takes rows, the columns to give the agent and the one that holds the reference answer, and a cap on its runs (`max_cost_usd`, required: each row's run, its look-back and its review's turn are capped at what is left, strict, so no request passes it on a cache miss; the grade of what a row's run learned runs under what that run's cap leaves and counts in the batch's cost, and a grade that doesn't fit is skipped, never run past the cap), and the server runs the agent on each row in order with learning on. When a run has answered and its learning has settled, the server sends it the review the learning bench sends, `Review: the reference answer is "X"; you answered "Y".`, the same words right or wrong, so it looks back again. One batch runs at a time per agent, a row starts only when what is left of the cap covers the mean of the rows done, and the batch stops `cap` there (or `cost_unknown` when a row's cost is not known, `learning_off` when the agent stops learning: learning is checked before every row). Its progress is the server's: `GET .../learning/batches/{batch_id}` answers rows done, right or wrong per row, the path each run took, the lessons kept (notes, skills, workflow revisions) and the cost so far, after a reload or a restart (a running batch takes up at its first unfinished row, and a row is counted done only once its review's turn completed); `POST .../cancel` ends it, its row's run stopped first. Its reads show what it saved cut of the server's secrets and the agent's sign-in pointers as they are now, as the agent's learning reads are, and withhold it (403) the same way when one of the agent's sign-ins can't be read here. The Learning tab's "Learn from a CSV" uploads a CSV, takes the input and answer columns and the cap, and shows that progress.
- An agent's Learning tab heads with its latest eval record: its held-out accuracy with the 95% Wilson interval and n, and the cost a task with learning against by hand; "Not measured yet" until one is recorded. Under the cost per run, on its run axis, the execution mix shows the share of runs each path took, block by block.
  `POST /v2/agents/{id}/learning/evals` appends a record of a held-out test's counts (`name`, `label_source`, `n`, `correct`, `cost_per_task_usd`, `baseline_cost_per_task_usd`, `learned_revision`); the server computes `accuracy` and its Wilson `ci`, and refuses a body that sends either. `GET` answers the `latest` and the list, newest first, the latest 20. Only what was posted is shown: nothing is computed from the agent's own runs. `agentrun learning record-eval --body @eval.json` and `agentrun learning evals` do the same.
- A run can start with `learning: "use"` (POST /agents/{agent_id}/runs and POST /runs). It starts from what its agent learned (notes, learned skills and learned workflows, as a run that learns is given them) and keeps nothing: no end-of-run turn, no proposal, no grade and no merge, at its end or after a follow-up. Its `learning` reads `seeded` while it runs, then `dropped` with the new reason `use`. Many runs of one agent then read one learned state, frozen, however many run at once (a held-out evaluation). A server whose learning is off still gives it nothing. Any other value is a 422 at the field.

  A follow-up message to a finished run of an agent that learns now learns from the follow-up. Before, the run answered the message, but its new end reused the first end-of-run turn's answer, and the store dropped the new proposal and learning run, so a reviewer's correction never reached learning. Now each end after a follow-up is a new round. It asks the model again, with the follow-up in what the person said and a prompt saying it looked back before. It keeps its own proposal beside the earlier rounds', and its own learning run (`<run>-learning-<n>`) grades and merges it. The run's `learning` reads its newest round. A later round's proposal also keeps `follow_up_usd`: what the follow-up's own turn cost, kept apart from the job and the look-backs.

  - **Breaking for a SQLite data directory.** Upgrading: the store's SQLite schema is now version 7 (a run's learning is kept by run and round). A server or runner of this release refuses a data directory an earlier release set up, with `SchemaVersionUnknown`: start this release on a new, empty data directory, or keep the old directory with the earlier release. A Postgres store migrates itself (migration 0005).
- An agent's Learning tab replays how its learned workflow changed: the workflow it runs now is drawn as the console's workflow graph, with a step for each revision that changed it. A step shows the graph as it was then with each node marked NEW (first in that revision) or EDITED (its prompt, code, inputs or tier changed), one line saying what changed, and the revision's date and author. Play steps through them; the slider and the arrows go to any one.
  `GET /v2/agents/{id}/learning/workflows/{name}/revisions` (`learning/1`) answers the latest revisions (`?limit=`, at most 50), oldest first, each with who made it, when, why and the workflow.json text it had then; `agentrun learning workflow-revisions <agent> <name>` prints them.
- An MCP server whose sign-in lets no app register itself (GitHub's hosted MCP, whose login has no dynamic client registration) is no longer a dead end. Starting its sign-in with no Client ID is 422 on `client_id`, reason `registration_unavailable`: "<host> doesn't let apps register themselves: create an OAuth app with that provider and enter its Client ID and Secret here". GitHub is named for its hosted MCP. A preview of such a server says so up front, as `details.oauth.registration: false` on its `auth_required` refusal.

  The console's MCP server form acts on either one. It turns to Sign in with OAuth, shows the Client ID and Secret fields and puts the cursor in the Client ID, and says what to do: create an OAuth app with the provider, using this server's callback URL, then enter its Client ID and Secret. A saved server whose sign-in is refused this way offers "Enter a Client ID".
- A learned note must hold beyond the one input it came from, and a run past the learning budget reads the notes that bear on it whole. Before the grader, one Jev question per new note (the Jev model and keys decision nodes use) asks whether it states a method, a source, a fact or a preference that holds for the job's other inputs; a note rated below 0.5 (`AGENTRUN_SERVE_LEARNING_GENERAL_THRESHOLD`, 0 to 1) is dropped there, its reason on the verdict, and when Jev cannot run the grader reads every note. The grader now answers `general` for every item, and an item it says is not general is never kept. Past the budget, whole notes take the room before rule lines do, so an agent with hundreds of notes no longer gets one line per note and nothing whole; the notes the section leaves out are named in the run's log and kept on its launch (`learning.notesLeftOut`). A learning budget of 0 now serves no notes, and a run whose notes none fit its budget is told they are there (and, with the read tool, where) instead of "Nothing learned yet."; an agent without the read tool gets the room its line would take. When Jev cannot run, the run's learning says so and the grade's cost is unknown.

  Upgrading: nothing to do; set `AGENTRUN_SERVE_LEARNING_GENERAL_THRESHOLD=0` to keep every note the grader passes.
- The pi family and Chord move from 1.5.0 to 1.5.2 together (pi-ai, pi-agent-core, pi-coding-agent, pi-codemode, pi-durable, chord). Pi's model catalog now lists `claude-fable-5-2`, so a pi run can use it. Chord's package root no longer exports `Context` or `JsonValue`; they come from `@earendil-works/chord/context` and `@earendil-works/chord/json`, which a host that imports them from the root must follow.
- Applying a template that grants a GitHub tool (release-notes' `issue_write`) on a server whose GitHub MCP server runs on the GitHub App now warns from the App's real permissions, not from what its manifest asks for. Apply reads each installation's own permissions map from GitHub (`GET /app/installations/{id}`), says per tool and per account what is missing ("has Issues: read on acme"), and says nothing when the installation holds it. When the map cannot be read (no App connected, none installed, GitHub out of reach), the warning says the check could not be made (`reason: not_set_up_here`) and never states that GitHub refuses the tool. The reads run four at a time within one four-second limit, so many or slow installations never hold Apply's answer (the agent and triggers are already created; only the warning is best-effort): an account not read in time, or whose map was refused or malformed, is named in a `not_set_up_here` warning as one the server could not check, never passed as holding the permission. Before, an App whose settings showed Issues: read was told it could not write issues even where the call went through.
- Setting a tool to allow now answers a call of that tool that is waiting for its owner's approval. Before, if the setting moved to allow while a call waited (say the second of two calls in one answer), the run's next pass ran the call on the setting and never closed its ask, so its Timeline rows read "Not run: the run ended while it waited" and "Withdrawn when the run ended" for a call that ran. Now the ask closes with a row reading "Allowed by the tool's setting", the call runs, its outcome reads "ran, as its setting allows it", and the person is never asked again. A tool set to deny since is still refused, and a deny the person already sent still stands. The same holds on pi, Claude Code and Codex runs.
- A run near its cap is told to wrap up again, on the runner, for every harness (part of #2080).
  - Once what is left of the cap is about one typical request, the run's next model request tells the model, inside that request, to finish now ("This run's budget is about $X, …"). The note goes to the model only and never into the run's transcript.
  - It is worked out from everything the run has spent and holds, including requests still in flight. A Claude Code or Codex run whose requests overlap is told on time, not late or never.
  - It is told once per cap. A raised cap is told again when the run comes near the new cap.
  - It composes with the cap's wrap-up as one story: the note tells the model what is left, and once what is left no longer covers what the run keeps back to answer (one typical step and the least answer), its tools stop. The note also comes due on that same rule, so the model is told no later than its first refused call.
  - Kernel: `requestFigures(request, mode, now)` in the cap gives a main-model request's least, step-0 typical and worst cost, which the run's reserve is priced from.
  - The Timeline shows the note as AgentRun's own row ("AgentRun: This run's budget is about $X, …"), written only once a request carrying it has been admitted.
  - Kernel: `ModelPort` and the model proxy's hooks gain `noteReturned?(note)`. The proxy calls it when a request that took the host's note leaves before its admission (its client gone, a refusal, an error), so the host can give the note to the next request at once.
  - Kernel, a change for anyone reading or implementing `ModelBooking`: it gains `heldUsd(): number | null`, the holds of the session's requests still in flight. It returns null (unknown, never 0) while one of them has no hold, and a reader must treat null as unknown. `spentUsd()` still counts answered requests only, so the run's total is `spentUsd()` plus `heldUsd()`. It also gains `boundUsd(): number`, what a cache miss adds to those holds (0 with none): the run's tools stop on the holds plus this, so the note counts both.
- A runner whose claim commit the store's Postgres left unanswered no longer leaves the run stuck for the lease. The claim may have landed, so the runner reads back what it holds (`runs.claimsOf`, judged on the store's clock), retrying the read with a doubling wait, and releases at once any claim of its own that nothing holds, fenced on its epoch, so another runner (or this one, on its next poll) takes the run. A release answered Unanswered is read back the same way and sent again only if the claim is still held at its epoch.
- A Claude Code, Codex or OpenCode run whose runner was killed mid-turn no longer leaves the dead claim's files on the runner's disk. The killed claim never ran its own sweep, so its folder (`<data>/scratch/<agent>/<run>/harness/<epoch>`, the CLI's home and session state) stayed after the run ended. Now each claim of a run removes every earlier claim's folder of that run when it starts and again when it ends, and the run's scratch folder goes once its last claim ends. A later claim's folder and other runs' folders are left alone. A sweep that is itself cut off partway is finished by the run's next sweep. An agent's emptied `scratch/<agent>` folder now goes with its last run's.
  A claim that fails in its setup (its computer cannot be had, its install fails) now still sweeps the earlier claims' folders, and a runner sweeps at its start the scratch folders of runs that ended after their runner died (the run's final epoch and below, at most 500 run folders per start, said in the runner's log).
- A claude-agent or codex run's turn is visible while it runs, as a pi run's is: `GET /runs/{id}` reads `working` with a `last_progress_at` that advances as the turn writes calls and results (never `working`/`idle` with none), and the model's answer is on the timeline as soon as its request is over, not at the end of the turn. A turn that fails with a message queued behind it keeps its error in the timeline and goes on to the queued message's turn, so the run ends with that turn's status. A turn the harness ends interrupted on its own, with no stop and no error, leaves the run `input_required` (a message goes on) instead of failing it with "the run gave no answer (interrupted)". A cancel accepted before such a stop is stored still wins it: the run ends `cancelled` and takes no further message.
- On Postgres, a command written while another command of the same run was still being written could be skipped by the runner holding the run: the two rows could commit out of id order, and the runner, which reads the rows past the last id it handed on, never saw the lower one (not at the next command poll either, so it waited for the run's next claim). Every write of a run's command row (a command, a trigger's message, a reopen) now takes a per-run lock first, so a run's rows commit in id order, as they do on SQLite.
- Settings → MCP servers in the console offers GitHub App as a credential, beside None, Bearer token, Headers and OAuth. Choosing it fills GitHub's hosted MCP address (the only one a GitHub App server may have), takes optional static headers, and saves `auth: {type: "github_app"}`; a server saved that way, through the API or the console, shows as GitHub App and is changed as one instead of falling back to None. A preview or save with no GitHub App connected says so in words and points to Settings → GitHub.
  A template's Apply screen now says, before Apply, when an MCP server the template names is not set up here: a required one says Apply is refused until it is, an optional one says the agent is made without its tools, and each links to the add form with the server's name filled (the `github` server opens with GitHub App chosen), at `#/settings/mcp?add=<name>`. Applying the code review template no longer leaves an agent without its GitHub tools unseen.
- The console reads on a phone held sideways and in half a page. On a short screen (a phone at 844x390 or 932x430) the desktop sidebar gives way to the top bar and its menu, as in portrait, and a run's page scrolls as a whole, so a run waiting on a question shows the question, the Report and the Timeline in full instead of a body 0 px tall. Where a run's header is narrow (the Playground's Response panel at about 1500 px), the title keeps at least 16rem and its actions (Raise the cap, Stop, Cancel run, Archive) wrap onto their own row instead of squeezing it to a letter; the title shows two lines at most and its full text on hover.
- A call refused before it ran no longer reads as an error. Its `tool_result` row on `GET /v2/runs/{id}/timeline` now carries `refused: true` (an additive field: absent on every other row, `tool_status` stays `failed`). That covers a tool set to deny, a pin, a person's deny, or a call held for an approval the run stopped or ended without, on pi and on Codex and Claude Code, whose refused calls now read "Refused: …" as pi's do. The console shows it with a neutral Refused chip, never the red Error chip.
  Also in the console:
  - status badges keep their words on one line at their own width, so a narrow window no longer cuts "Input required";
  - web_search's `auto` help names Parallel: the harness's or the model provider's own search, else Parallel where the server holds its key, else keyless Exa.
- Three small wording and rendering fixes. An opened Answer row on a run's Timeline renders its Markdown as the Report does (links clickable, code fences as code blocks, no raw HTML) in place of raw fences and `[text](url)`; the New agent Computer step says "This computer adds these tools: ..." in plain text in place of an uppercase "THE LOOP GETS"; market-monitor's `lookback_days` help says what the number does (how many days back a run looks, kept equal to the gap between runs) instead of "when you change cron".
- A runner's close, or a lost claim, while a resumed pi run opens its session no longer ends the runner process on an unhandled rejection. pi-durable answers a wait registered after its signal aborted with a promise it rejects at once and hands back only after the commits before it are published, so on Postgres that rejection could go unhandled: the standalone runner exited 1 on it with its claims left to lapse, and a runner beside the server took the server down. Every wait on a pi-durable submission or task (the pi turn, a steer's turn, a subagent, a workflow node and task, a host tool's waitForTask) now runs on a signal of its own that never aborts and is cut by the caller's signal here, so the turn ends interrupted as before. A waiter pi-durable made and never handed back because its Session failed (a commit's storage error) no longer rejects unhandled either.
- A run's answer is its last turn's own: a follow-up whose stop shows no text (a thinking-only or contentless stop, a `/compact`) now reads `result.final_answer: null` instead of the previous turn's answer. A cancel reads `cancelled` from the `202` on: `GET /runs/{id}` reports the run as cancelled as soon as its cancel is written, before the runner has cut the turn, never `working` or `completed` in between. The run stays unsettled (`ended_at` null, `poll_after_ms` 1000, its timeline not final) until the runner's end is stored, and a normal end that commits with an accepted cancel still waiting is the cancel's: the run ends `cancelled`, never `completed`.
- A web search on a GPT-6 model (gpt-6-luna, gpt-6.1-sol, gpt-6.1-terra) is booked at OpenAI's $0.01 a call, as on GPT-5. Before, its search had no known price. A pi run's native web_search on a GPT-6 model under any spend cap was refused before it was sent ("the size of the next model request's input is unknown, so the run's cap cannot be kept"). A Codex run with `webSearch: "live"`, or an uncapped pi run, booked an unknown cost for any response that searched.
- A run's grade of what it learned runs under what the run's cap leaves, so a capped run never goes past its cap by its grade.
  - When a capped run that learns ends, its learning run gets its own cap: the run's cap now (a raise counts), less what the run spent (its job, its follow-ups, every look-back) and what each earlier round's grade spent. An uncapped run's grade is capped by nothing, as before.
  - Each grader call is checked against that cap before it is sent, at its worst case: its whole input uncached and its whole output bound. It is never cut down to fit, so a verdict is never lost to a short answer.
  - A grade that doesn't fit is not sent. The run's learning ends `dropped` with reason `no_budget` and the words "Not graded: no room under the cap." (or "Not graded: the grade's cost can't be kept under the cap." when its spend or the grade model's price is unknown), which the run page shows. It is a skip, not a failure, and spends nothing.
  - The generality check's Jev requests count as the grade's spend under the same cap. Before they are sent, their worst case is checked against what the cap leaves; a check that doesn't fit is skipped, and the run's learning says "The generality check had no room under the cap, so the grader read every note." Each grader call's room leaves out what the check spent, and the grade's cost is the check's dollars plus the grader's.
- A message sent to a run right after `POST /v2/agents/{id}/runs` answered (`POST /v2/runs/{id}/messages` before the runner had sent the run's input) now lands after the run's own input. Before, on a pi run the runner placed the message as the session's first prompt and sent the input after it: the Timeline showed the message first and the model answered the two in that order. The runner now holds such a message until the run's input is sent, then places it into that turn as any later message. Claude Code and Codex runs already ran it after the input's turn; a test now holds all three to it.
- A pi run whose request was stopped or cancelled mid-answer now reads its cost as unknown with what is known so far, never $0: the request is marked when it is sent and its end is marked when it did not answer at a price. A workflow that parks at its spend cap names the node it parks at, also for a map's items. A map whose items are held at the cap at once parks only after every item's held end is committed, so the raise resumes them instead of failing on an effect left unknown, and a polled call held for a raise has its poll window moved back by the time it was held.
- A web_search setting of deny or ask now applies to a Claude Code or Codex run's own web search at its next search, including a run that started while it was allow. Before, the setting was read only when the run started, so a run that started with native search kept searching after the setting changed.
  - Claude Code: each WebSearch asks the run's gate before it runs, as a host tool's call does. A deny refuses it in the gate's words. An ask parks the run on the person with nothing searched; once they allow it, the model's next search with the same query runs once, with no second card.
  - Codex: its search runs inside the provider's model request, so its proxy reads web_search's setting before each request and offers the provider its search only while the setting is allow. A failed read offers no search.
  - `SessionIO.permission(tool)` (agentrun-kernel) is the host's setting for a harness's own tool at the time of the read. The runner reads it from the store each time. `ProviderPolicy.apply` may return a promise.
  - A runner run whose plane resolves web_search to native now gets the harness's own search (#2458). The runner had built the run's environment without its plane, so Claude Code and Codex runs on a runner never had it on.
- A run's context reset and its summarized older context show on the Timeline with no held key in their text: the new context and the summary are words from the run, redacted by the host before the row is cut, as every other row a run's words reach.
- A web_search that resolves to the model provider's own search works again on the runner for pi (#2458). It used to answer "web_search has no model to search on" every time:
  - A pi run's own web_search on an Anthropic or OpenAI model. That is what `auto` picks for pi, and `native` too. Each search now goes through the run's model proxy with the provider's search tool, and its searches are booked at the provider's price on top of its tokens.
  - A learned workflow's call node whose web_search resolves native, on any harness.

  Each run's search uses that run's own model route, never one shared by the whole process. Hand-written workflow agents were not affected: their web_search never resolves native. Both harness packages now export their `withWebSearches` price wrapper, and the Codex one its `webSearchUsd`. A claude-agent or codex run's own search is not switched on by this change.

  A capped run holds a hosted search's fees with its tokens before the request is sent, at the most searches the request allows, so the fees can't pass the cap. The kernel's model proxy takes a policy's `feeMaxUsd(body)` and holds it as the request's `feeUsd`; a fee it can't bound leaves the request unmeasured. The proxy also hands `usageOf` the sent body as a second argument, so a pi request on OpenAI's Responses that offered no search reads 0 searches from its body, even when its answer names a search call.
- A gateway model written with its version's separators flipped (`gpt-5-4`) is priced when the catalog's entries differ only in a long-context `tiers` table: they are compared on their base price, and the entry that carries `tiers` prices it. Different base prices, or different tiers tables, still leave it unpriced.
- The server's log prints `event=run_started` (run, agent, kind) when a run is first claimed and `event=run_ended` (run, agent, status, cost_usd) when it ends, again after the run engine's removal dropped them. Each run has one of each, a reclaim after a lost runner prints no second start, and `AGENTRUN_LOG=quiet` keeps them. The runner beside the server writes them to the same stdout; a separate `agentrun-serve runner` process writes them to its own.
- A run started by hand (the console's Send request, `POST /agents/{id}/runs`) now reaches a GitHub repository. Before, only a run a GitHub trigger started, or one whose first message held a `https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>` URL, had one, so every github MCP call of any other run failed with "this run names no GitHub repository". The start body takes an optional `repo` (`owner/name`), which must be one the agent is bound to (a repository its GitHub triggers' `accept` names on `/repository/full_name`): another is 422 in words naming the repositories the agent is bound to, and a run's reach never grows past its agent's triggers. Left out, an agent bound to exactly one repository takes it, unless the first message names a repository itself. The console's start form has a `repo` field. The refusal a run with no repository gets now says to start it with a repository or bind the agent to one, and no longer reads as a connection problem.
- A capped run on the runner is priced the way the cap's `expected` mode says: each model request from the previous request of its session. The cache that request read or wrote counts at the cache-read price, and only its other input plus what the body grew by since counts at full price. Before, the runner gave the cap no previous request, so every step was held as a whole cache miss, and a run needed a cap several times what it spent (a 5-step Sonnet run that spends $0.04 needed $0.11). `strict` mode is unchanged: every token uncached. A side call (a title, a summary) is priced as a cache miss, as a host's own request already was.
- A pi run's cost counts every request it made. A learned workflow's model node, or a request on another model than the run's, is booked beside pi's own answers as a side call, and the run's view, its Timeline usage row and its stored cost now add it, where they read pi's answers alone (three requests booked at $0.000014 each read $0.000028). A request a lost runner left unanswered is booked cut once, however many of the next claim's bookings read it open: its hold and bound count once toward the cap, and its cost is unknown once, where a second booking could count it twice. A pi run's stored cost is now its booking's, as a CLI run's is: a run cancelled or stopped while its model's answer streamed reads its cost unknown (the cut request may be billed for what it streamed), never the $0 its cut answer carried.
- The console's Screen tab no longer says "Waiting for the browser" for a run that never opened one. `GET /v2/runs/{run_id}/computer`'s `none` answer now carries `session`, read from the run's journal: `unopened` (no browser step so far, so a run that only used `web_fetch` while it waits for its person), `opening` (a browser step that opens one has no result yet; a desktop or a phone from the run's start until its screen is up) or `closed` (the run opened one, which is not up now). The tab waits only while it is `opening`; it says "This run hasn't opened its browser. The agent's page shows here if it opens one." for `unopened`, that the browser isn't open now for `closed`, and "This run didn't open its browser." on an ended run that never did. A desktop or a phone is said in its own words.
- With accounts off, the API token can't write secrets. The console's cookie on a server with no accounts was a MAC of the token, and the printed link carried the token, so anyone holding the token (a run's process, an MCP client, a script) could compute that cookie or fetch it from the link, and save, replace or remove a secret as the console does. Now each start makes a launch code at random and prints the console's link with it (`Open <url>/?launch=<code>`, never the token); opening it gives the browser a console session, an id made at random and kept by the server, and only that session (on a loopback-bound server) writes secrets. A `?token=` link signs no browser in, and a cookie computed from the token is no session. The session lasts until the browser closes or the server stops; the next start prints its own link. A wrong launch code is logged as `auth_failed reason=wrong_launch_code`.
- `agentrun-serve import` titles a Claude Code run the way Claude Code shows it: the person's `/rename` (`custom-title`), else its own `ai-title`, else (in older files) the `summary` of this session's last message. A session with none is titled by the person's first words, never by a slash command's `<command-name>` markup, its `<local-command-stdout>` output or the "Caveat:" preamble before it. A session with no words of the person's at all (only `/resume` and `/model`, or a Codex or pi session kept by `--all`) is titled "Session in <folder>" in place of the markup, "codex session" or an empty title; when a held key touches the folder's name (one across the folder and its parent included), it keeps the generic "<source> session" and names no folder. An imported run with no answer no longer keeps a slash command's markup as its summary.
- A server started on a store an earlier release set up is still refused, but the refusal now says what to do: start on a new, empty data folder (`--data <new folder>`, with the Docker image's flags; on Render the Docker Command must be the whole start command, as it replaces the entrypoint too), add agents, MCP servers, keys and sign-ins again, and keep the old folder to stay on the earlier release; a store a later release set up says to run that release or later.
- A Timeline row for the agent's words that open with a fenced code block (a JSON answer written as ```json … ```) previews the code itself, on one line, up to the summary's 500 characters. Before, its summary was the fence's first line, so the console's Answer row read only "json…". The row's text, and the run's answer, keep the words whole, fence included.
- Setting a tool to allow now ends a run's wait on that tool at once. A run waiting for its owner's approval of a call went on only when someone answered it (or sent the run another message), even when the tool's setting had moved to allow since. Now `PUT /v2/settings/tools` wakes every run waiting on a call whose tool reads allow for that run, with its agent's own tool settings over the server's: the call runs, and its approval row reads "Allowed by the tool's setting". A run whose agent still sets the tool to ask, or whose tool still reads ask or deny, keeps waiting for its person. The same holds on pi, Claude Code and Codex runs.
- `web_fetch`'s text (a page read directly, `readPage`) leaves out what the page hides from everyone who reads it: an element with the `hidden` attribute, an inline `display:none` or `visibility:hidden`, a closed `<dialog>`, a class the page's own `<style>` sets to `display:none` or `visibility:hidden`, and the common pop-up and display-none utility classes (`mfp-hide`, `modal`, `d-none`, `hidden`, `hide`, `invisible`, `is-hidden`, `u-hidden`). A record page's help pop-ups, hidden until a click, were read as the record, so an agent took their boilerplate ("notice of intent to dissolve") for the company's own. Text only a screen reader reads (`sr-only`, `visually-hidden`, `wb-inv`, `screen-reader-text`) and text marked `aria-hidden` stay in the text: each is shown to someone. Only the page's live style elements count (none in a comment, a script, a template or a noscript, and only those for the screen); a later declaration or rule that shows the element wins (inline over a class, an author `display` over the `hidden` attribute), and where the outcome is unclear (an `!important` mix, classes in conflict, a class a compound selector shows) the text is kept.
